Given Healey’s message of ‘continuity’ around the UK’s overall fiscal stance and with likely more restrained and limited increases in taxation and spending, we are less con- cerned that the Budget will result in a significant increase in market pricing of UK fiscal risk premia. records.text: 4 The Global Thinker | 10 September 2026 At the same time, a series of adverse supply shocks pushed real interest rates below their equilibrium levels and generated substantial excess liquidity. Combined with persistently expansionary fiscal policies, these conditions fueled a massive rally in asset prices, with associated wealth effects feeding back into the real economy. A broken record…with a new track Over the past several years, we have extensively discussed the limits of fiscal policy and their implications for interest rates in the United States, the United Kingdom, the Euro Area, and Japan (see the report The Global Thinker: The case for no Fed cuts and The Global Thinker: Around the world in 5 questions). The underlying issue is therefore not new. What differed in the post-crisis period was the macroeconomic environment. Limited investment opportunities, abundant global savings, and ongoing central-bank purchases allowed markets to absorb growing fiscal deficits while keeping borrowing costs at historically low levels. What has fundamentally altered the global savings-investment balance over the last 18 months is the AI-driven investment boom, centered largely in the United States. Persistent fiscal deficits remain important in explaining the level of interest rates across advanced economies. However, they are less useful in explaining the recent acceleration in rates. In fact, for August, the basis between the overall IG index (including 144As) and the index excluding the AI ecosystem was unchanged (Figure 4). In HY, spread duration, carry, and quality outperformed. The outperformance of spread duration and carry was consistent with what has historically occurred in tight and range-bound environments. In contrast, the outperformance of quality continued to buck the historical trend, as CCCs remain a significant laggard amid persistent idiosyncratic concerns. In the near term, we expect investment grade and high yield valuations to remain well supported amid strong corporate fundamentals, moderate economic growth, and robust yield- driven demand. However, with spreads still at historically tight levels, we remain of the view that the potential for further tightening remains limited and expect spreads to remain range- bound. Downside risks to our view include a broadening of AI-related concerns to the rest of the market, a resurgence in inflation as the Iran conflict continues, and financial tightening driven by higher long-end rates. 11 September 2026 6 Barclays | US Credit Alpha: Credit hasn't blinked

These readings put core CPI inflation at 2.45% y/y and headline CPI inflation at 3.35% y/y (SA). Using today's CPI data, we revised our August core PCE inflation forecast up to 0.25% m/m from 0.24% prior to the release. On a 3-, 6-, and 12-month annualized basis, core PCE is now tracking at 2.74%, 3.19%, and 3.26%, respectively. The upward revision reflects somewhat firmer core goods inflation than we anticipated following yesterday's PPI release. Our forecast incorporates our best estimate of the methodology changes that will be introduced with the September 30 PCE release. For comparison purposes, we also report the PCE estimates that would have prevailed absent the annual revisions. On that basis, our core PCE tracker stands at 0.23% m/m, consistent with 3-, 6-, and 12-month annualized rates of 2.50%, 3.11%, and 3.34%, respectively. Although today's CPI report had little effect on our core PCE translation, the upside surprise in core CPI inflation reduces the likelihood of our call that the Fed will remain on hold through year-end. The 3- and 6-month annualized measures of core PCE still show enough progress that some FOMC participants may be inclined to hold rates in September. The slope in the linear portion of the fly has also flattened considerably (Fig. 3). As such, we would enter next year’s political risk events with reinforced caution. Low risk premia makes the EGB market susceptible to important repricings, should fiscal and political concerns start to dominate more the price action. Not to say that nothing is currently discounted in spreads. In fact we do believe that idiosyncratic risk is currently embedded in OAT spreads considering the isolated widening of the spread despite unchanged credit fly parameters. However, should the market start to price the risk of a downgrade into the BBB bucket, according to our analysis, a plausible range for the 10y OAT-Bund spread could become 77-150bp, all else equal, and will depend on the broader market risk sentiment (Fig. 4). The range widens as we transition from the linear portion of the fly (akin to the AAA/AA slope), to the convex one (proxied by the AA/A/BBB fly). The 10-year inflation swap (1.91%, 4 September) is 5bp below the cash BEI, the reverse of the textbook liquidity discount, which points to tight supply of the cash bonds under BoJ holdings, issuance cuts and buybacks. One caveat is essential: the yen inflation swap market is extremely illiquid, quotes are updated sporadically, and in Japan the swap is not much of a reference for BEI, so fair value cannot be argued from swap-cash arbitrage as it can overseas. We use the swap only as an auxiliary input to close the IRP identity; the judgement rests on the cash BEI curve and the survey. Three yardsticks give three answers for the 10-year BEI. The DCF fair value on our CPI path (long-run inflation 1.91%, seasonally adjusted) is 1.79%, so the market is 17bp rich. What the regression learned is the post-2021 relationship that BEI follows the yen and equities; a shift in pricing behavior is not among its drivers. records.text: Unusually large primary deficits, the rise in the debt-to-GDP ratio to nearly its n post-WW2 peak, and the rebound in interest rates from much lower rates last cycle have driven concern about the fiscal trajectory for a while. The sharp rise in interest rates this year amid continued high inflation and strong demand for capital from the AI boom has heightened those concerns. We update our projections of the fiscal path using our forecasts for federal n deficits, GDP growth, and interest rates. We project that the debt-to-GDP ratio will rise from 100% to 123% by 2035. We consider three perspectives on the burden the debt imposes. Nominal n interest expense as a share of GDP has reached its 1990s peak and is set to surpass it substantially in coming years. Real interest expense—the cost of stabilizing the real value of the debt—remains low but is on track to approach its 1990s highs. A third measure is the interest expense that must be paid to stabilize debt-to-GDP . That perspective has been less concerning in recent years, when the average interest rate on debt outstanding has been below nominal GDP growth (r<g). That would remain true in our forecast but would not if current interest rates held indefinitely. There are two reasons to worry about fiscal sustainability even when interest n rates are below nominal GDP growth. However, over shorter timescales this relationship is imperfect; the residual behaviour in price can largely be explained by forward-looking expectations reflecting in net long fund positioning. The copper market’s global “call-on-scrap” (end-use consumption net of mine supply) adjusted for the cost of scrap recovery (proxied by real diesel pricing) can explain most of real price action over the last 20 years The residual can mostly be explained by forward-looking expectations around copper’s market balance (as expressed by the scale and direction of investor net long copper positioning) Prepared for Cayla Buettner

records.text: is experience led many economists and policymakers to conclude that substantially higher debt levels were sustainable and, in some cases, desirable. The argument was often framed within the secular stagnation paradigm, in which insufficient aggregate spending justified a more active role for fiscal policy. The intellectual foundation for this view rested on the debt-sustainability condition commonly summarized as (r - g). As long as the real interest rate (r) remained below the economy's growth rate (g), debt dynamics appeared manageable and governments could maintain higher debt burdens without triggering explosive debt trajectories. The problem with this argument is that if debt is being issue to finance permanent increases in spending, such as entitlements, then it is politically very costly to reverse policy to put the fiscal house in order. A classic time inconsistency problem. Central banks sometimes help too much Central banks became an essential part of this equilibrium. Through successive rounds of quantitative easing and other unconventional policies, they absorbed large quantities of public and private debt that financial markets may not have been willing to finance at prevailing yields. By warehousing duration risk on their balance sheets, central banks compressed term premia, lowered borrowing costs, and eased financing conditions across the economy. Should birth rates instead stagnate, the shrinking working-age population would push pension costs toward 21.4% of GDP by 2070 – well above the Commission’s 16.7% estimate for the same year (Figure 1). Reading that against the EC debt sustainability framework, it would mean persistently worse primary balances, reaching almost a 5pp hit to GDP by 2070, pushing the debt ratio 120pp higher by then, as the economy shrinks faster with a lower population. On the other hand, the EC is failing to fully account for the recent migration flows that have boosted Spain’s working-age population, which could partially make up for the hypothetical lower-than- expected number of births. Should net migration stagnate at current levels, we estimate the pension burden would sit at 17.5% by 2070, even still assuming a smaller fertility rate than the Commission. While still worse than the EC’s 2070 baseline, these greater migration flows could shrink the impact from a smaller natural population growth on the primary balance to a fifth. More importantly, they could even deliver better primary balances along the way, which would compound and lead to a debt level around a quarter lower than the one expected by the official estimates for 2070. Spain’s long-term fiscal stability is thus closely tied to demographics, akin to its recent economic performance. That said, it is worth remembering that alternative policy tools remain available to the administration, including 45X tax credits and other measures designed to incentivise domestic production. Our preferred copper-exposed names, combining attractive valuations and clear catalysts, are GLEN, Anglo, FM, and FCX. Mine supply weakness persists As well as potential US tariffs, a key fundamental driver behind the price strength over the past year has been the persistent weakness in global copper mine supply, reflecting years of underinvestment and disruptions at several major mines in recent years. The latest company updates and high frequency data show that mine supply could decline this year for the first time since 2017 following anaemic growth (less than 1%) last year: n Chile reported monthly production data for July yesterday. Production from the world's largest copper producing nation fell 9% YoY in July (Fig 9-10), marking a further deterioration from the 7% decline recorded in H1. As rate hikes were rapidly priced in, currencies with better starting points in terms of output gaps, policy restrictiveness and energy exposure (USD, AUD & NOK) outperformed. This was particularly evident against the EUR, even though the ECB was among the first central banks to hike. On a y/y basis, we estimate trimmed mean PCE inflation at 2.17%, compared with 3.26% for core PCE. Recent research from the Dallas Fed argues that trimmed mean PCE is a reliable measure of underlying inflation trends but primarily when the skewness of monthly price changes is negative. As shown in Exhibit 8 , skewness moved back into negative territory in June and July, supporting a more favorable interpretation of the trimmed mean signal during those months. records.text: M Idea 2 Select Committee earlier this week. We find it difficult to see any meaningful inflection in pay growth and forward-looking pay surveys at this level of labour market slack, absent regulatory decisions (i.e. NLW hike above 5% or similar). Should the BoE hike rates in the coming year, we don't think it would be due to pay pressures emerging as a more material operational cost for UK businesses. There are, however, indirect inflationary effects stemming from the energy shock that can be facilitated and amplified by more robust demand, should the savings rate fall further. In addition, should inflation rise beyond 4%Y with the economy growing at ~0.2%Q, we suspect Chief Economist Pill's argument - risk management hikes to recalibrate inflation expectations - might become difficult for the core of the committee to push back against. Our base case is still for the BoE to hold through year-end and cut once next year should commodity price pressures subside before the end of the year. Should that not be the case, and should broader global growth tailwinds continue to counter already exceptionally tight financial conditions, keeping the economy supported, we would expect 2 hikes at forecast meetings, perhaps in 1H27. Two hikes have been our risk scenario since May this year (see here). We will preview the next week's BoE meeting by the end of this week. For our thoughts on the QT decision, see here.

records.text: 1 We define the duration factor as an outright exposure, where a long spread-duration basket is traded against a short spread-duration basket. As duration amplifies credit spread movements, this definition introduces directionality to credit market excess returns (ie, the isolated spread return component). Some investors may instead prefer a spread duration-neutral definition, in which a long-duration basket is traded against a short-duration basket on a duration- neutral basis. Such an approach would make duration and market factor returns significantly less correlated. IG Quality: Negative Being Negative Quality earns a positive expected return in our base case. Although there is a meaningful negative expected return in our adverse scenario, given the constellation of other factor choices and their performance expectations, we are Negative on Quality. IG Spread Duration1 : Negative The Duration factor screens very rich ( Figure 12), and as we discuss here, considering the relative break-evens of curve trades versus down-in-rating trades, we do not favour going out further than around the 5y point. The government has already announced additional spending cuts worth EUR 3bn (in addition to the EUR 6bn already announced in March) and plans EUR 2bn in savings on social security to keep expenditure on track. However, extra costs due to the heat wave and lower growth raised risks of fiscal slippage in H2. The risk of a higher-than-expected budget deficit this year and lower growth complicates the equation for building the 2027 budget. We now see the budget deficit coming back down to 5.0% of GDP (vs 4.5% in our previous forecast when the 5% 2026 target was still on track), which would still require significant budget adjustments. According to government estimates, given the adverse impact of higher interest rate payments and structural trends in social spending, not passing the budget and thus no fiscal consolidation would imply a risk of a budget deficit widening from 2026 balance by around 0.5% of GDP next year and thus closer to 6% of GDP in our view, and even 7% by 2030. The Prime Minister has indicated that next year's budget will keep taxation stable, which implies, in our view, that the surtax on big corporations will be rolled over for the third year in a row. Tighter spending at the central state level will be needed, according to recent government papers, but addressing social security may also be required but where parliament majority is hard to get. But, for now, the build-up of slack in the UK economy looks to be slowing, which means policymakers are more likely to get more worried about these external price pressures eventually driving a pick-up in underlying (domestic) inflation. This need not come through wage growth cost push - considering the slack in the UK labour market we are fairly confident wage growth in the UK will continue to hover around 3% over 2026 and 2027, absent any inflationary regulatory decisions (i.e. NLW hike of 5% or more). And while the pace of slackening in the UK does look to be slowing, we think the output gap does remain between 0.5% to 1.0% of GDP. But with more robust demand, and commodity prices at these levels, there are clear and very strong risks that the BoE acts to lean against external price pressures. We still think the plausible cumulative tightening the BoE would deliver should commodity prices remain at today's levels is 50bp, at forecast meetings, and from November at the earliest. A sharp decline in fuel prices, with petrol prices falling by almost 7% in July, more than offset upward pressure from other categories. The disinflationary impact of lower fuel prices outweighed the effect of the near 9% increase in electricity tariffs implemented in July. August CPI data will be published on 23 September, a few hours ahead of the SARB decision. We expect headline CPI to remain unchanged at 4.3% in August before edging up to 4.5% in September. Thereafter, we forecast inflation to stabilise at around 4.7% through the remainder of 2026. Under our baseline, headline CPI reaches 4.8% in March 2027 before resuming a gradual downward trajectory. Structurally, inflation remains driven more by services, at over 5% year on year, than by goods inflation, at close to 4%. Recent inflation dynamics have been dominated by movements in fuel prices, administered costs such as electricity and water tariffs, and periodic rental adjustments. By contrast, food inflation has remained relatively subdued, supported by a favourable 2025/26 agricultural season and improved domestic food supply conditions. Core inflation also appears to have peaked at around 4.2% and should remain broadly stable through the remainder of 2026, with little change expected before 1Q27. Bond allocations have risen from a low of 11.6% in March to 12.2% now, although they remain below the peaks reached in 2023. • Collateral scarcity remains an important driver. records.text: M Idea 8 Rates Strategy: Terminal Rate Too High, Balanced Risks at the September MPC Fabio Bassanin The Monetary Policy Decision Our economist expects a 6:3 vote split for a hold, with the minutes likely to continue to stress that risks to inflation remain skewed to the upside amid elevated energy prices, and that the risk of second-round effects could increase, the longer those pressures persist. That said, we also expect the MPC to continue to highlight the significant tightening already repriced into financial conditions, as well as the degree of slack in the UK economy, which should help limit the risk of more persistent second-round effects. How strongly the balance between these two considerations has shifted, if at all, will be our key focus in next week’s minutes and is likely to be the key driver of the market reaction. Beyond that, the individual paragraphs will also be important. Any indication that the decision to hold was “finely balanced” for a core MPC member — i.e. the Governor or Deputy Governors — could also be interpreted hawkishly. Any explicit indication that a November hike is becoming the base case for the core of the Committee could also drive a hawkish repricing, although this may be more about a redistribution of tightening across the strip, with additional tightening brought forward into early 2027, given that the market already fully discounts a 25bp hike in November and around two cumulative hikes by end-2026 (see Exhibit 9 ). records.text: 2 Global Emerging Markets Weekly | 10 September 2026 The View David Hauner, CFA >> MLI (UK) david.hauner@bofa.com Not to get carried away EMFX carry remains popular, but JPY induced volatility is increasingly being raised as a risk. We worry less about this factor but more about the potential implications of the midterms on energy prices and equities. Stay long FX carry but add hedges against risk- off through asymmetric credit spreads. Stay cautious EM rates given high energy prices. JPY unwind: not so worried EM carry is very popular, including among Japanese investors: TRY is particularly big with a position amounting to several billion USD, followed by MXN and ZAR (Exhibit 1). But we aren’t too concerned about JPY outflows from EM as long as the USD remains weak. An EMFX carry basket funded in JPY was hugely profitable in 2025 and would still be in the money for 2026 even accounting for our end-year USD/JPY target (Exhibit 2). A bigger concern could be outflows from EM local bonds as global sovereign bonds in JPY terms have had major losses (Exhibit 2). Eg, a simulation by our Japan strategists shows that a 5% reallocation of pension funds away from global bonds could affect Poland, Mexico and Korea most meaningfully (Exhibit 3). On the investment side, our updated framework suggests the contribution is already material. In our recent note, Building a better mousetrap: AI spending and its contribution to US GDP growth, we refined our estimate of AI investment's contribution to GDP. In our new estimates, we broadened the set of investment categories included, improved the treatment of imports, and distinguished between AI-related spending and spending that is incremental to the AI boom. Translating AI spending into growth is difficult since capex does not translate one-for-one into US GDP. GDP captures domestically produced final output, whereas corporate capex can include imported and intermediate goods. In the case of AI investment, spending on imported equipment used in data center construction is included in corporate capex plans but does not contribute to US GDP. Using our broad measure, AI-related investment has contributed about 0.6pp on average to annualized real GDP growth since 2025; the narrower incremental measure, which we call “AI-only” spending, puts the contribution closer to 0.4pp. Our new treatment of imports raises our estimate of the growth impulse versus our prior calculations, as we adjust for re-exports and also estimate the share of computer imports being used for person

records.text: US Rates Weekly 11 September 2026 Citi Research 10 Beyond September, we could see a marginal increase in SOFR/IORB, particularly towards the end of the month, as we expect ~$240bn of net T-bill supply. Further, the October month-end move in TGA could also push SOFR fixes temporarily higher. We’re penciling in a TGA balance of $1.04tn by 10/28, in line with Treasury’s refunding guidance. This increase in TGA and temporary drain in reserves could pressure SOFR to fix around 5bp above IORB on the day. In Figure 19 we show two potential paths for SOFR/IORB. The dotted orange line corresponds to the estimate using the recent sensitivity of SOFR/IORB to liquidity needs, while the brown line shows the estimate using last year’s sensitivity. In practice, we think SOFR is likely to fix somewhere between these two estimates. Quick note on buybacks and RMPs Yesterday, Treasury conducted their first upsized buyback operation and bought $5.19bn out of the $6bn maximum amount announced. While the updated buyback schedule guides for a “= or > $4 billion” maximum for the rest of the quarter, we think Treasury is likely to keep maximum sizes at $6bn going forward. We continue to think these will be funded via T-bill issuance as we don’t expect Treasury to alter their TGA target. As for their effect on T-bill supply, as we discussed in US Rates Weekly - Can Secretary Bessent and Chair Warsh save the curve?, even with the $6bn size we see the impact on T-bill supply as relatively small. As we have argued in our recent labour market notes over this past year, and as the BoE, we think, deduced in July - pay growth in the UK looks to be largely target-consistent. While AWE remains an important data point, the focus now turns to the survey evidence on pay settlements in the year-ahead. The initial - albeit scant - information we have suggests target-consistent pay rewards. Into year-end, more information should start to trickle in. First, on Friday, we think the Agents' Survey ought to have a preliminary range, which we see at between 2%Y and 4%Y. We also note that traditionally, the Low Pay Commission tends to provide an update on their National Living Wage tracking in either August or September. We are not sure if such an update will come this year, where the final recommendation has to be provided to the government before the end of October. NLW for April 2027, in other words, could only be announced at the Budget. We stress that we see little reason why the recommended NLW hike, as things stand, would be higher than ~4.25%. This is in line, we think, with corporate expectations, and would solidify pay settlement surveys for the year ahead at 3%Y-3.5%Y. This, of course, is target-consistent and ought to allow the BoE to model inflation returning to target as the energy shock dissipates. records.text: upee problem. Asia: Back to School outlook The macro picture in Asia has largely remained similar to that in June when we published our mid-year outlook. Amid elevated geopolitical uncertainty, robust global demand for tech goods continues to offer support to resilient regional growth. Thanks to strong 2Q26 performance in some economies, we upgrade Asia growth forecast to 4.8% in 2026 (from 4.7% previously). Vietnam: Unlocking Vietnam’s capital markets Despite Vietnam’s compelling growth story, global portfolio investors have often found it challenging to gain meaningful access to its capital markets. In July 2026, the government unveiled a comprehensive long-term blueprint that signals a stronger commitment to deepening capital markets and improving investor access. The impact could be even greater if accompanied by a faster pace of capital account liberalization, in our view. Week ahead In the coming week, we turn out focus to monetary policy meeting in Japan and Taiwan, as well as Aug activity data in China. In Japan, we expect the BoJ to raise the policy rate by 25bp to 1.25%. Our base case is a unanimous vote, with the policy statement likely retaining the July language acknowledging the risks of underlying inflation overshooting the 2% target. In Taiwan, we expect the CBC to raise its policy rate by 12.5bp, an out of consensus call, against the backdrop of above-trend growth and above-target inflation. In China, we expect industrial production growth to edge up to 4.7%

By offering a $20 billion swap line to Argentina, the US Treasury became the ultimate backstop in case of a run against the currency, effectively changing the expectations of investors. Instead, the surge in AI-related investment has materially increased demand for capital. At the same time, rising asset prices have supported consumption through wealth effects, reducing effective saving. The combination of stronger investment and lower saving has placed additional upward pressure on equilibrium real interest rates (see Exhibit 3). AI is the canary in the coalmine Importantly, AI-related investment should not be viewed as the root cause of higher rates. Rather, it has exposed pre-existing vulnerabilities associated with persistent fiscal imbalances across advanced economies. In this sense, the AI boom has acted as a catalyst that revealed constraints that had previously been masked by an environment of excess savings and abundant liquidity. This adjustment has been reinforced by the gradual reversal of quantitative easing across many advanced economies. As central banks reduce the size of their balance sheets, private investors are required to absorb a larger share of sovereign debt issuance. The return of market-based price discovery, particularly at the long end of yield curves, has therefore amplified the upward pressure on interest rates at a time when investment financing needs are rising. More importantly, unlike Italy, it seems to be in a position where migration flows could be enough to compensate for a stagnant fertility rate. Conversely, the stakes are higher in Spain when considering changes to migration policy, as any change could have significant long-term implications for the country’s fiscal sustainability. Ensuring a more resilient fiscal position and less dependence on external flows will require more aggressive reforms, such as linking the retirement age to life expectancy and reducing the gap between statutory and effective retirement ages; this looks hard to achieve given the current fragmentation of national politics. Growth-enhancing reforms would help if they translated into higher wage growth, decreasing the weight of average pensions on average wages (the benefit ratio). As the situation stands, the migration/structural reforms trade-off seems clear, at least in the long run; the willingness to face it less so. M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 27 Updated Loan Pricing for VS4 Released This is a reprint of a previously published note, which you may find here. After FHFA Director Bill Pulte's initial post on X on September 3, 2026 that announced all lenders are allowed to deliver loans with VantageScore 4.0 (VS4), Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac have released letters today confirming all lenders may deliver eligible loans using VS4. In conjunction with the announcement, the GSEs have also released their updated LLPAs/Credit Fees. The updated LLPAs are equivalent for each Classic FICO cohort and a 20-point higher VS4 cohort, across loan purposes. Though agency borrowers, on average, score ~20-points higher with VS4, we've previously found <700 Classic FICO borrowers tend to score ~40 points higher. As a result, we expect the updated loan pricing to be negative for existing FICO pools, as these borrowers would likely be able to qualify into a lower-LLPA cohort with VS4 and access a lower mortgage rate. records.text: 3 Nelson Jantzen, CFA AC (1-212) 270-1169 nelson.r.jantzen@jpmorgan.com North America Credit Research 11 September 2026 J P M O R G A N Credit Strategy Update High-yield bond yields rose 24bp to a five-month high this week as an escalating conflict in the Middle East produced sharply higher Treasury yields, a spike in Oil prices, and weaker equities. And this morning’s August CPI report came in firmer than expectations with the core rising 0.29% m/m which would bias the Fed towards a hike next week. And as investors grapple with the inflationary ramifications of the spike in Oil, OIS forwards are pricing in more than a cumulative 45bp of hikes by YE26. records.text: 12 The Global Thinker | 10 September 2026 That environment is now changing. As central banks shrink their balance sheets and market-determined risk premia normalize, fiscal authorities face a very different set of constraints. Higher debt levels that appeared sustainable in a world of near-zero interest rates may prove considerably more difficult to finance in a regime characterized by structurally higher real rates. The key implication is that the limits of fiscal policy are becoming increasingly visible. The issue is not simply the size of existing debt stocks, but the interaction between elevated debt levels, higher borrowing costs, and reduced policy space. Governments that fail to restore more sustainable fiscal trajectories may find themselves entering the next downturn with less room to support growth, while central banks face increasing pressure to account for fiscal sustainability concerns when conducting monetary policy. Ultimately, the post-crisis lesson may not be that debt constraints disappeared, but rather that they were temporarily obscured by an extraordinary combination of financial repression, quantitative easing, and exceptionally low equilibrium interest rates. As those conditions fade, the underlying trade-offs of fiscal policy are re-emerging. US fiscal policy Fiscal backing is a necessary condition for price stability. records.text: We added a 25bp rate hike at this week’s September FOMC meeting to our n forecast last Friday following the August CPI report. The report had little impact on our inflation view but pushed market pricing of a hike to nearly 90%, high enough that the FOMC will likely want to avoid the market reaction that would likely follow from remaining on hold. We continue to expect two cuts in 2027 but now expect them in September and December (vs. June and December previously). We have also raised our forecast for the terminal rate to 3.25-3.5% (vs. 3-3.25% previously). We do not see a strong economic case for raising the funds rate. We think that all n of the overshoot of 2% can be attributed to one-time factors whose impact is likely to fade, that the improvement in core PCE inflation to a roughly 2.5% pace over the last three months is an early sign of this, that high inflation looks broad-based mainly because of tariff effects, that inflation expectations are not at immediate risk of unanchoring, and that the economy is not overheated, which is the usual rationale for raising rates. We think that some FOMC participants will sympathize with these points and as a result will be reluctant to signal any additional hikes. We expect the FOMC to make only the minimum necessary change to its n statement, which will likely note that it is hiking to return inflation to 2% but will likely avoid providing guidance on the path forward or the criteria for further hikes. records.text: M Idea 2 Market Recap Markets looked at two things this week and repriced Fed expectations - higher oil prices amid increasing concerns around the uncertainty of resolution for the Middle East tensions, and inflation data that surprised to the upside. As of this morning, markets are pricing in roughly an 85% chance of the Fed hiking in September and almost 2 full hikes this year along with an extra 1.5 hikes next year. Rates bear flattened, vol was up, and stocks were down modestly, though credit spreads were slightly tighter. Perhaps not surprising given how mortgages normally act to higher vol and bear flattening episodes, mortgages widened materially. We had moved underweight the basis after the Jackson Hole speech, targeting mid-30s OAS on the index to cover the underweight. We were also worried about how vol was trading directionally, and into higher rates floater spreads would widen as the combination of cap risk/higher vol/wider MBS would weigh on them. Well, since Jackson Hole, 6.5 cap floaters have widened 15-20bp while 6.0 cap floaters have widened 50-60bp into increased cap risk, underperforming CLO AAAs. Stating the obvious, TBA 6.0s below par isn't a great thing for demand for 6.0 caps. Over that same time period, IG credit is unchanged while MBS is 7bp wider, and we think mortgages are more fairly valuing the risks, Thus, we move to neutral on the basis here, finding risks roughly balanced. We divide this target by the strategy's expected one-year return to arrive at the notional required. ° We apply this notional to the P&L generated if spreads were to retrace instantaneously to our chosen retracement date. The result is our (D/S) measure: the loss incurred, for a position sized to generate 100bp of income, if spreads were to move to the retracement scenario today. ° For the option trades we apply a similar logic. However, given our option strategies are based on 3-month expected returns, we first scale the 100bp of income target down to the specific option tenor before sizing notional. The richness is even more pronounced when considering the roughly $40bn of BB data-center bonds issued over the past year, without which the index would trade at ~143bp. Duration adjustment does not materially improve the compensation picture, as both BB OAS and spread-per-unit-duration (SPUD) sit near their 3rd percentiles since 2021. ° Single Bs: Single-B spreads have largely behaved in sync with BBs and are under their 6th percentile since 2021, reflecting overall strong demand for performing credits. When it seeks to offset fundamentals, it merely delays the adjustment and increases the risk of larger distortions later on. US Treasury buyback: Lost in translation The recent expansion of the U.S. Treasury's buyback program, often described as an Operation Twist-style strategy because it involves the purchase of long-dated securities financed through the issuance of short-term liabilities, highlights the distinction between desirable and undesirable forms of market intervention. records.text: 6 The Global Thinker | 10 September 2026 Financial-stability externalities constitute a third category. Fire sales, balance-sheet constraints, and liquidity shortages can generate feedback loops that amplify market stress and widen the gap between prices and fundamentals. By alleviating these constraints, policymakers can prevent temporary dislocations from evolving into broader systemic risks. The key principle is that intervention is most effective when it addresses a genuine distortion that prevents prices from reflecting fundamentals. When prices are primarily conveying information about changes in underlying economic conditions, attempts to resist those signals are unlikely to succeed and may ultimately undermine policy credibility. When does intervention work? A few success cases In many cases intervention is justified and properly executed it works. We will illustrate it with 3 relatively recent examples. The first one is the liquidity crisis of March 2020, which is an example of limits to arbitrage combined with fire sale. The second one is the intervention of the US Treasury in the FX market in Argentina ahead of midterm elections. The third one is the famous Draghi’s “Whatever it Takes” to save the Euro. In each case, although not very visible, there are hidden costs that are important to consider. A central lesson is that the way in which a decision problem is presented can materially affect the choices people make. The question posed at the conference provides a good illustration. It implicitly treats the existing pay-as-you-go system as the risk-free status quo and asks whether adding a funded component would introduce an unacceptable new risk. But the status quo is not risk-free. The return on a pay-as-you-go pension system ultimately depends on the future contribution base – the number of contributors and their taxable earnings – and is therefore exposed to domestic demographic and economic developments. So the actual choice is not between a safe pay-as-you-go system and risky capital markets. It is between concentrating pension financing on domestic demographic and wage risks and combining those risks with a second source of returns from diversified financial assets. Seen in this way, the introduction of a funded component does not simply add risk; it also diversifies risk. Short-term capital-market losses would undoubtedly be highly visible. The gradual effects of demographic ageing are much less apparent, but economically no less painful. This brings us to an even more fundamental point about framing in the political debate: the starting point for a reform discussion matters. We expect dovish Policy Board members Asada and Sato, both nominated under the Takaichi administration, to vote against the hike (resulting in a 7-2 vote), but uncertainty is especially elevated around Sato. Asada was the sole dissenter against the June rate hike. In a Reuters interview on 7 July, he said that demand-driven inflation accompanied by wage growth would need to be confirmed before he could support another hike. Since then, key components of domestic demand, including consumption and capital expenditure, have weakened somewhat, so we do not expect him to have sufficient grounds to reverse his previous judgment. Sato, on the other hand, emphasizes the need to distinguish cost-push pressures stemming from import prices from sustained price increases driven by wages and inflation expectations, but has also said that the impact of the strengthening pass-through of exchange-rate movements to prices on underlying inflation warrants close attention. The less clearly the Fed communicates its reaction function, the harder it becomes to disentangle those two effects and extract meaningful information from market signals. In this sense, a well-articulated reaction function complements rather than undermines market discipline. By reducing uncertainty surrounding the policy framework, it allows asset prices to reflect economic news more efficiently and improves the informational content of market signals. If the objective is to maximize what the Fed can learn from markets while minimizing unnecessary noise, then providing a clear description of the reaction function is not a substitute for market pricing but a prerequisite for interpreting it correctly. Forward guidance is not necessarily needed at this stage of the cycle. A clearly communicated reaction function is. Is Bessent making Warsh’s job more or less difficult? Bessent's attempt to influence conditions at the long end of the Treasury curve can only operate directly through nominal yields. Whether real interest rates ultimately decline depends on the response of inflation expectations. If inflation expectations remain relatively contained, lower nominal yields would translate into lower real yields, resulting in an effective easing of financial conditions.

Source: Barclays Research JPY outlook (last updated 23 June) • We expect USDJPY to remain elevated around 160 as Japan’s policy risk premium and net• capital outflows are offset by FX intervention (and fears thereof). Specifically, Takaichi administration’s “high pressure economy” policies, alongside higher oil prices, have pushed USDJPY via inflation risk premium well above our mid‑140s fair value estimate. At the same time, FX flow dynamics remain negative for JPY, as outbound investment (~JPY40trn) continues to exceed the current account surplus (~JPY20trn), reinforcing sustained net selling pressure. Household portfolio reallocation into foreign assets (including ~JPY10trn annual through NISA) and robust outbound FDI should keep capital outflows elevated. FX interventions are unlikely to shift the trend in USDJPY amid hawkish Fed pricing, while the BoJ is unlikely to accelerate its rate hiking cycle. We see room for some break above 2024- high of 162 in USDJPY due to greater headwinds for the JPY and a failure or perceived unwillingness to intervene risks an even greater upside in USDJPY. broadly fits this pattern, with an initial rally in Treasuries subsequently giving way to a reversal. The notion of asymmetric information is particularly delicate. If policymakers possess information that is materially different from that embedded in market prices, then transparency is generally more valuable than intervention. Market prices are informative precisely because they aggregate dispersed information from millions of participants. To the extent that policymakers attempt to influence prices without revealing the underlying information that justifies their view, price signals may become less informative and less efficient as guides for capital allocation. Crucially, possessing privileged information does not necessarily imply a superior ability to process and aggregate information relative to financial markets. The risk is therefore that intervention weakens the informational content of prices without improving the market's understanding of fundamentals. If policymakers believe markets are mispricing risk because they are operating with incomplete information, the most effective remedy is often greater transparency rather than stronger intervention. There is also a risk that such interventions create a coordination problem. In the absence of clear evidence of market dysfunction, repeated efforts to influence yields can be interpreted as a signal that authorities are increasingly concerned about the sustainability of current financing conditions. records.text: ss in business investment. In the April balance of payments data, receipts from R&D services exports increased sharply. As net imports of R&D services are included in capex in the GDP statistics, the increase in exports likely continued to weigh on GDP-based capex in the second estimate by reducing net imports. Revisions to the other components were mixed. Specifically, consumption, which had fallen well short of market expectations in the initial estimate, was revised up slightly from -0.1% to 0.0%, while government spending was revised up from +6.7% to +6.9%. By contrast, residential investment was revised down from -1.8% to -2.3% and public investment from -0.4% to -1.8%. In terms of overseas demand, both exports and imports were revised down, leaving the contribution from net exports unchanged at +1.8pp. Reflecting the latest data, including the second GDP estimate, we keep our real GDP growth forecast unchanged for FY26 (+1.0%) and revise down for FY27 (to +0.8% from +1.0%). On a calendar year basis, we revise up for 2026 (to +1.1% from +1.0%) and down for 2027 (to +0.6% from +0.7%; Figure 18 and Figure 19). 11 September 2026 14 Barclays | Market Strategy Japan: Focus on BoJ and JPY beyond next week

records.text: South Africa (SOAF) We are Marketweight on South Africa EXD, based on valuations and its beta to global risk. The bonds are BB and at current levels we believe they are trading fairly, while the valuations reflect the current risks. Upside risks lie in continued fiscal consolidation, higher precious metal prices, and improving global growth. Downside risks lie in weaker growth, resurging global inflation, and globally-driven credit risks (given South Africa's high beta to overall EM risk) Turkey (TURKEY) We are Marketweight (MW) on Türkiye External Debt (EXD). Valuations look fair to us given fundamentals, and in the context of inflation and political backdrops which are growing more salient. Upside risks are geopolitical resolution in the Middle East, improving fiscal and stronger reserve buffers. Downside risks are weaker fiscal backdrop and a more hawkish Fed Ukraine (UKRAIN) We have an Overweight recommendation on Ukraine EXD, as in our view current valuations have already priced in mid-term risks well and have asymmetrically positive risk/reward. Any sign of improvement in the geopolitical outlook could support valuations. Downside risk is: a continued prolonged conflict, which could further boost associated fiscal, economic and all other costs, potentially triggering a new round of restructuring. More recently, however, supply has re-emerged as an important driver. Growth in the CLO market has once again outpaced that in the leveraged loan universe, further widening the collateral gap ( Figure 5). While FRNs have remained the natural first destination, FRN market growth has stalled since early 2026, coinciding with a more volatile rates backdrop following the start of the Iran conflict. As a result, CLO managers have increasingly had to look beyond FRNs and into fixed-rate bonds, contributing to the broad-based increase in overall bond holdings since late 2025 ( Figure 6). Bond-loan price differentials have turned negative again More recently, relative value has reinforced the shift into fixed-rate bonds. Rising rates volatility, driven by a confluence of factors, has weighed on high yield bond prices while leveraged loans have remained comparatively resilient. As a result, the bond-loan price differential has moved back into negative territory this week ( Figure 7). The asymmetry between Warsh and Waller is not only explained by potentially different readings of the economy. There is a relative skin in the game component. The seat of the Chairman has more skin in the game. And the Chairman speech was to some extent path-dependent. Waller had more flexibility to be transparent about conditionality. Paradoxically, the policymaker arguing against forward guidance ended up giving more of it, while the policymaker who openly describe the conditional nature of his reaction function gave markets less information about the actual path of rates. The lesson: more transparency means less commitment The hiking analogy captures the distinction neatly. Warsh effectively hinted that the Fed might have waited too long, so be prepared for the Kohn trail. Waller effectively hinted that here is the trail map, if the terrain stays benign, take Bernanke trail, if it deteriorates, take Kohn trail. The first tells market which trail is becoming more likely. The second tells markets how the Fed will choose between them.

We have been arguing for a while that the UK economy is being supported by the global capex/AI cycle, with clear evidence of productivity growth picking up in the private sector (see here and here). Governor Bailey acknowledged, at the Treasury Select Committee hearing this week, that there were signs of an improvement in productivity growth, but stated this was not related to AI. We disagree, and see today's print as further evidence that tech adoption is the primary driver of the now very clear cyclical rise in output per worker across the private sector. We also flag this interesting note from the ONS on how data centre build-out is recorded in the UK national accounts. Per the ONS: "Once operational, data centres will typically contribute to economic output through the services they provide, such as data storage and cloud computing. This activity is recorded within...the Information and Communications Sector". Apart from AI adoption-related consultancy activities, hence, data centres are probably boosting ICT GVA. Elsewhere, consumer facing services were down on the month, while manufacturing output surprised to the upside, with pretty solid broad-based gains across the electronics and machinery sectors. On the other side, midterms are often a check on the party in power as the sitting President typically loses seats in Congress, and gridlock has been historically positive for stocks. In our view, midterms are a litmus test on party agendas and momentum. The risk to equities is that a more progressive US political narrative gets repriced post midterms: 1) higher odds of progressive policies (e.g. tax on wealth, AI regulation) being implemented on a Democratic landslide led by progressives, 2) the loss of momentum for GOP pro-business policies (e.g. corporate tax rate, deregulation) if the Senate is also lost, and 3) increased questions about the Trump coalition/agenda going into 2028 presidential elections. The near-term path for stocks though is likely to be driven by the policies of the Trump administration over the next 6-12m. A continued decline in policy uncertainty amidst strong profit growth could fuel a rally and volatility compression into year-end, as seen in the average midterm year. Prior to her latest interview (see here), we thought there was some chance that Mann reverts to voting for a 50bp hike. But her Jackson Hole messaging, to us, sound consistent with another 25bp dissent. We are fairly comfortable with calling for the rest of the Committee to vote for a hold, with our view informed by Deputy Governor Ramsden's Treasury Select Committee appearance. records.text: 13 The global copper market is reliant on rising scrap supply in 2026/27 to meet structural demand growth given flat anticipated mine output. However we expect weaker scrap elasticity to copper prices given the recent hikes to energy and fuel costs, softer goods trade-in-support in China relative to last year and domestic policy headwinds including a crackdown on provincial subsidies for secondary producers and scrap invoicing changes. We also see the global scrap supply chain as likely relatively depleted given broader shortages of raw copper inputs for smelters in recent years and strong scrap growth in 2025. China scrap import data shows ~8% y/y growth for Jan-Jul and ICSG data suggests ~6% y/y growth in secondary refined output in 1H’26. This compares with 12% y/y growth that might be anticipated given copper prices are ~40% higher year-on-year. Local experts also estimate China domestic scrap generation fell 200-300kt y/y in 1H’26 China scrap imports provide a broad measure of global copper scrap supply response that broadly correlates with price (although can also be influenced by trends in China domestic scrap generation) China Cu-in-scrap imports show 8% growth in Jan-Jul, This lags annualised growth of ~12%+ that historical price-to-scrap recovery might impact at current copper prices and likely also reflects slower growth in domestic scrap generation Scrap supply growth lagging historical price elasticity Source: Citi Research, Bloomberg, China Customs, TDM Prepared

COVID relief funding through the CARES Act boosted hospital cash from 2020 to 2023, leading to dampened issuance and M&A activity. As issuers struggled to understand HR 1 policy uncertainty, NFP hospital mergers slowed to their lowest levels in 2025 (Figure 5) with a record share involving a distressed hospital. 46% of announced transactions were divestitures and 44% of transactions involved a distressed party, signaling financial pressure and a shift in strategy from national scale towards regional concentration or high margin services (Figure 6). Now, in 2026, we have seen a strong M&A rebound with announced transactions up 208% compared to last year (Figure 7). 22 transactions were announced in the first quarter of 2026 and 18 more in the second quarter. Divestitures drove the transaction number in Q1, accounting for more than two thirds of transactions, but normalized in Q2 when that share decreased to one-third. records.text: What Would It Take to Get to a Sustainable Fiscal Path? There are two reasons to worry about fiscal sustainability even when interest rates are below nominal GDP growth. First, the large primary deficits we expect in coming years (Exhibit 7) will very likely keep debt-to-GDP growing steadily, and government borrowing rates tend to rise with debt levels, which together could increase r-g over time. Second, the recent jump in interest rates is a reminder that a genuinely sustainable path should be robust to uncertainty about future interest rates, growth, and deficits, and higher debt increases vulnerability to unfavorable surprises. What would it take to get on a sustainable fiscal path? Exhibit 8 shows that in our baseline projection, the primary deficit accounts for all of the growth in the debt-to-GDP ratio well into the future. Without policy action, the budget points to a 9.4%-of-GDP deficit (4.5% primary) in 2027, although the government plans a fiscal adjustment that could partially offset the deterioration. Government unveils a more challenging fiscal outlook The new government re-drafted the 2027 budget bill and submitted it to Congress, accusing the previous administration of misrepresenting the fiscal deficit and borrowing needs. We expect job growth to average 77k/mo in ‘26, comfortably above breakeven, allowing the u- rate to edge down to 4.2% in 3Q26. The labor market remains stable, and we expect that to persist, with only modest effects from policy tightening in ‘27. We forecast job growth to average around 60k in ’27 and ‘28, with the u-rate falling to 4.1% by 1Q27. While immigration-related constraints should keep labor supply growth subdued, easing tariff uncertainty has reduced downside risks to labor demand. We expect AI's labor market impact to remain limited through 2026, with broader job reallocation more likely emerging in 2027. Fed: Hike now or get asked questions later • Growth is solid, the labor market is roughly in balance, inflation is too high for comfort, and monetary policy has become too easy. Hence, we maintain our out-of- consensus call that the Fed will hike by 75bp this year, starting in September. We have long been of the view that rate hikes were the right policy prescription in the US. Weak Jul data made a rate hike in September marginally less likely. However, following Chair Warsh's hawkish remarks at Jackson Hole, likely to correct for the dovish July presser that led to increasing concerns around Fed credibility, the bar not to hike in September is high. And we expect more to follow.

records.text: Last year after the 2026 budget was announced, we have taken the reform of the debt brake and introduction of the SVIK at face value (see Germany: Laying groundwork for growth acceleration, dated 3 Oct 2025). So far, we have learned that the German government only delivered around 65% of their target for SVIK spending in 2025 (EUR24bn out of EUR37.2bn planned). Yet, we see reason that spending should be easier in 2026 compared to last year. Much of the shortfall was attributed to disbursement of the states for which the enabling law was only enacted in mid-December 2025. Monthly spending data on defence and investment shows that spending is at 1.1% of GDP for both investment and defence over H1. This means the government is on track to meet their 2026 spending target for defence (2.3% of GDP) but lags slightly on investment (2.7% of GDP). We think the recent passing of the procurement and infrastructure future act, significantly reducing red tape around procurement and getting projects started, should facilitate spending in H2. Additionally, government data suggests that 2/3 out of the projects for which disbursement started are still in the planning stage, which means further spending should follow suit. Thus, looking ahead we remain optimistic that the full EUR500bn envelope of the SVIK will be deployed, albeit we see risks for further delay in deployment. Case 2: US Treasury intervention in Argentina ahead of midterm elections Last year, ahead of the Argentine’s October midterm elections, investors became worried that a poor result for the incumbent Javier Milei would weaken his presence in Congress and derail the much-needed fiscal adjustment and structural reforms, generating a self-reinforcing negative dynamic. Expectations of political defeat leading to policy reversal and devaluation of the currency, which triggered a hedging demand for dollars by households and corporates, higher sovereign spreads, tighter domestic financial conditions, weaker economic sentiment and recession. In turn, this was increasing the probability of President Milei’s party doing poorly in the midterm elections. This case represents a good example of multiple equilibria. As labour market slackened, and pay growth slipped towards 3%Y, underlying inflation normalised. records.text: Japan Rates Weekly 10 September 2026 Citi Research 8 Lending to JBIC was $34,958mn, up $1,341mn since July. If we assume that half of the JBIC contribution to the additions to the $550bn facility for investment in the US announced on August 14 are from the Foreign Exchange Fund Special Account, the amount would be a somewhat large $787mn. However, this is an item in which some change is to be expected, so it is not something of concern. Based on a somewhat longer-term perspective, even under the current framework the Foreign Exchange Fund Special Account will need to contribute more than $90bn, so the amounts lent so far are only a fraction of this. It therefore looks likely there will need to be a drawing down of deposits and sale of securities, or other fundraising. While the situation differs, the big drawdown of foreign currency reserves is reminiscent of China in 2014–2016. Over 18 months, China’s foreign currency reserves fell by 25%, from $4trn to $3trn. The decline in the market value of Japan’s reserves due to rises in interest rates started from the peak of $1.4trn in 2021, and they fell further due to intervention in 2022. A peak of $1.4trn means a fall of 25% would leave the total at just over $1trn, so there is a buffer that provides leeway for further intervention. records.text: he China slowdown and lockdowns, commodity price volatility, the EM pandemic response and Fed rate hikes – have periodically dampened inflows, they have not reversed the longer-term growth of the international investor base. Prolonged quantitative easing in global developed markets in Europe, Asia and the US in previous years, with ultra-low or negative interest rates, fueled demand for high- yielding EM assets. The inclusion of China local debt in major global bond indices in 2020 also increased foreign demand, although political and economic concerns since 2022 have driven net outflows in a few recent years. Volatility has not shaken investor commitment Despite volatility and periodic retail outflows in 2013, 2018 and 2020-24, investors in local debt markets (LDM) have remained committed to the asset class, as it offers opportunities for income through coupons, price and FX appreciation. Beware of capital controls Opportunities may remain abundant over the medium term, but understanding the characteristics of each market is key. A major concern for various governments amid Fed tightening has been sudden outflows, which have depressed lending and triggered domestic financial volatility. In response, some policymakers have intervened, imposing measures to discourage such flows, adding to the investment challenge.

records.text: European Rates Weekly 10 September 2026 Citi Research 2 Rates volatility has woken up from its late summer sleep – with top-left posting the highest two-day increase in two months. Not only was Thursday’s hike a “no brainer” for the ECB but, as long as energy prices keep rising, further hikes seem to be the most logical consequence. In the absence of a neutral rate or any other guidance beyond energy prices, “markets do what they have to do” – by bear flattening the front-end and injecting uncertainty around future policy outcomes. More hikes to come also infer a higher probability of reversals: We close our 2s5s bear steepening recommendation and rather tactically recommend buying 3m right-hand skew via 1x1.5 structures on 1y rate. A no-brainer hike. Gas and oil prices rose jointly for a 4th session this week on the day where the press conference that followed the well-telegraphed 25bp hike read pretty hawkish – such that our economists now expect a cycle peak of 3%. With President Lagarde re-iterating the meeting-by-meeting approach and playing down the neutral rate as policy guide, it seems that not only was Thursday’s decision a “no brainer” but that, as long as energy prices keep rising (Figure 1), further hikes seem to be the most logical consequence. In the absence of any other anchor than energy prices, in other words, “markets do what they have to do” by injecting uncertainty around future policy outcomes and raising the probability of U-turns. Caution is warranted due to eroded risk premia in the EGB complex, which make EGB spreads more prone to substantial repricing on a negative shift in market sentiment or on a rise in French idiosyncratic risk. However, flows from the neighbouring country have come under pressure in recent weeks. As a result, Mongolian coking coal prices have continued to rally, rising a further $30/t (13% WoW) to $265/t free-on-truck (FOT) in the week ending 28 August. The disruption is particularly significant given Mongolia's growing importance in China's import mix following the Australian coal ban in 2020. Mongolia now accounts for more than 60% of China's metallurgical coal imports. Unlike seaborne suppliers, however, the vast majority of Mongolian coal enters China by truck through border crossings such as Ganqimaodu, leaving supply highly exposed to logistical bottlenecks. Recent diesel shortages, environmental inspections and weaker customs clearance rates have sharply reduced truck movements. According to Mysteel, border clearances on 22 August were 54% below the January-July average, with little evidence of a meaningful recovery so far. Chinese domestic production is likely to remain constrained, making a normalization of Mongolian flows the key downside risk to our constructive coking coal outlook. Exhibit 6: China

records.text: The Global Thinker | 10 September 2026 15 The communication lesson is evident: the more clearly the Fed explains the rule governing the choice between the slow pre-emptive hike and the delayed aggressive hike, the less it needs to guide markets about which trail is will actually take. Fed's search for the optimal degree of transparency Chairman Warsh's speech at Jackson Hole was a welcome development at the margin, but substantial work remains to be done. As the July press conference demonstrated, moving from extensive forward guidance to virtually no guidance at all risks generating unnecessary volatility. The market immediately priced the shift through a bear steepening of the Treasury curve, wider inflation breakevens, and higher rates volatility. Rather than reducing uncertainty, the new communication framework increased uncertainty about the Federal Reserve's reaction function. Excessive forward guidance can distort price discovery, but the absence of guidance can create its own inefficiencies (see Exhibit 9), and higher risk premia (see the report Global Economic Weekly: Anna Karenina Principle of Monetary Policy). The combination of a steeper yield curve, lower equity prices, and a weaker dollar is uncomfortably close to the market reaction typically associated with credibility shocks in emerging-market central banks. The new silk route In contrast to the growing strain China’s upgrading places on advanced manufacturers, deeper trade dependence and broad- er cooperation with China has, so far, been constructive for most EM Edge economies. The reason is structural: many EM Edge markets export commodities and basic intermediates and maintain relatively small or low-tech manufacturing sec- tors. In this setting, an influx of medium‑ to high‑tech Chi- nese imports (autos, machinery, electrical equipment, elec- tronics) is less likely to displace domestic production at scale than it is in advanced manufacturers where overlap with Chi- na is highest in precisely these higher value-added segments. Put differently, the competitive shock is asymmetrical: advanced economies compete with China; the EM Edge mostly complements it. Complementarity also runs through the external accounts and near-term macro outcomes. EM Edge export baskets typically do not compete with China’s, while China’s import substitu- tion in manufactured inputs and its push for supply-chain resilience raises the premium on reliable commodity suppli- ers—supporting demand for energy, metals, and other prima- ry inputs and, in some cases, strengthening the leverage of exporters of “strategic” materials. Consistent with this, Chinese investment is increasingly extending downstream into mineral processing, not just mine ownership, particularly across the copper, cobalt, and lithium value chains. Host-country priorities are also changing. Governments are pushing for jobs, tax revenue, and value-chain upgrading: Zambia’s critical-minerals strategy emphasizes building “val- ue chains” rather than exporting raw copper; Kazakhstan is seeking investment in metals processing, industrial produc- tion, and logistics, alongside a sharp rise in Chinese FDI. Logistics has become a central pillar across Central Asia under the China–Central Asia framework launched in spring 2023. Manufacturing relocation is clearest in Vietnam (China+1) and, to a lesser extent, Serbia (a potential EU gateway). Beyond those two, evidence of broad-based relocation is thin- ner, though there are pockets of local industry build-out— e.g., Kazakhstan in metals/coal/wheat processing, power gen- eration, and logistics; Uzbekistan in renewables, autos, and logistics. In this model, host countries capture more value-added and infrastructure, while China secures longer-term access to stra- tegic resources and end-markets—often retaining control of the higher-end processing know-how and downstream appli- cations. In a sense, Bunds are being dragged higher by both global factors and European energy/inflation considerations. On the US side, US Treasury buyback activity proved irrelevant, with USTs selling off after news of the €6bn longer-dated buybacks. Away from this unease bleeding into broader risk assets, it adds to the impetus in European rates, and in particular in CDS indices. The higher – and faster – rates go, the more important is the effect on total returns. €IG total returns are now -40bp YTD. Although €HY total returns YTD are positive at 1.5%, the rolling 2mth total return stands at -35bp. Last time total returns turned negative to this degree was in early March 2026, when we saw five weeks of consecutive outflows, for about 4% of AUM. In short: watch HY demand technicals. Supply is also up: Wednesday-to-Wednesday, €IG saw €21.5bn in supply. While the composition of this supply is much-discussed, the amount of supply is in line with historical norms ( Figure 1). records.text: 18 The Global Thinker | 10 September 2026 Under that scenario, the intervention would place additional pressure on the Federal Reserve to tighten monetary policy. The front end of the curve would need to reflect not only a stronger policy response to easier financial conditions, but also the fact that the buyback program is financed through the issuance of short-term liabilities. In effect, part of the duration removed from the long end would reappear at the front end of the curve. However, the opposite outcome is also possible. If the intervention leads investors to demand a higher risk premium, either because of concerns about fiscal sustainability or because policymakers are perceived as interfering with price discovery, long-term yields could ultimately rise rather than fall. In that case, financial conditions would tighten, providing the Fed with greater scope to wait and assess the impact on economic activity before adjusting policy. This asymmetry underscores the importance of understanding the drivers of market prices. A decline in yields driven by improved market functioning has very different implications from a decline driven by reduced term premia. Similarly, an increase in yields driven by stronger growth prospects sends a very different signal than an increase driven by rising fiscal or inflation risk premia. These technical factors can introduce noise into prices and complicate the process of extracting information about underlying fundamentals. This distinction is critical when assessing whether policy intervention is warranted. Intervention is justified when market outcomes are distorted by failures in market functioning, coordination problems, or financial-stability externalities. It is far less compelling when the objective is simply to push prices toward levels preferred by policymakers. Market failures can emerge when dealers and arbitrageurs are unable or unwilling to intermediate. Under such conditions, forced sales may drive asset prices significantly away from their fundamental values, while spreads reflect liquidity shortages and market plumbing constraints rather than new information about economic prospects. In these circumstances, temporary intervention can help restore market functioning and improve price discovery. Coordination failures provide another rationale for intervention. When multiple equilibria are possible, self-fulfilling expectations can push markets toward an inefficient outcome. A classic example is a sovereign debt market in which fears of default lead investors to demand higher yields. Similarly, we had flagged upside risks to airfares (+2.7%) given that the seasonal factors were expecting a roughly 3% decline in non-seasonally adjusted prices. As jet fuel prices have reversed most of their 2 3% decline in June, this made it very easy for airfares to outperform on a seasonally adjusted basis in the August data. The details within last Thursday’s PPI data also skewed hawkish, with notable strength in international airfares as well as hospital prices. Combining the component-level data within the CPI and PPI , we are tracking August core PCE to increase by 0.27%, a pace that is not consistent with further progress towards the Fed’s target. Interestingly, the upcoming methodology changes for the PCE components will likely add a couple basis points to the core PCE print relative to the current methodology. Legal services in the PPI rose by about 1.8% seasonally adjusted versus likely declining by a tenth in the CPI , so switching to the PPI for legal services will add about 2bps to August core PCE. The Ugly The greatest risk is that repeated intervention generates increasingly severe policy inconsistencies. Japan could find itself simultaneously defending the yen while maintaining a monetary and fiscal policy stance that remains fundamentally inconsistent with the desired exchange-rate objective. Such contradictions are rarely sustainable. Over time, they can distort capital allocation, weaken market discipline, and undermine price discovery. Moreover, persistent intervention may ultimately shift pressures elsewhere in the financial system. If exchange-rate adjustments are suppressed while underlying imbalances remain unresolved, the burden of adjustment could fall on domestic bond markets. In that scenario, attempts to support the currency might come at the cost of greater volatility at the long end of the Japanese government bond curve, particularly as monetary normalization proceeds and private investors are required to absorb a larger share of sovereign issuance.

As in the previous example, the rise in yields made the sovereign debt less sustainable, weakening the banking system that had exposure to those bonds, tightening financial conditions, worsening the recession and fiscal position, in the end making the default event more likely. In this sense, it was an example of multiple equilibria, where a country can be solvent at normal interest rates but insolvent at crisis interest rates. Markets could coordinate on a bad equilibrium even if the country might have remained solvent at normal borrowing costs. On July 2012, the ECB Governor Mario Draghi announced the ECB was ready to whatever it takes within its mandate to preserve the euro. The commitment was made concrete in September through the announcement of the OMT (Outright Monetary Transactions), where the ECB stood ready to purchase unlimited quantities of eligible sovereign bonds in the secondary market, particularly maturities of one to three years. Crucially, OMT was conditional on the government entering and complying with an EFSF (European Financial Stability Facility) and ESM (European Stability Mechanism) adjustment program. The adjustment program was designed to mitigate moral hazard considerations and put fundamentals in order. Interestingly, the OMT was never executed. After two months of upside surprises in June and July, Swedish inflation surprised to the downside in August. With CPIF excluding energy broadly in line with the Riksbank's expectations, we believe the pressure to normalize the policy rate to 2.0% as early as September has eased materially. As a result, we now expect the Riksbank to hike by 25bp in December. The inflation outlook remains highly uncertain Key inflation risks stem from energy price developments, but also from the potential fiscal policy changes following the September general elections. On balance, we view the risks around our call for the policy rate at 2.0% throughout 2027 as broadly balanced. Should geopolitical tensions ease, and energy prices normalise, the Riksbank could then remain on hold for longer, adopting a wait-and-see stance. Higher energy prices than assumed in June, together with the stronger GDP growth outlook, have pushed up core inflation forecasts for 2028. The ECB now sees core inflation at 2.3% in 2028, including in 4Q28, which is c 10bp above the June forecast (Exhibit 2). This is all despite the forecasts now being based on 3m Euribor assumptions of three policy hikes (perhaps a tad more). Implicitly, the ECB is signalling that a December hike may be warranted, if its base case materializes (we are not convinced its core inflation forecast of 2.6% in 4Q26 will, so we keep our call unchanged for now). The “mild” scenario could justify keeping current policy rates on hold, while the “adverse” scenario would open the door to a fourth hike. We would still point out that all scenarios, except the particularly severe one, point to a less hawkish outcome than markets are currently pricing. Why? Today’s energy price futures are above the ECB’s base case, but well below the adverse scenario (Exhibit 2). records.text: Methodology: Adding option strategies to the framework We extend our existing curve trade framework to include carry-generating option strategies. In addition to considering outright longs, our curve trades under consideration are: • 3s5s and 5s10s forward – selling protection at each tenor, notional-neutral • 3s5s and 5s10s DV01-neutral steepeners Our options strategy analysis is based on 3-month options, and we construct four strategies – payers, payer spreads, straddles and strangles, using the following set of deltas across strategies: • Payer: 25-delta • Payer spread: 25-delta/10-delta • Straddle: 50-delta payer/50-delta receiver • Strangle: 25-delta payer/25-delta receiver In our analysis, actual option strategy returns are based on the nearest 3-month options corresponding to the target deltas (eg, the November 65bp strike for a 25-delta Main payer). While historical percentile rankings for the strategies are calculated using a normalised constant-maturity, constant-delta series, constructed via interpolation of the option surface, ensuring comparability across time. We then evaluate these strategies against each other, and against our existing curve strategies, using the following metrics: • Expected Return ° For curve trades and outright longs, the expected 1yr return from carry and roll-down on assumed unchanged curves. ° For option strategies, the expected return is the premium received for selling the strategy over its 3-month tenor, expressed in bp of notional –
