Following a sharp ~20bp move in the front end of the UK curve yesterday alone, the BoE is priced to deliver a hiking cycle - 100bp by the June meeting, with 2 hikes to be delivered in November and December. Chief Economist Pill - who has been voting for rate hikes since April - has stressed in his latest speech that an imminent rate hike "...need not be the start of a prolonged and aggressive series of increases". In any case, financial conditions in the UK are exceptionally tight. In this environment, we think, any indication that a core member of the MPC thought about voting for a hike in September already, or a very clear hint that a hike in November is coming, could, in our view, open the door for market conversation around a 50bp move in November, or push the pricing of the terminal rate to 5% or higher. This, we think, is the clear lesson of the March meeting. This is why we ultimately think that a repeat of the July messaging which leaves the door open to act, but remains non-committal on the timing and the pace, is probably the optimal strategy, and one the BoE will pursue. In an environment where commodity prices are as elevated as they currently are, and the ECB might deliver further hikes, it is highly unlikely that financial conditions will ease significantly if the BoE fails to deliver more hawkish messaging. records.text: is no parliament majority, it is hard to get. Beyond this, considerable uncertainty surrounds the fiscal trajectory following the presidential election (second round: 2 May 2027). Given rising interest rate payments, stabilising the debt-to- GDP ratio would require fiscal consolidation worth around EUR120bn (4% of GDP) by 2032, as now forecast by various presidential candidates. At this stage, the various candidates in the presidential election have not yet clearly outlined their medium-term fiscal policies, although several have announced that they would roll back the pension reform. This could prove costly and would require strong fiscal arbitration elsewhere to finance it (see page 10). The capacity of any newly elected president to deliver on their economic policies requires a supporting majority in parliament. This is still uncertain. Any new president would likely call for new parliamentary elections, to take place possibly in the second half of June 2027. In the past, French voters have been rather consistent, voting for a majority – or close to it – of the same party as the president. We expect this will be still the case, helping to provide more visibility on the pace of fiscal consolidation. However, given the political fragmentation, we can not rule out the risk of a lack of a ruling parliamentary majority, forcing the formation of a coalition government. records.text: Sector Fundamentals: Some reversal of fortune Earlier this year, as we framed our methodology for approaching sector allocations, we highlighted how net leverage at the sector level informs these views. We focused on sectors within each market where net leverage had been trending lower vs. higher. In the exhibits below, we refresh these charts, now with the benefit of two additional quarters of earnings reports, and find that, for many of these sectors, the trend has reversed or stagnated. We find several noteworthy sector developments in North America that are less evident in Europe; accordingly, we focus on North America below. Energy, for example, had experienced steadily rising net leverage in both the North American IG and HY markets since 2022, but—not surprisingly given the evolution of energy prices during the current middle east conflict—2Q saw net leverage decline for both IG and HY Energy issuers (Exhibits 11 and 12). Perhaps more surprisingly, despite the range of headlines about the weakness of the consumer, retail and consumer-focused firms also saw net leverage improve in 2Q. records.text: 2 Japan Viewpoint | 11 September 2026 Japan’s economy: Resilience amidst the Middle East shock Japan’s economy absorbed the immediate shock from worsening Middle East tensions surprisingly well in Apr-Jun, with real GDP rising +1.4% QoQ SAAR and marking a third consecutive quarter of expansion (Exhibit 3). It is worth noting that 2Q CY26 GDP was also lifted by a range of temporary factors, including a surge in durables consumption reflecting policy-driven boosts to auto and air conditioner sales, a large one-off increase in service exports attributable to an overseas transfer of patent rights, and a temporary boost from lower oil imports (see Apr-Jun GDP (Prelim): Underlying growth remains resilient despite distortions, 17 August). However, even after accounting for these distortions, underlying growth likely remained broadly flat, in contrast to widespread fears of a contraction. We attribute the resilience to several factors. First, the economy entered the year with solid momentum, including record corporate profits and a positive wage outlook. Second, the direct energy shock proved smaller than expected. Japan secured alternative supplies faster than we anticipated, including a sharp increase in oil imports from the US, while the government released strategic inventories. Together, these measures limited disruptions to production (Exhibit 3). At $220bn year to date, HY issuance remains $160bn below our $380bn full-year forecast, implying that 42% of the 2026 supply will price after Labor Day. records.text: Rethinking the details One of the most asked about sections of our Inflation-Linked Daily is our detailed CPI fixings analysis. In this section, we look at the CPI swap fixings, which are in NSA terms, translate what those imply for market-implied SA fixings, and then calculate a proxy for market-implied "core" fixings. Calling that final step "core" is slightly misleading, as it really is ex-CPI energy commodities, and even then, practically derived from a pure focus on motor fuel. Up until now, we have been comfortable with stopping there, and calling the result a "core" proxy, given the complexity in deriving a high-conviction market-implied electricity and food path. However, the world has changed, and our sense is that sophistication of the market has grown in recent years. In essence, our previous parsimonious approach to tracking market-implied "core" fixings is too simplistic at this point. In this publication, we rethink our methodology for tracking market-implied "core" fixings (or, at least ex-energy) and demonstrate what that implies for the upcoming market-implied CPI inflation path. Rather than focusing only on ex-energy commodities, we provide a framework to track market-implied energy more generally across the four major CPI energy categories, specifically: fuel oil & other fuels, motor fuel, electricity, and utility (piped) gas service. We find that our deepened framework presents a more realistic market-implied CPI energy path and a smoother ex-energy fixing

In justification of the hike, the ECB said: "The conflict in the Middle East continues to generate inflation pressures, and inflation is set to remain well above target for an extended period." According to the ECB, the economic outlook "remains highly uncertain, with risks to the upside for inflation and to the downside for economic growth." As regards the policy outlook, the ECB stuck to the now familiar statement according to which the Governing Council "will follow a data-dependent and meeting-by-meeting approach to determining the appropriate monetary policy stance. (...) The Governing Council is not pre-committing to a particular rate path." The ECB said that "[w]ith today’s decision, the Governing Council remains well positioned to navigate the uncertainty caused by the conflict", without indicating whether it sees a necessity for further rate hikes. That said, the updated macro projection in our view conveyed a somewhat hawkish impression. To start, a draft budget needs to be sent to parliament in time to allow for approval, and parliament has 70 days to vote on the budget bill (40 days for a first reading in the National Assembly, 15 days in the Senate, and the remaining time to find agreement between both chambers). To ensure a budget is in place at the start of the following year, this time frame requires this year's budget draft to be sent to parliament by 6 October 2026 ( first Tuesday in October ). This would allow parliament to adopt the budget by mid-December. Before being promulgated, Art. 61 of the Constitution allows the budget bill to be referred to the Constitutional Council at the request of 60 deputies or 60 senators (as well as the President of the Republic, the Prime Minister, or the presidents of the assemblies). In case the 70-day period is not respected, and no bill is voted before the end of the year, the Constitution distinguishes between whether this delay is due to parliament or the government. If a delay can be attributed to parliament, i.e. if parliament fails to reach a decision, Art. 47(3) allows the government to bring the provisions into force by a "budget ordinance", which is adopted by the Council of Ministers and does not require parliamentary ratification (unlike the usual procedure in Art. 38, whereby ordinances require parliamentary approval). Attorney General Approval & State Regulation Some investors have begun asking whether AGs may start promoting acquisitions or mergers. In our view, AG regulatory attitudes are increasingly split depending on why an acquisition is happening. In cases when a community could potentially lose its only hospital, AGs have shown that they will not just permit a deal, but actively expedite it through: • Oregon (August 2026): AG Dan Rayfield granted emergency, expedited approval of Salem Health's $61mn acquisition of Santiam Hospital after the two systems filed an emergency appeal, saying Santiam faced imminent collapse without it. His office explicitly worked "swiftly" because closure would have dumped ~22,000 ER visits onto Salem's flagship. • Minnesota (August 2026): AG cleared Sanford Health's takeover of the financially strained North Memorial (which lost ~$50mn last year), though only after negotiating a 10y guarantee that trauma, cardiac and safety-net services stay open. • Courts have grown more receptive to letting distressed hospitals be acquired even in concentrated markets. In the 2024 Novant/Community Health Systems case, a judge denied the FTC's request to block the deal because both target hospitals were "likely to close soon" anyway, reasoning that a hospital exiting the market entirely harms competition more than the merger would. records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 9 Exhibit 15: Cash withdrawals from the DHS - CBP , as a proxy for tariff refunds 0 20 40 60 80 100 120 140 160 Cash Withdrawals from DHS, CBP (Fiscal YTD, Bil $; 4-wk avg) Source: US Treasury, Haver Analytics, Morgan Stanley Research Tariff refunds represent cash returned to importers when customs duties were previously overpaid or later determined to be refundable, for different reasons, including a tariff exclusion or court-ordered refund or a drawback claim tied to goods that are exported or destroyed. The process generally runs through CBP, where importers or brokers submit the relevant claim and supporting documentation; CBP then reviews eligibility, confirms the entry and status, and certifies approved refunds for payment. In Treasury cash-flow data, we monitor these payments at high frequency through CBP-related withdrawals in the Daily Treasury Statement. We interpret this as a tariff-refund proxy.

records.text: ustment program was designed to mitigate moral hazard considerations and put fundamentals in order. Interestingly, the OMT was never executed. The credibility of the unlimited backstop changed investor incentives. Markets quickly coordinated into a good equilibrium where spreads tightened. Fiscal conditionality through EFSF/ESM compliance ensured the good equilibrium was fundamentally sustainable, while ECB commitment prevented markets from coordinating on the bad equilibrium. Will intervention works this time? Japan meets US The Treasury's recent interventions, first in support of the yen and later through the expansion of long-dated Treasury buybacks, have a common underlying objective: influencing prices in markets that are sending increasingly uncomfortable signals about underlying macroeconomic conditions. While some aspects of these measures may be justified by liquidity or market-functioning considerations, others appear aimed at dampening information contained in market prices. History suggests that distinction matters. Interventions can mitigate temporary dislocations, but they rarely succeed in reversing trends driven by fundamentals. When prices reflect deteriorating fiscal dynamics or a shift in the savings-investment balance, intervention is not a cure. It merely delays the adjustment. Ultimately, fundamentals tend to prevail.

A path like that would imply an average policy rate over the next decade of roughly 3.6-3.7%, not far from what is currently discounted. A decade is a long time. Markets are not pricing a single policy path. They are pricing an average across a wide distribution of outcomes. A recession would almost certainly pull policy rates materially below the modal path for a brief period of time. Equally, a world in which inflation proves more persistent, or growth remains more resilient than expected, could keep policy rates above the modal path for longer. Bottom line, investors often anchor on nominal yield levels. A 5% 10y Treasury yield feels high because it is high relative to most of the post-GFC period. But the post-GFC era was also characterized by unusually low policy rates, compressed term premia and strong demand from price-insensitive investors. The relevant question is not whether yields are high relative to the last decade, but whether they are high relative to the world we now inhabit. On that basis, we do not think a 5% 10y Treasury yield is, by itself, sufficient evidence that USTs are cheap. FIGURE 5. records.text: 14 The Global Thinker | 10 September 2026 brisk style of Kohn vs the more leisurely style of Bernanke. And then he asked "Is this a Kohn Day or a Bernanke Day?". After listening his relatively hawkish speech and moreover, after listening Waller's relatively dovish speech, it is becoming evident that Chairman Warsh was trying to tell us more than an innocent joke with that analogy. The Bernanke trail is the slow, pre-emptive route: start hiking earlier, move gradually, and reduce the risk that inflation or financial conditions get far enough out of line to require a more painful tightening later. The Kohn trail is the alternative: wait longer but if the inflation outlook deteriorates, be prepared to hike faster and more aggressively. The question is then not really whether to hike, but whether to hike slowly and pre- emptively today or risk having to hike much faster tomorrow. Forward Disguidance This framing helps explain why Warsh's Jackson Hole speech was so forceful. records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 5 Oil tracker: Elevated prices, falling inventories We continue to track the evolution of petroleum-product inventories, production, trade, and prices. The latest data suggest that crude oil inventories in the Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) fell further, and the total US crude oil and petroleum-product inventories were relatively flat. US domestic crude oil production rose, while net imports of crude oil and petroleum products have moved sideways recently. Meanwhile, oil prices moved higher. As of September 4, US stocks of crude oil and petroleum products, which represent the EIA's estimate of how many barrels of crude oil and petroleum products are physically sitting in US storage at period-end, remained broadly unchanged from a week earlier. The stocks of crude oil in the Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) continued to fall to around 285 million barrels, the lowest level since April 1984. The Energy Department said the SPR's minimum inventory is determined by "cavern mechanics," which, when applied across the full system, translates to a conservative operational minimum of about 70 million barrels. If the SPR continues to decline at roughly its recent pace of 30 million barrels every four weeks, inventories would approach the operational minimum by the end of February 2027. records.text: Please refer to important information at the end of the report and MAR disclosures Italy has performed two significant reforms to the pension system in the last 30 years or so: the 1995 so-called Dini reform and the 2011 Fornero reform. These have introduced (and then accelerated) the transition from defined benefit to defined contribution schemes and the second one in particular has linked retirement age to life expectancy. Both these reforms have contributed to stabilising the pension system, which is now projected to show rising expenditure until the middle of the century but then decline. However, we note that these official projections (from the state account general and the European Commission) are based on some relatively optimistic assumptions. First, the GDP/employment ratio is assumed to grow significantly faster than in the recent past. While a productivity shock – such as the one led by the AI revolution – could make this trend a reality, there is no guarantee. Second, looking beneath the surface, both the RGS (state account general) and the European Commission appear to assume a rising fertility rate – a key driver of population projections – although this has been dropping over the past few years (Figure 2). Maternity and paternity policies could help reverse the trend, but no significant reform seems to be in the pipeline. records.text: The Global Thinker | 10 September 2026 3 policymakers seek to pursue multiple objectives in an environment characterized by elevated debt levels, persistent uncertainty, and heightened market sensitivity to policy signals. Why are interest rates moving higher? Two stylized facts stand out. First, while attention has naturally centered on the United States, the increase in interest rates is a global phenomenon spanning both advanced and emerging economies (see Exhibit 1). Second, the adjustment has been driven predominantly by rising real rates rather than by higher inflation expectations (Exhibit 2). Together, these observations point to a conclusion that is becoming increasingly difficult to ignore: global interest rates are unlikely to revisit the extraordinarily low levels that characterized the post-Global Financial Crisis era. Rather, rates appear to be normalizing toward levels more consistent with those prevailing before the Lehman collapse. Yet periods of rising rates often expose underlying vulnerabilities. As in the late 1990s and early 2000s, important imbalances are once again emerging beneath the surface. Assessing their significance requires understanding the forces shaping both short- and long-term interest rates globally. For both strategies, weights are linear representations of the input signals, reweighted to sum to zero, and for positive and negative weights to sum to +1 and -1, respectively. On a full-sample basis, while both strategies deliver positive total returns, vol-adjusted performance in both cases is only particularly strong in certain periods (such as the sharp G10 tightening cycle of 2022-2023). We see the driver of positive total returns in the ‘Hikers vs Cutters’ strategy as mostly a function of persistence in the pricing-in of hiking and cutting cycles over time. Daily average total FX returns from the strategy (~2.3bps/day) are around 4-5 times the size of the daily average shifts in rate differentials from following the same signals (~0.5bps/day). That ratio is slightly above the beta of daily returns in G10 Dollar pairs to shifts in rate differentials, and we suspect that a gradual underlying tailwind to currencies where more policy tightening is expected helps support the strategy’s average FX returns versus the moves implied by shifting rate differentials. records.text: 9 Visible copper inventory at record, we see build as part-shift, part-surplus (2) Source: Citi Research, Bloomberg, CME Group, ShFE, LME Stripping out seasonality, most gains in visible copper inventory over the last year have been deliveries to COMEX-registered warehouses in the US The US implied inventory build since March 2025 (initiation of S232 investigation) totals ~1.1Mt, including ~0.3 Mt implied shadow stock build With a no-tariff decision (or loss of belief in tariff by market) we could see some unwind of visible inventories in the US over the next 6- 12 months which can partly absorb forecast 2027 deficits. Such drawdowns would mostly reflect a rebalancing of global inventory distribution back to pre-Section 232 levels (including ex-US shadow restocking). The bull case risk is tariff imposition fuels further builds, or the US administration takes alternative steps to try and disincentivise a reversal of inventory flows and draws for strategic reasons. (Note the US had a strategic copper inventory of close to 1Mt in the early 1960s, at that time visible global inventory totalled ~3 months of consumption!) Prepared for Cayla Buettner

If the Fed moves in that direction, it risks de-anchoring inflation expectations and pushing the market to build up higher risk premium in the long end of the curve, eventually increasing real interest rates and with that the cost of servicing the debt. A Fed hike next week likely supports our long-end view T oday’s CPI print paints the perfect picture for the long end of the curve even if it does justify a rate hike at next week’s FOMC (our economists changed their call today to a hike; see US Economics - Disinflationary details of stronger August core CPI). The bulk of the 0.29% MoM core CPI print was the exceptional increase in wireless services (5.9% MoM which equates to almost 0.1% for the MoM core CPI print). The wireless story appears to be a one-off as vendors ended some unlimited grandfathered plans. The remainder of the CPI print limits the risk that the ‘neutral’ rate is above the implied Fed funds forwards of 4.5%, in our view. Shelter inflation continues to slow and there are no signs of higher energy prices passing through into goods prices (core goods only rose 0.11%MoM). Weaker shelter prints support our view as well, with primary rents up only 0.17% MoM and a 0.19% increase in OER (both down from 0.26% MoM). Note that on a YoY basis core CPI is still rapidly normalizing (Figure 4). Longer-term normalization should continue as well. For instance, airfares in core CPI YoY would be lower without high oil prices from the Iran conflict (Figure 5). This would eventually decline if WTI prices fall. records.text: M Update 4 Watch: Import Prices Swiss inflation surprised substantially to the upside this week while PMIs and GDP numbers were better than expected. Despite these surprises, EUR/CHF rallied through the 0.9450 level following a rise in front-end European yields after the September ECB meeting. We continue to expect CHF to strengthen broadly by year end as spot converges to long-term fair value, but the speed of convergence will likely be modulated by near-term movements in European energy prices, which have tracked closely with ECB pricing and euro area - Switzerland rate differentials. This week, we will be attentive to import prices, which may modulate the SNB's concern about EUR/CHF movements and potentially introduce the prospect of SNB purchases of CHF; we note that President Schlegel's recent communication has eschewed previous language regarding intervention.

FX: higher rates could prove counter-productive The ECB meeting was more hawkish than we expected, largely due to hawkish forecast revisions. The communication itself was broadly in line with our expectations, with the ECB declining to endorse market pricing. FX price action was mixed. The initial EUR reaction – shortly after the statement – was modestly positive, better seen in the crosses than in EUR-USD. However, despite higher yields, subsequent FX price action became more nuanced, particularly against the backdrop of higher energy prices. OAT and the peripheral spreads widened, while FX liquidity slightly worsened – higher yields may well prove counter-productive for the EUR from here. US PPI data likely provided some support to the USD as well. An ECB committed to preserving its inflation-fighting credibility while other central banks appear less committed has been supportive of the EUR. However, an ECB that ultimately over-tightens could dampen growth and become counterproductive for the currency. To be sure, our economists do not expect the ECB to deliver anything close to what is currently priced by markets. We retain a constructive medium-term view on the EUR but remain neutral for now, awaiting greater clarity on (1) energy prices and (2) the reaction function of other central banks, including the Fed.

BoJ hike expectations, technical factors and FX supply-demand behind the recent sharp JPY appreciation The recent sharp JPY appreciation was likely driven by BoJ rate hike expectations, technical factors and FX supply-demand, including anticipation of pension repatriation. USDJPY fell from around 164 to nearly 155 following coordinated US-Japan intervention at end-July, then rebounded to around 160 in early September before reversing again and briefly plunging into the 152s on 8 September. We believe the renewed JPY appreciation reflected stronger BoJ rate hike expectations, technical factors and anticipation of pension funds shifting back toward domestic assets. First, hawkish remarks by BoJ officials including Board Member Takata pushed market pricing for rate hikes by year-end from around 40bp in August to 45-50bp in September. Second, from a technical perspective, the break below the 155 support, which held through both the Golden Week and July interventions, opened the way for further downside. Third, JPY's FX supply- demand has improved with rounds of interventions. On the meeting itself, we see risks as broadly balanced, although ahead of the MPC, energy prices, global central-bank expectations and domestic data could materially alter market pricing and the skew of risks. On QT, we expect the decision to be largely a non-event for the gilt market, with the next-cycle envelope and maturity split likely to be broadly aligned with both our call and market consensus. LLC US Daily: Adding a Hike in September 11 September 2026 | 4:49PM EDT We now expect a 25bp hike at the September FOMC meeting next week (vs. a n hold previously). Additional hikes at later meetings are possible but are not our baseline. While today’s CPI report only raised our August core PCE forecast slightly to 0.26% and has not changed our fundamental inflation view, we think that the FOMC will want to avoid the market reaction that would likely follow from remaining on hold when the market is pricing a nearly 90% chance of a hike. We do not see a strong economic case for raising the funds rate. We continue to n think that all of the overshoot of the 2% target can be attributed to one-time factors whose impact is likely to fade, that the improvement in core PCE inflation to a roughly 2.5% pace over the last three months is an early sign of this, that the economy is not overheated, that inflation expectations are not at immediate risk of unanchoring, and that limited rate hikes are unlikely to appreciably offset the impact of supply shocks. We suspect that some FOMC participants will agree with this, and for that reason we see the Fed’s decision as less clear-cut than market pricing implies. But we suspect that most FOMC participants will worry about the potential n market reaction to not delivering a hike that recent Fed communication has guided the market to now almost fully price. It looks like minimal negotiations between Iran and the US are going with the US promising a patient strategy of sanctions and blockade while Iran is doing something similar in terms of military pressure on the GCC and US regional bases plus the imperfect blockage of the Straits. What we learned from the Russia-Ukraine war is that investor impatience for a solution and the “obvious” fact that the conflict is economically irrational does not mean a peace is coming before the next month-end/quarterly earnings/hedge fund redemption schedule. Tolls are our base case with the question for local investors only about the size of the toll What was unthinkable pre-war is now the CEEMEA Strategy base case: that the GCC will pay tolls on energy shipped through the Strait. Our best guess is $3/bbl for now and likely to rise going forward. If we rely on economic theory to assume that in the long term the oil price is the marginal cost of production and GCC oil production is at the bottom of the cost curve, then even a large toll does not change the cost of the marginal barrel. It will only change who keeps the profits, with energy buyers not paying the toll via higher prices. The Russia-Ukraine war shows us how a determined great power can keep fighting long after its ability to win a decisive victory has disappeared and can be sustained to avoid the appearance of a defeat. records.text: Adding a Hike in September We now expect a 25bp rate hike at the September FOMC meeting next week, rather than our previous expectation of no change. While today’s CPI report did not change our fundamental inflation view, we think that the FOMC will be reluctant to surprise a market now pricing a nearly 90% chance of a hike. Additional hikes at later meetings are possible but are not our baseline. We suspect that a majority of FOMC participants would prefer not to hike again at the October meeting, both because it comes just before the midterms and because those participants skeptical of the case for hiking would likely prefer that it at least be limited to a more gradual pace. By December, we think that further evidence of improvement in the inflation trend and greater distance from some of the key drivers of higher inflation, especially tariffs and the Iran war, will make another hike seem unnecessary. We do not see a strong economic case for raising the funds rate. We continue to think that all of the overshoot of the 2% target can be attributed to one-time factors whose impact is likely to fade, and that the improvement in core PCE inflation over the last three months is an early sign of this. Accounting for the likely effects of the methodological revisions that will be implemented this month, we estimate that the three-month annualized pace of core PCE inflation will be around 2.5% through August, though the exact impact of the revisions is uncertain. The Ugly The most adverse interpretation is that the program could potentially be interpreted as an early step toward a broader regime of financial intervention. Under this scenario, policymakers increasingly rely on balance-sheet policies and market intervention to contain borrowing costs rather than addressing the underlying drivers of fiscal deterioration. Such an approach would weaken price discovery, create a de facto fiscal policy put, and amplify moral hazard by reducing incentives to confront the fundamental issue: the trajectory of the fiscal deficit. Ultimately, the success of the buyback program depends on whether it addresses genuine market imperfection or attempts to counteract a market signal. If the problem is liquidity, intervention can help. If the problem is the fundamentals, intervention can only postpone the adjustment. What are the limits of fiscal policy? Fiscal positions deteriorated significantly across advanced economies in the aftermath of the pandemic. For several years, these vulnerabilities remained largely hidden by exceptionally low interest rates, abundant liquidity, and central-bank balance-sheet expansion. records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 3 backdrop in our current forecasts does not look strong enough to fuel inflationary pressures on its own. At the same time, we also see an upside risk to our inflation and growth projections. Energy prices, primarily natural gas, have moved higher, and the 2Q26 GDP print was revised up, with a composition, notably on the exports side, that looks supportive. Incorporating these risks, our view on the euro area economy could end up rather similar to the one presented by the ECB today. In such a scenario, the ECB might well decide to hike in December, provided actual inflation data would start to show signs of indirect effects. Focus on the data: The incoming data between now and the December meeting will be key ( Exhibit 2 ). What does the ECB need to see in the data to tighten further? Aside from energy prices remaining high, the growth data would need to continue to indicate strong activity. Here we would focus on the PMIs staying around the current levels and 3Q26 GDP remaining solid (MSe: 0.25%Q). As mentioned, core inflation should start showing signs of indirect effects of higher energy prices in the prints leading up to December - absence of these is an indication against further hikes. Food inflation and/or signs of a pass-through to wages will also be watched closely by the ECB in the run up to the December meeting. Nonetheless, the country is expected to continue showing good fiscal outcomes, driven by high nominal growth. The lack of a working majority has prevented the Spanish government from approving a state budget since taking office. Despite the willingness of the cabinet to make one last attempt to approve a 2027 budget – its final chance before the elections – earmarking a 1.8% deficit target, we think this target will be hard to achieve. We consider 2.1% more likely (closer to the deficit expectations of 2.3% from Banco de España). Looking ahead, next year’s general elections are unlikely to unblock the situation. Currently, polls suggest a minority government as the most likely result, but with little certainty on which side of the spectrum it will fall. Centre-right PP is leading the polls at 32%, with the incumbent centre-left-led coalition of PSOE + Sumar tracking a total of 32% of voting intentions as well (Politico poll of polls). records.text: 2Q Credit Fundamentals: Mostly Steady With 2Q earnings now largely in hand, we take stock of how aggregate fundamental credit metrics have evolved for North American and European IG and HY rated issuers. At the index level, fundamentals remain in a solid place. That said, under the surface, we find that the trend of elevated dispersion persists. Leverage and interest coverage Leverage for the median issuer in the North American market can be described as range-bound in IG and modestly worsening in HY. For example, while IG net leverage remains well below the pandemic era peak of 2020, excluding that period of disruption it has steadily climbed higher since 2011 (left panel, Exhibit 1). In our view, this reflects an increased willingness of management teams to strategically add leverage to their capital structures while staying firmly within IG territory. This can be seen in the steady growth of average deal sizes in the USD IG market from $792 million in 2010 to $1.7 billion in 2026. For the median HY issuer in North America, leverage has climbed higher over the past several quarters (again, left panel Exhibit 1). That said, it remains well below the peaks seen in the 2015 commodity disruption and the 2020 pandemic, and generally towards the lower end of the range of the post-financial crisis period. records.text: European Economic Perspectives11 September 2026 ab 11 (2) Request parliamentary authorisation before 19 December for a special law to collect existing taxes and – once the special law has been passed – adopt decrees to implement the appropriations established in last year's budget, essentially ensuring budget continuity. This happened at the end of both 2024 and 2025. The same option to request a special law applies if the Constitutional Council were to reject the implementation of a budget (that had been adopted by parliament) before 1 January. Lastly, in case of any other rejection of the budget law not foreseen by legislation, such as a systematic rejection of the budget bill or emergency measures, a Constitutional Council ruling from 1978 could apply. This requires the government and parliament to find a solution to ensure the functioning of the state, in essence by extending the previous year's budget. As a very last resort, the Constitution's Art. 16 grants the president exceptional powers in case "the institutions of the Republic, the independence of the Nation, the integrity of its territory or the fulfilment of its international commitments are under serious and immediate threat, and where the proper functioning of the constitutional public authorities is interrupted". However, it is unclear whether a budget crisis would qualify for such measures. Despite years of both fiscal and market-driven periphery outperformance, our fiscal scores indicate further narrowing between core/semi-core countries and the periphery (Fig. 1). This trend is driven by a "pincer movement": continued fiscal improvement in the periphery coupled with further deterioration in the core/semi-core regions (Fig. 2). What this means for the market is unambiguous: a further tightening of lower-rated countries’ spreads towards higher-rated ones, or in other words, a further flattening of the credit fly (Fig. 3). We have ran various forms of ‘convergence themed’ trades over the last 2-3 years. The last one held in portfolio is a short France in the Germany/France/Italy fly (see EGBs: Short belly in 10y ITA–FRA– GER credit fly), entered on 8 May. records.text: Please refer to important information at the end of the report and MAR disclosures What’s the purpose of this note? Our objective is to use a “quantamental” approach to identify 1–3 month directional ideas. We combine positioning and flow data with macro/idiosyncratic catalysts to move beyond purely discretionary or quantitative models. Positioning (stock vs flow): ’Stock’ measures crowding, identifying tomorrow’s vulnerabilities and potential contrarian opportunities. ‘Flow’ measures current directionality, helping us decide when to ride momentum or when to go against it. Roadmap: This is a work in progress, not a finished product. We will continue to integrate and enhance the data further to ensure our insights remain timely, relevant and tactical. Expect additional, high-frequency data to feature in these notes in the coming months. Metrics in focus*: We combine, normalize and standardize (z-score) various flow metrics across 1- and 3-month trailing windows: • Retail cash equities: 1-month trailing sum in stocks and ETFs, using data from our retail flow dataset (see launch note here) • Option premia: 1-month and 3-month trailing sum of net option premium traded (calls minus puts), normalized by total premium traded • ETF flow: 1-month and 3-month trailing sum of ETF flows, normalized by the AUM at the start of the trailing window • Short interest: shares held short, normalized by market cap • Crowding ranking: combined percentile scores derived from the above metrics. records.text: Although we do not think that it is necessary to raise the funds rate, we would expect a single 25bp rate hike to have only a modest effect on the economy. We suspect that some FOMC participants will agree with this assessment, and for that reason we see the Fed’s decision as less clear-cut than market pricing of a nearly 90% chance of a hike implies. But we suspect that most FOMC participants will worry about the potential market reaction to not delivering a hike that recent Fed communication has guided the market to now almost fully price. Chairman Warsh’s Jackson Hole speech, which took a hawkish angle on a range of topics, led the market to expect a hike if the inflation news was imperfect, and while today’s CPI report was not concerning, it was imperfect. As a result, the FOMC might worry about the consequences of not hiking for market perceptions of the Fed’s credibility and about the immediate reaction of longer-term interest rates. Recent increases in oil prices might also make FOMC voters who had previously been ambivalent a bit more open to hiking. And even some of those who share our inflation views have signaled fatigue with explaining why continued high inflation is not evidence of overheating and is likely to fade on its own, which might lead them to not oppose a hike even if they are skeptical of its purpose. Episodes of JPY strength always lead to concerns around potential unwind of EM carry positions. Carry strategies have done well for much of the year, even though with yen implied yields having risen, the overall realized carry-vol profile for funding in yen has moderated (Figure 4). Data from Tokyo Financial Exchange shows Japanese investor positioning most stretched in TRY (Figure 6). 3. The 'portfolio rebalancing' channel - vulnerability to Japanese repatriation. Japanese IIP holdings as of end 2025 put the biggest portfolio debt holdings within EM for Japanese investors in China, Mexico, Singapore, Poland, Korea and Malaysia (Figure 7). These amounts are relatively small compared with the overall size of local markets and/or total offshore bond holdings in Asia; but in terms of relative yield on offer – on a FX hedged basis – for Japanese real money investors, Asia is relatively poorly placed vs the likes of MXN, PLN and ZAR (Figure 8). BoJ: Faster hikes, higher terminal The continued rise in inflation expectations and the fact that inflation risks remain firmly tilted to the upside mean that monetary policy has entered a new, more difficult phase. Now that underlying inflation is around the 2% target, we believe the BoJ needs to pay greater attention to the risk of a structural overshoot. At the same time, the rate hikes delivered so far have not materially tightened financial conditions. The July surge in USD/JPY and subsequent US- Japan coordinated intervention have also raised the stakes around Japan’s defense of the yen. With fiscal policy retaining an expansionary bias, the burden of adjusting Japan’s policy mix falls primarily on the BoJ, at least in the near term. the sharp increase in real interest rates has brought debt sustainability back to the center of the policy debate. Absent meaningful fiscal consolidation, higher financing costs threaten to erode fiscal space and reduce governments' ability to respond to future economic downturns (see Exhibit 4, Exhibit 5). The recent AI-driven investment boom has accelerated this process, but not because it created the fiscal problem. Rather, it exposed it. By contributing to a rise in equilibrium real interest rates, the investment surge acted as a stress test for public finances. In this sense, AI is best viewed as the canary in the coal mine, not the root cause of the problem. The underlying challenge is that many advanced economies entered this period with fiscal positions that had become increasingly reliant on an environment of unusually low borrowing costs.

records.text: US Rates Weekly 11 September 2026 Citi Research 17 6m30y contingent payer as cheap hedge for higher rates/lower SPX As an alternative to owning long-dated vanilla swaption payers that have already meaningfully outperformed on the swaption surface and in skew, we recommend owning hybrid OTM payers on 30y rate contingent on lower SPX as a cheap hedge for the fiscal tail risk. We find the hybrid 30y payers with SPX contingent feature particularly attractive because its pricing is reflective of the current cross asset correlation, which could realize at a much more negative level in a worsening fiscal tail risk scenario. Looking at the realized 1m correlation between the daily Tsy 30y yield change and daily SPX % change, we see that it has fluctuated between positive and negative and center around 0% (Figure 33). More importantly, the realized correlation appears to have inversely tracked the change in the Tsy 30y yield, where rate sell-offs have corresponded with decline in the yield/equity correlation. The most notable instance was earlier this year in May when 30y yield reached a new multi-year high and the realized correlation turned extremely negative before normalizing. While this inverse relationship between 30y yield and yield/equity correlation might be counter to the convention thinking of higher yields/higher growth/higher risky assets, it makes intuitive sense given the unresolved long-run fiscal/supply worries that is currently dominating the market narrative. records.text: Gauging the Impact of Government Bond Supply on Bond Yields China’s growth momentum has softened notably in recent months, and the pace of fiscal spending was sluggish in the first seven months of the year. Against this backdrop, the July Politburo meeting called for “accelerating the progress of fiscal expenditures and the spending of bond proceeds”. Government bond issuance – including both central and local government bonds – has started to accelerate. In addition, the RMB800bn New Policy-Based Financing Instrument (NPBFI), announced earlier this year, has started to be allocated. We expect total bond net issuance (both central and local) to rise meaningfully in the coming months, with the monthly net issuance reaching 1% of GDP per month during September–October1, up from a monthly average of around 0.6% of GDP in H1; Exhibit 1). The recent rise in 1-year CGB yields, alongside still-subdued long-end yields, raises the question of how a heavier issuance calendar may affect the level and shape of the CGB curve (Exhibit 2). In principle, additional long-term government bond supply should point to a bear steepener, but the transmission in China is less straightforward. PBOC liquidity accommodation, the pace at which fiscal proceeds are disbursed, and the extent to which markets have already priced in additional fiscal easing all matter. July MAS core CPI (excluding accommodation and private transport) rose 2.0%yoy, below the market consensus of 2.2%. In annual terms, while core goods inflation rose to the mid-2% level due to a 17% increase in electricity tariffs, core services inflation remained below 2%. On a 3M/3M SAAR basis, a key indicator utilized by MAS to gauge inflation momentum, both headline and core inflation moderated somewhat (Figure 2). This may imply that the positive output gap arising from the AI cycle is still not translating into demand-side inflationary pressure, amid negative growth in unit labour costs (Figure 3). July retail sales also missed market consensus, rising by only 1.5%yoy due to a contraction in food & alcohol sales. Overall, whilst Singapore’s economy is benefiting significantly from the global AI boom, we do not see the recent economic data are strong enough for MAS to tighten monetary policy for a third consecutive quarter. In mid-August, the Ministry of Trade and Industry (MTI) upgraded its 2026 growth forecast to 4.5-5.5% from 2.0-4.0%. MAS is now forecasting both headline and core CPI inflation to average 1.5-2.5% this year. records.text: ab 11 September 2026 Global Research US Equity & Derivatives Strategy Midterm elections cheat sheet: What do equity markets typically do and what is priced? Midterm election rally anomaly The S&P 500 has rallied an average of 14.5% (median 16.4%) from end-August to end- March during midterm election years since 1950. The market has typically been choppy from August-end until early October, with a median decline of -1.4%, before the market starts to rally through year-end and into the next year. The rally in US equities around midterm elections has historically been much stronger than the average returns in all other years. Equity volatility follows a similar course – September and October have historically been the most volatile months on record since 1928, particularly during midterm election years, but volatility ultimately normalizes significantly post-elections into year-end. Gridlock is good Midterms have resulted in the President's party losing an average of 25 House seats and 3 Senate seats. The incumbent President has lost one or both chambers in 8 midterms (5 of which have occurred over the last 5 elections). Betting markets show the odds of Democrats winning the House at >85%, while Senate odds show just above 50-50, slightly in favor of the Democrats (~49% implied odds for full Democrat control of Congress). Setting aside the midterms, a credible case for passing in October is that it takes time to observe the effects of the hike on the economy. Inflation continues to look supply-shock driven, and as such we don’t foresee a protracted hiking cycle extending into next year. The case for a hike next week is simply that core PCE inflation has been above 3% every month this year and has made little recent progress heading towards 2%. There is a case for patience. We estimate that through August three-month annualized core PCE is 2.7%—not great, but moving in the right direction. Inflation expectations are stable and there are no signs of overheating in the labor market. That case might have won the day, but so far, the new Chair has not spelled out why one should expect a return to 2% inflation. Colombia’s bond yield fair value We estimate the fair value for Colombia’s 10-year government bond yield using an ordinary least squares regression. The model is based on monthly data from January 2008 through August 2026 and includes three explanatory variables: the US 10-year Treasury yield, Colombia’s 12-month-ahead consensus inflation expectation, and the country’s primary budget balance. Together, these variables capture the main external, inflation, and fiscal drivers of long-term Colombian rates. The model has an R-squared of 0.87, indicating that it explains a large share of the historical variation in the 10-year yield. Our baseline scenario implies modestly lower bond yields The scenario analysis points to a wide range of possible fair values, driven by Colombia’s inflation and fiscal outlook. In our baseline scenario, 2027 inflation reaches 4.9% and the primary deficit stands at 3.0% of GDP, generating a fair-value estimate of 12.15% for the 10-year bond yield. In the bullish scenario, inflation falls to 4.5% and the primary deficit narrows to 2.3% of GDP, lowering fair value to 11.5%. In the bearish scenario, inflation rises to 5.5% and the primary deficit widens to 3.5% of GDP, pushing fair value to 13.0%.

Following our Q&A note from mid-July, this note focuses on four themes, along with 25 charts and two boxes. First, we expect the upcoming 2027 budget round to deliver only marginal deficit reduction, with the primary objective likely to be securing parliamentary approval (with the risk of a higher budget deficit in 2027 if no budget is passed). Second, we review the latest opinion polls (and the UBS Evidence Lab Political Probability Monitor, based on betting markets), which show Marine Le Pen from the far-right Rassemblement National (RN) leading. Third, we summarise what we have learned in terms of policy proposals by the main candidates. And fourth, we outline key dates to watch (with party primaries and congresses as well as upcoming ratings decisions in focus). Our rate strategists argue that fiscal concerns and increasing inflationary pressures could see OAT-bund spreads exceed 90bp in the near term. See also this note from our credit strategists. Despite this rapid increase in collateral funding needs, SOFR fixes have remained relatively low. We show this divergence in Figure 16, where we plot our preferred liquidity needs proxy (private T-bill outstanding minus reserves) against SOFR/IORB. These two series moved relatively close together through most of last year; however, they have been diverging this summer. In our view, the Fed’s RMPs pushed reserves back to a lightly abundant regime, which in turn reduced the sensitivity of repo rates to changes in T-bill supply. In Figure 17 we plot weekly changes in private T-bills minus reserves against changes in SOFR/IORB, and we find that the correlation between the two series has fallen significantly since July and is now near zero. With reserves likely to move sideways for the rest of the year, we expect this low-correlation environment between private T-bill outstanding and SOFR fixes to persist for the upcoming months. Or in other words, we think we’ll continue to be in a lightly abundant reserves regime for the rest of the year. records.text: 16 The Global Thinker | 10 September 2026 As a result, markets may view the Fed as having implicitly raised the bar for remaining on hold in September. Absent a meaningful downside surprise in inflation, the Committee could find it increasingly difficult to avoid validating the signal embedded in Warsh's remarks. The reaction function is the nominal anchor Why is it so important to explain the reaction function? Because inflation is ultimately a monetary phenomenon, and every monetary regime requires a nominal anchor. Under monetary targeting, the money supply served that role. If money growth was fixed at 3%, inflation would converge in the long run to money growth adjusted for the economy's trend growth rate. Under an interest-rate-based regime, however, the price level is not pinned down by the money supply itself. Instead, determinacy requires a systematic feedback rule describing how policy responds to the evolution of inflation and economic activity. In practice, the reaction function becomes the nominal anchor of the economy. A poorly understood reaction function weakens that anchor, increasing uncertainty not only about the future path of interest rates but, more importantly, about the future path of inflation. The result is greater macroeconomic volatility and a higher risk that inflation expectations become unanchored. records.text: financial conditions being sufficiently accommodative to support a surge in investment demand. Viewed through this lens, the increase in real rates reflects a rise in the equilibrium real interest rate, or r*. As r* increases, a given policy rate becomes less restrictive over time. Put differently, the policy stance may be easing relative to the economy's underlying equilibrium even as market interest rates move higher. This interpretation is particularly relevant for the United States, where investment demand appears to be the dominant driver of higher real yields. The picture is different for economies that are not experiencing a comparable investment boom. In those cases, the increase in real interest rates resembles more closely an exogenous tightening of financial conditions imported from abroad. Higher global yields raise borrowing costs, tighten financial conditions, and weigh on economic activity without the offsetting benefit of stronger domestic investment demand. A different interpretation is required when rising yields are driven by higher risk premia rather than by stronger demand for capital. In that case, the market is requiring greater compensation to finance a given level of investment, whether due to fiscal concerns, inflation uncertainty, or other sources of risk. The economic implications are materially different. An increase in real rates driven by higher r* reflects stronger underlying demand and may imply less restrictive policy than commonly assumed.

That interpretation became more difficult to sustain once subsequent communications were considered. A program originally presented as a market-liquidity tool increasingly appeared to be associated with an effort to influence the pricing of long-term government bonds. The shift in perception intensified when Secretary Bessent suggested that the Treasury could ultimately repurchase as much as $1 trillion of long-dated securities while arguing that market participants were operating with incomplete information. The implication was that long-term yields were deviating from values consistent with underlying fundamentals. When combined with concerns that Japanese intervention could result in Treasury sales and spill over into the U.S. rates market, the broader narrative surrounding the intervention changed considerably. The challenge is that intervention cannot permanently offset weak fundamentals. Indeed, if markets perceive an intervention as inconsistent with underlying economic realities, the opposite effect can occur. Investors may choose to test policymakers' resolve, resulting in greater rather than lower volatility. The market reaction following the announcement broadly fits this pattern, with an initial rally in Treasuries subsequently giving way to a reversal. records.text: icy. In other words, there are expectations in the market for either rate hikes at consecutive meetings or for a 50bp hike. We think this goes too far. Now that the yen has stopped depreciating this is even more the case. While the BoJ has no need to deny market pricing for a rate hike each quarter, it also has no incentive to encourage even stronger pricing. The policy rate is expected to reach 150bp either at the December meeting or the January meeting, and this will depend upon the market environment at the time, including forex. The biggest focus is whether or not the Fed will hike by year-end. Where the Japanese policy rate goes after reaching 150bp will also depend considerably on the Fed. If the BoJ is forced to hike each quarter, it would be appropriate for pricing to reflect a high terminal rate. However, whether or not the policy rate will actually reach that level would be a separate issue. We continue to forecast a terminal rate of 200bp. This is consistent with the potential growth rate comparison with the US and eurozone and with the medium- to long-term outlook for the economy. In addition, the Takaichi government targets high-pressure economics. The BoJ will not want to foster inflation, but we think it will probably put up with slightly high inflation and a slightly weak yen. records.text: What risks would waiting for too long to address the fiscal trajectory present? A classic debt crisis where falling confidence in the ability or willingness of the government to repay its debt drives up interest rates and worsens debt dynamics is unlikely because the US issues debt in dollars, sets its own monetary policy, and has a flexible exchange rate. But we see two other risks. The main risk for investors is that if debt servicing costs or the necessary deficit reduction become large and painful enough, there could be pressure on the Fed to keep rates too low, resulting in high inflation. Another risk is that an unfavorable debt situation might limit the willingness of policymakers to fight recessions with fiscal stimulus. Could AI Offer an Easier Way Out? How much would a larger productivity boost from AI help? Our baseline economic forecast assumes that AI will lift real GDP growth to 2.3-2.4% through 2035, above most consensus and institutional forecasts but close to the median forecast for a moderate AI adoption scenario from a recent survey of economists, AI professionals, and expert forecasters. We consider an alternative in which AI instead raises GDP growth to 3%, with a five-year phase-in, five years of 3% growth, and a five-year phase-out. records.text: Across US Treasuries, agency MBS, and USD IG we expect longer-term (i.e. ex-Treasury bills) net supply to the private sector of $2.6tn in 2026, up about $50bn from 2025. We expect that to rise to $2.85n in 2027 (Exhibit 1). In 10y equivalent terms, we estimate that gross supply to the private sector (adjusting for UST buybacks) will be $5tn in 2026 (up $450bn year-over-year) and $5.2tn in 2027 (Exhibit 2). To put those numbers into historical perspective, both would be record highs in dollar terms, but are more typical of the post-pandemic issuance picture after normalizing by nominal GDP . We estimate the prior peak in notional net supply across these markets was just above $2.8tn in 2024, which saw a much sharper jump in longer-term net supply with the Fed in the midst of quantitative tightening and Treasury concluding its most recent round of auction size increases. Our expected composition of longer-term net supply this year and next is far more balanced between Treasuries and IG in particular, reflecting both Treasury’s heavier reliance on T-bills and the meaningful rise in IG supply. Normalized by nominal GDP , 2021 was the peak in net supply at 10.8% versus our 8-to-8.5% projections for this year and next. 2021 was also the previous peak for gross supply in 10y equivalent terms, both on an outright basis and normalized by GDP . records.text: M Idea 8 The effective tariff rate, tariff receipts, and refunds Tariffs averaged 6.7% over May-July, and we expect that it will rise to near 10% USTR's final forced-labor Section 301 action was broadly in line with our expectations. Effective July 24, the agency imposed additional tariffs on imports from 60 economies, setting a 10% duty on economies that have adopted, partially adopted, or committed to adopt a forced-labor import prohibition and a 12.5% duty on most others. The final action also preserves several key carve-outs, including goods already subject to Section 232 tariffs, USMCA-compliant imports, and a range of general and country-specific product exemptions. Overall, both the tariff structure and the principal exemptions closely resemble the proposal, reinforcing our expectation that Section 301 would serve as the broad country-level tariff floor. We continue to expect that the statutory effective tariff rate will converge toward ~10% by year-end. In the July 2026 data, the effective tariff rate is estimated at ~6.5%. Over the past three months of detailed trade data (May, June and July), the tariff rate has averaged 6.7%. There has been a recent escalation of trade disputes with Canada, and section 338 tariffs have been applied on approximately $20bn of Canadian imports. records.text: more recent joint intervention by Japan and the United States differs from previous episodes and can be analyzed through three lenses: the good, the bad, and the ugly. The Good The participation of the United States enhances the credibility of the intervention and strengthens its signaling and coordination effects. Market participants are naturally more reluctant to challenge an intervention that carries the backing of both countries. Moreover, access to the Federal Reserve's FIMA (Foreign and International Monetary Authorities) repo facility allows Japan to obtain dollar liquidity without liquidating its Treasury holdings. This reduces the risk that foreign-exchange intervention translates into large-scale Treasury sales, thereby limiting potential spillovers into the U.S. bond market and improving financial-market stability. The Bad For intervention to have durable effects, it must ultimately be supported by changes in underlying fundamentals. While the Bank of Japan is expected to continue normalizing monetary policy, there is little evidence that Japan is prepared to implement the magnitude of monetary and fiscal adjustments required to alter the longer-term outlook for the currency. As a result, intervention is unlikely to address the root causes of yen weakness. Instead, it risks creating moral hazard by encouraging market participants to expect periodic official support while delaying the necessary adjustment process. We think the 10y OAT-Bund spread could reach 130bp in the RN-win scenario, if we assume that the market tests the credibility of the government’s spending plans – known increases in pension spending and tax cuts, weighted against unknown spending cuts. In a centrist-win scenario, we think the spread could fall to 50bp, assuming that the budget is viewed as credible, alongside an assumption that structural reforms end up being passed. We cannot rule out the possibility of another hung parliament, which could mean that the 10y OAT-Bund spread goes back to its post-June 2024 trading range (55-90bp). Developments in the polls will be key for how spreads move as the election approaches. Italy: Unlike France, we think the range of fiscal outcomes arising from Italian elections is small. records.text: The Global Thinker | 10 September 2026 19 Is the steeper curve signaling less policy credibility or a policy mistake? Conventional wisdom holds that a bear steepening driven by higher inflation breakevens reflects concerns about central-bank credibility, whereas a steepening driven by higher real rates reflects either an increase in the equilibrium real interest rate, r*, or a higher fiscal risk premium. While this distinction is useful, it can also be misleading. If markets believe the Federal Reserve is falling behind the curve but remains ultimately committed to restoring price stability, then fewer hikes today imply more aggressive tightening tomorrow. In that scenario, a steeper real yield curve, particularly at the front end and in the belly of the curve, may simply reflect expectations of a more forceful policy response in the future rather than a rise in equilibrium real rates or fiscal concerns. A similar logic applies to inflation breakevens. Their behavior cannot be interpreted independently from expectations regarding the Fed's reaction function. When Warsh assumed the chairmanship, his initial press conference was perceived as more hawkish than expected. Inflation breakevens declined as real yields rose by more than nominal yields. records.text: would make us change our mind? If 10y USTs are not cheap today, what would make them cheap? The most obvious path would be a material deterioration in the growth outlook. As we have argued, most of this year's repricing has come through the expectations component rather than term premium. A weaker labor market or a more meaningful slowdown in activity would likely pull down the expected path of policy rates and, by extension, yields. That does not appear imminent. Economic data are no longer surprising to the upside as consistently as they did earlier in the year, but consensus expectations do not look optimistic enough to leave much room for a large downside surprise. A second possibility is a further rise in term premium. A meaningful increase, whether driven by domestic concerns or spillovers from global bond markets, could push yields to levels that begin to weigh on broader financial conditions. At some point, higher yields would tighten conditions enough to weaken risk assets, slow economic activity and ultimately create demand for duration. We do not believe we are there yet. Bottom line: We think the Fed will hike, and we’re comfortable with our forecast that it will. Barring a very weak August CPI print, markets are likely to i) view a hold as a policy error, i.e., an unduly dovish stance in the face of sticky inflation, and ii) impact the Fed at the long end of the yield curve. Statement: tweaks to justify the expected hike We see a few potential tweaks to the FOMC statement. If the Fed hikes, we think the language around inflation will be modified to rationalize the move. For example, the statement might note that progress on inflation has slowed or that the rate increase was aimed at delivering price stability. records.text: Japan Viewpoint | 11 September 2026 5 BoJ: The policy challenge has changed The continued rise in inflation expectations and the fact that inflation risks remain firmly tilted to the upside mean that monetary policy has entered a new, more difficult phase. For the first two years of the BoJ's normalization process, the focus was on re-anchoring inflation from below. This also justified a gradual pace of policy normalization. However, now that underlying inflation is around the 2% target, we believe the BoJ needs to pay greater attention to the risk of a structural overshoot. At the same time, the 1ppt cumulative rate hikes delivered so far have not materially tightened financial conditions. In fact, bank lending is accelerating (Exhibit 9), while real borrowing costs remain below pre-COVID levels (Exhibit 10). This is one reason behind growing support for faster rate hikes among Policy Board members in recent months, as moving too slowly risks leaving financial conditions overly accommodative at a time when underlying inflation is already close to target (see BoJ Watch: Faster hikes, higher terminal, 14 August 2026). The Federal Reserve was beginning to face a growing credibility challenge, and the Jackson Hole speech appeared aimed at arresting that deterioration. Nevertheless, markets are likely to continue testing the Fed's commitment to restoring and maintaining price stability. Chairman Warsh's initial press conference was not particularly informative. While reaffirming the Fed's commitment to price stability, it offered little insight into the strategy required to achieve it. The Jackson Hole speech represented an improvement by explicitly re-establishing 2% PCE inflation as the policy objective. However, it still fell short of clearly articulating the Fed's reaction function. Although Warsh reiterated that the policy rate remains the primary instrument for delivering price stability, he provided little discussion of how balance-sheet policy fits within the broader framework. More importantly, while he shared his assessment of the economy and suggested that inflation currently represents a greater concern than employment, he stopped short of explaining how those views would translate into future policy decisions. In practice, a reaction function is not defined by policymakers' objectives, but by how policy responds to incoming data and evolving risks. records.text: The Global Thinker | 10 September 2026 17 stated objective and the available instruments. Ignoring that tension risks undermining the credibility of the target itself. Central banks can have predictable reaction functions without having predictable policy paths. Good central banking does not require telling markets where interest rates are going. It requires explaining why rates will ultimately go wherever they need to go. When the reaction function is well understood, markets can form their own expectations without relying on explicit policy commitments. Viewed through this lens, the Jackson Hole speech largely compensated for the uninformative and confusing July press conference. The positive market reaction may therefore have reflected the low bar established after July rather than a fundamental improvement in communication. Warsh is now effectively back to square one. records.text: A Hike Without a Signal? On Friday, we added a 25bp rate hike at this week’s September FOMC meeting to our forecast following the August CPI report. The CPI report had little impact on our inflation view but pushed market pricing of the probability of a hike to nearly 90%, which puts pressure on the FOMC to deliver a hike to avoid the market reaction that would likely follow from remaining on hold. Our key expectation for this week is that the FOMC will be careful not to signal that further hikes are necessarily coming, either in the statement or in the dots, where we expect a narrow majority to show one hike this year. We Do Not See a Strong Economic Case for a Rate Hike We do not see a strong economic case for raising the funds rate. We estimate that all of the overshoot of the 2% target can be attributed to one-time factors whose impact is likely to fade (Exhibit 1), and we see the improvement in core PCE inflation from June through August to an annualized pace of around 2.5%, inclusive of the likely impact of the upcoming methodological revisions, as early evidence of this. We also do not see high inflation as particularly broad-based. While more categories than usual have seen prices grow at a 3%+ annualized rate over the last six months (Exhibit 2, left), as Chairman Warsh noted in his Jackson Hole speech, the share looks more comparable to past periods of 2% inflation once we net out estimated tariff effects (Exhibit 2, right), which are likely now largely behind us. Meanwhile, CPI inflation edged higher, with CPI rising to 0.8% yoy and PPI accelerating to 3.8% yoy, supported primarily by supply-side factors and higher upstream prices. That said, after the oil spike, we expect disinflationary pressures to re-emerge, as weak domestic demand continues to weigh on underlying price dynamics. Japan: Strong wage growth data; What we learned at Japan Conference 2026 The preliminary July Monthly Labour Survey showed robust wage growth, as total cash earnings per worker rose 4.7% yoy, the strongest growth in roughly 30 years and above the 3.8% market consensus. Case 1: March 2020 liquidity crisis in the US In March 2020, the US Treasury market went under a lot of pressure as the COVID shock intensified and the demand for cash exploded. Institutional investors, in particular leveraged hedge funds, foreign official institutions and mutual funds sold Treasuries aggressively to raise cash and meet redemptions and margin calls. The flow of selling was so big that dealers quickly hit their balance sheet constraints and could not absorb the unprecedented volume of selling. Liquidity in the Treasury market collapsed and bid-offers increased sharply, and with that volatility, feeding back into higher margin calls and the need for fire selling Treasuries. Cash-futures pricing got severely distorted, forcing leveraged hedge funds exposed to arbitrage the cash-futures basis to sell. The key point is that the selling pressure on US Treasuries was not driven by a deterioration in fundamentals but a need to raise cash. To restore market liquidity, the Fed intervened by massively expanding repo operations and purchased all the US Treasuries and agency securities that the market wanted to sell, effectively using its balance sheet as a replacement of the dealers’ balance sheets, becoming the buyer of last resort until liquidity was restored. records.text: M Idea 14 FX Strategy David Adams, Alex Scholefield With little priced for action from the BoE at this meeting, we think the bigger driver of GBP’s performance in the coming weeks will relate to carry, fiscal risk premium, and energy prices. Carry remains an important factor that has limited weakness despite what we think is a generally bearish investor perception around the currency. While Bank rate fails to offer similar carry as other G10 currencies like NOK and AUD, it remains elevated compared to most European peers which, coupled with low implied volatility on crosses, implies that GBP shorts are expensive to hold. For example, the implied negative carry on a vol-adjusted basis for EUR/GBP longs is roughly equal to that of USD/JPY shorts, a popular pair for carry trades (Exhibit 17 ). The result is that, in the absence of clear negative catalysts or a rise in implied volatility, GBP shorts are expensive and challenging to express. This can keep GBP supported all else equal. That said, we do see scope for risks for GBP to rise, both in the near-term and medium- term. In the near-term we see capacity for GBP-negative risk premium to increase by 3 percentage points. Exhibit 18 shows EUR/GBP’s trading relative to what 2y OIS implies as its fair value using this methodology. records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 7 Labour market: The key release will be the LPC's Volumes | Stabilising at 0: The REC, the PMI and the DMP survey are (for now) signalling a flatlining, as opposed to a declining headcount in the year ahead. The robustness of UK growth - we think largely a result of global growth tailwinds - in face of the energy shock this year does leave us a bit less worried about the labour market risks. Ongoing repricing in commodity markets will test the said robustness, however. But, all in all, labour demand seems to have stabilised at stagnating levels. To us, this still looks bearish, particularly given firming evidence of rising labour productivity growth and declining unit labour costs growth. For next week's data, we forecast -5k payrolls, a drop in vacancies to 700k, and a jobless rate at 4.9%, although with risks of the number rounding up to 5%. The slack keeps on building, slowly and steadily. We note that per the ONS, recent sampling errors that impacted LFS data ought to be resolved in the July variant. Workforce Jobs Survey should also be released next week. Pay growth | More of the same: We see private sector ex-bonus pay growth at 2.8%3M/Y, with whole economy regular pay growth at 3.5%3M/Y; both unchanged vs. 2Q26. We expect whole economy total pay growth (i.e. bonus inclusive) at 3.9%3M/Y. records.text: Please refer to important information at the end of the report and MAR disclosures 11 September 2026 1 EM rates: Stopping out of ZAR front-end flattener Our ZAR year-end vs 1y1y flattener has reached its stop-loss and we close it for a 21bp loss. With the start of the war in the Middle East, the South African Reserve Bank’s initial reaction function was to remain proactive and deliver policy tightening in response to the energy price shock. Hence, we initiated a front -end flattener trade idea ahead of the May MPC meeting (see South Africa: Proactive SARB to flatten front-end rates, dated 6 May). Despite May’s rate hike, the SARB did not follow through in July and kept rates unchanged despite market pricing a full hike ahead of the meeting. We still expect the SARB to revert to a more hawkish reaction function on 23 September (see South Africa: SARB stays on hold, but likely to hike in September, 23 July). However, the curve is struggling to price front-loaded hikes after the dovish surprise in July, and the FRA curve remains steep. As a result, our year-end vs 1y1y flattener (dates: 5 February 2027 start 3m vs 5 May 2027 start 1y) has reached its stop-loss level. We close the trade with a 21bp loss (or USD210,000 for USD10,000 DV01) at 11bp. records.text: Euro Area Watch | 10 September 2026 3 The link to US term premia is something we had flagged as part of the price action in Jun-mid August (see Liquid Insight: US bond pressures Europe rates 26 August 2026). However, when we examine the additional selloff of the past month, we find that the 32bp rise in 10y Bund yields can be fully explained by the 47bp repricing in 1y1y €str OIS, considering the beta of c.0.7 recorded since March, at the start of the US-Iran war. To us this means that without some change in ECB communication that would reduce the sensitivity of front-end rates to energy prices, 10y EGB yields are likely to remain under sizeable bearish pressure. Lagarde noted that the ECB “are monitoring attentively what is happening [in bond yields], particularly in the long-end”. This also includes country spreads although she declined to comment on it in more detail. That language could represent the beginning of a shift to a more supportive communication, but concrete options would still need to be mentioned (eg. willingness to reconsider the path of QT / provide new tools to support bonds). Lastly, no comments regarding changes to MRR (Minimum Reserve Requirement) or reserve renumeration were made, thus we look forward to the October meeting when more information may be provided given their previous communication of a decision being made “by autumn”.
