records.text: BoJ Monetary Policy Meeting Preview 11 September 2026 Citi Research 2 A rate hike at next week's BoJ meeting is widely expected. We revised our BoJ outlook in early August following the coordinated US-Japan currency intervention (see: Japan Economics - Regime shift in BoJ policy). Previously, in order to align with the reflationary Takaichi administration, we had assumed two further rate hikes—in December this year and June next year—at a pace of once every six months, with a terminal rate of 1.5%. Following the coordinated intervention, however, we judged that the containment of yen weakness by the US and Japanese authorities had entered a new phase, and we now expect four rate hikes—in September this year and January, June, and December next year—with a terminal rate of 2.0% (Figure 1). That said, the future path of BoJ rate hikes will depend significantly on Fed policy. Our house view assumes the Fed will remain on hold for the remainder of this year, but should the Fed raise rates within the year contrary to our forecast there is a high likelihood that the BoJ would also hike in December rather than January. Should the Fed enter a rate hike cycle, the BoJ would likely be compelled to hike at a quarterly pace, increasing the probability of the terminal rate exceeding 2%. Forward guidance is in the eye of the beholder There is considerable confusion about what forward guidance actually means and how it differs from a reaction function. Forward guidance provides information about the future path of policy. A reaction function, by contrast, explains how policymakers will adjust policy as economic conditions evolve. The distinction is important because one concerns future outcomes, while the other concerns the decision-making process that generates those outcomes. Forward guidance is a communication tool designed to influence expectations about future monetary policy, particularly policy rates. Importantly, there is a significant difference between calendar-based and state-contingent guidance. An example of the former is: "rates will remain at their current level for the rest of the year." An example of the latter is: "rates will remain low until unemployment falls below 5%." The second statement preserves substantially more flexibility because it conditions future policy on the state of the economy rather than on a predetermined timeline. Explaining the reaction function is a different exercise altogether. It requires describing how the Federal Reserve evaluates the state of the economy, weighs competing risks, and responds to evolving macroeconomic conditions. The top 20% income cohort, college-educated group, and 55+ cohort each account for around 80% of household equity wealth. For the top income cohort, equity wealth is roughly six times annual labor income, so relatively modest asset-price gains can offset the spending effects of a temporary decline in labor income. Warsh's justification for abandoning forward guidance is that he wants markets to process information independently and form their own expectations. In his view, the Federal Reserve can learn from market prices only if those prices reflect investors' independent assessments of the economy rather than attempts to reverse-engineer Fed communication. The challenge is that market participants respond to incentives. Their objective is not to price what the Fed should do, but rather what they expect the Fed will do. If the Fed fails to provide a sufficiently clear description of its reaction function, that uncertainty will inevitably be reflected in asset prices. As a result, market prices will contain not only information about economic fundamentals, but also uncertainty about the Fed's own decision-making process. This makes the Fed's inference problem more difficult rather than easier. Markets are perfectly capable of pricing policy mistakes. Even when investors disagree with the likely policy path, they have every incentive to price the path they expect policymakers to follow. Consequently, observed market prices may reflect anticipated policy errors as much as underlying economic conditions. The less clearly the Fed communicates its reaction function, the harder it becomes to disentangle those two effects and extract meaningful information from market signals. In

BOND WATCH Mexico Bonds: Attractive Long-End Value Figure 6 5yr bond yield vs. 1yr implied rate gap We continue to see relative value in Mexican bonds. The gap between the five-year government bond yield and the one-year implied policy rate indicates how investors are compensated beyond front -end carry: a narrow gap suggests returns are concentrated at the short end, while a wider gap reflects additional term compensation for macro risks, including inflation and fiscal risk premia . Mexico currently has the widest gap in our EM sample, well above that of the US. Although fiscal risks remain, the 2027 budget reduces the near-term likelihood of a downgrade to speculative grade; as an investment -grade sovereign, Mexico therefore offers an attractive long -end risk premium. In addition, we believe the market is pricing an overly aggressive policy -rate path, further strengthening the case for long-duration exposure. Source: State Street Markets, Bloomberg. Even taking official projections for granted, expenditure on old age in Italy is set to rise until around 2050, meaning that more fiscal adjustments will be needed. records.text: New York Fed reportedly sold EURJPY during the intervention at end-July, but no significant change has been observed in the SOMA account’s holdings of EUR or JPY. The intervention was therefore likely funded using the ESF’s holdings of foreign currency and foreign-currency-denominated assets (a combined USD4.4bn in JPY and EUR; Figure 13). If so, the effective size of the US intervention was likely well below the “USD5-10bn” reportedly noted in Treasury Secretary Bessent’s memo (Reuters, 31 July). In short, while the US again played an important signaling role in the coordinated intervention, Japan appears to have provided most of the actual funding. Although the need has receded, Japan still has ample capacity for further FX intervention. In a 31 August interview with CNBC, Treasury Secretary Bessent said, “it’s my belief that the Japanese government and that the BOJ will do the things that will lead to a stronger yen. ” This could be interpreted as signaling that the initiative for further JPY-strengthening measures and, if necessary, FX intervention now rests with the Japanese authorities. The JPY’s recent appreciation has reduced the need for intervention, but even after conducting the largest intervention on record in 2026, the MoF still held USD1.09trn in foreign reserves as of end-June (Figure 14). records.text: ab 11 September 2026 Global Research Global Strategy Rates Map - This repricing is not over Low bar for hikes given energy risks and growth We continue to think that the bar for further central bank hikes is low . The ongoing normalisation of monetary policy is bringing bond markets closer to their pre-2008 regime. Central banks are unlikely to look through another energy shock. Growth has remained surprisingly resilient, global equities are up 11% year-to-date, private-sector borrowing is stirring and capex is broadening. Against that backdrop, policymakers have little incentive to tolerate a renewed inflation impulse from the energy complex. Tversky and Kahneman (1974) warn that adjusting views from an anchor is usually effective, but can lead to systematic and predictable errors, very much in line with the persistence of the forecast errors of one-year ahead 10-year yields since the 2022-23 tightening cycle (Figure 2O n e - y e a r a h e a d f o r e c a s t e r r o r s o f B l o o m b e r g c o n s e n s u s ). Why repricing is not over yet? The move in oil prices back towards $70/bbl has proved temporary. As the US midterms approach, oil could remain near $100/bbl or move higher if supply disruptions intensify. Moving back from data-dependence to risk management is a tightening in financial condi- tions. We have held a steepening bias to the broader curve on the view that further RBA rates required inflation to realize stronger than RBA forecasts (which we haven’t expected). A pre-emptive tightening breaks that framework and so we close the ACGB 3s/10s futures steepener and paid position in AUD 10Y EFP at a small loss and gain, respectively. We raise the benchmark 3Y yield forecast by 20bp for Dec-26 and Jun-27 to reflect higher terminal and a delay before the market can price easing into 2027, along with a flatter 3s/10s curve (trough of +35bp in Dec-26) on tighter financial conditions/weaker growth. As we detailed our aforementioned FOMC preview note, the case for a rate hike is strong in our view. Growth remains solid, the labor market has rebounded and is showing some signs of tightening, and PCE inflation has demonstrated limited evidence of falling back towards target. Forward -looking indicators, including from energy prices, suggest the inflat ion overshoot is likely to persist for some time. Against this backdrop, it is not clear the Fed is sufficiently restrictive. Correspondingly, we recently added a third 25bp hike to our outlook – we now expect the Fed to deliver 75bps of tightening in total, with 25bp increases in September, December , and next March. This action would unwind the risk management rate cuts the Fed delivered last year. Risks to the view are two - sided. If recent data trends continue, there is scope for the Fed to hike again in October. Dovish scenarios include a sharper tightening of financial conditions and/or an unexpected softening in inflation or in the labor market. Thus far, we have learned that the German government only delivered around 65% of its target SVIK spending in 2025 (EUR24bn out of EUR37.2bn planned). Yet, we believe spending should be easier this year than in 2025: much of the shortfall was attributed to lack of disbursement to the states; the law enabling states to claim the money was only enacted in mid-December 2025. Monthly spending data on defence and investment shows that cumulative spending was at 1.1% of GDP for both investment and defence over H1 2026. This means the government is on track to meet its 2026 spending target for defence (2.3% of GDP) but lags on investment (2.7% of GDP). We think the recent passing of the procurement and infrastructure future act, significantly reducing red tape around procurement and getting projects started, should facilitate a pick-up in spending in H2. Unless supported by a sufficiently powerful and credible policy framework, interventions intended to reduce volatility can ultimately end up amplifying it. More broadly, intervention itself becomes a powerful signal. It can help coordinate expectations around a desirable equilibrium when markets are disrupted. However, it can also coordinate expectations around an erroneous assessment if policymakers' diagnosis of the problem proves incorrect. The larger the intervention and the weaker the evidence of market dysfunction, the greater this risk becomes. As with the discussion of Japan, the Treasury's intervention can be viewed through the lens of the good, the bad, and the ugly. The Good The buyback program may improve market functioning in specific segments of the Treasury market. By supporting liquidity in off-the-run securities and alleviating temporary segmentation, it can enhance price discovery and reduce frictions that are unrelated to fundamentals. The Bad To the extent that the program suppresses term premia that are correctly reflecting deteriorating fiscal dynamics, rising financing needs, or a higher equilibrium real interest rate, it risks obscuring valuable market signals. In that case, intervention becomes less about improving market functioning and more about resisting the information embedded in market prices. Without sufficient productivity growth to offset these shifts, financing social programs will become increasingly difficult over time, particularly in systems with inter-generational redistributive mechanisms. Aging impacts public finances through higher pension and healthcare expenditures and lower education costs (due to fewer young citizens attending school). We note that official projections, such as the European Commission’s aging report, may rely on overly optimistic assumptions. Specifically, the assumption that potential growth will stabilize above 1% between 2040 and 2060 relies on a productivity boom that is not guaranteed, given the drag of demographic decline. Furthermore, the degree to which these forces exactly impact public finances heavily depends on country specific characteristics, especially in the case of pension expenditure. For this reason, we analyse the situation of each economy separately. We expect the diverging fortunes that have characterised fiscal policy among the big-4 eurozone economies in 2025 and 2026 to persist in 2027 and probably in the few years that follow before the end of the decade. Germany continues its investment plan, raising questions about compliance with EU fiscal rules and potentially reshaping the broader EU architecture. For nonprofit hospitals, the proposed 2.4% OPPS (outpatient procedures) payment increase is largely offset by CMS's proposal to raise the annual 340B remedy clawback from 0.5% to 3%, so this headline while positive for for-profit hospitals, is neutral for NFPs. These proposals do not need to go through Congress, and next procedural steps include a 60 day public comment period before a final OPPS rule around November. Additional administration moves towards site neutrality would also likely be a credit negative for NFPs that benefit from higher hospital reimbursement rates. 11 September 2026 14 Barclays | Municipal Weekly

records.text: 14 Global Emerging Markets Weekly | 10 September 2026 A 9.4% budget deficit next year, if nothing is done The re-drafted 2027 budget targets a 9.4%-of-GDP overall deficit (4.5% primary) for 2027, from an estimated 7.2% deficit (3.3% primary) in 2026. The budget is done at the central government level; that means, excluding regional & local governments, state- owned enterprises, and social security institutions. Primary expenditures are expected to increase by 0.6pp of GDP between 2026 and 2027. This is where the fiscal consolidation should be visible. Interest expenditures (over which the government has little control) go up by 1.1pp of GDP, and revenues fall by 0.6pp of GDP (assuming GDP growth slows down to 1.8%, from 2.5% in 2026, the elimination of the wealth tax, inter alia). But government proposes adjustments of 2.2pp After the re-drafted budget was announced, the government communicated it intends to submit a separate bill to Congress – called “Fiscal Adjustment Law” (aka “Economic Rescue Law“) – which will aim at narrowing the primary fiscal deficit of 2027 by 2.2pp of GDP. With that, the government would be targeting a primary deficit at 2.3% of GDP for 2027. How will Congress respond? Our base-case is it will approve it, with some dilution (to ~1.5pp, from 2.2pp). This is the best moment to do it, at the beginning of the mandate, when political capital is higher and other parties are negotiating to get a share of power. India: Strong FCNR (B) flows, but may not completely fix the rupee problem In recent days, the RBI has disclosed its final Foreign Currency Non-Resident Account (Banking) swaps, which, at USD136bn, exceeded our expectations. This has also restored the efficacy of the balance of payments. Indeed, India's foreign reserves have jumped significantly and are set to climb past USD750bn soon. However, it may not have completely fixed the rupee problem. There is also a bigger question mark over the impact these funds have on India's economy, given the fact that they are not particularly long-term. The biggest opportunity, beyond the cyclical factors, is for the RBI and the government at large to reset India's foreign investment proposition, especially with growth efficacy restored, investment demand improving, and balance sheets remaining clean.

We expand our carry framework to include option strategies, but still find long forward curve trades to offer the most attractive risk-reward. Trades we recommend • Europe: Long 3s5s forward in iTraxx Main, sell 5y iTraxx Main protection @ 53.1bp, buy 3y iTraxx Main protection @ 29.5bp, notional neutral • US: Long 5s10s forward in CDX.IG, sell 10y CDX.IG protection @ 91.65bp, buy 5y CDX.IG protection @ 51.25bp, notional neutral A historically range-bound summer CDS indices traded in a remarkably tight range over the summer months despite a backdrop of persistent macro volatility. For iTraxx Main, the June-August trading range was among the tightest of the past decade, exceeded only by 2021, while CDX.IG recorded its narrowest summer trading range over the same period (see Figure 1 for Main and Figure 2 for CDX.IG). This resilience continues despite ongoing geopolitical tensions in the Middle East, with Brent crude back above $100/bbl, elevated rate volatility and ever-lingering uncertainty around AI-related risks. At Jackson Hole, Warsh had to convince markets that a switch to Kohn trail was still a real possibility. Despite insisting that he wants less forward guidance and more learning from markets, the need to repair July’s credibility damage pushed Warsh into a communication trap. Because he had more reputational capital tied to reversing the July message, he could not simply describe a neutral reaction function. He had to lean in the only direction that could restore credibility. By emphasizing that inflation remains too high, financial conditions are not restrictive enough, the labor market was fine, and the Fed still had work to do, Warsh effectively told markets that the default path had shifted toward the Kohn trail. He did not formally commit to a hike, but he gave much more directional guidance than his philosophy of communication would suggest. Our base case is still for the BoE to hold through year-end and cut once next year should commodity price pressures subside before the end of the year. Should that not be the case, and should broader global growth tailwinds continue to counter already exceptionally tight financial conditions, keeping the economy supported, we would expect 2 hikes at forecast meetings. Going into next week, our risk scenario would be for hikes in February and April. Two hikes have been our risk scenario since May this year (see here). The common pushback to this risk view is that the Taylor rule presented for the adverse scenario in the July MPR showed 75bp worth of hikes, with the Optimal policy projection consistent with 4 hikes. We do, however, flag that the MPR fairly explicitly noted that these policy rules should be viewed as a policy stance (i.e. Bank Rate and risk premium), and not an explicit guide for the Bank Rate trajectory. We also note that the end-point of the Contemporaneous Taylor-type rule is 4.2%. While the BoJ has no need to deny market pricing for a rate hike each quarter, it also has no incentive to encourage even stronger pricing. The biggest focus is whether or not the Fed will hike by year-end. Where the Japanese policy rate goes after reaching 150bp will also depend considerably on the Fed. If the BoJ is forced to hike each quarter, it would be appropriate for pricing to reflect a high terminal rate. As a result, modes have formed within the software sector's price distribution, coalescing around $20-30, the mid-$50s, and the mid-$90s. While there is still some cushion between now and the bulk of the sector's maturity wall (2027/28/29 maturities of $4bn/$36bn/$33bn), the refinancing (or LME) of these nearer-term maturities will likely remain focal between now and YE26. Given the weight in CPI, if one were to choose one energy subcomponent to track, it would be motor fuel, but if we are going to track market-implied energy prices, we should do a thorough job and expand to the other major subcomponents. Back to building blocks This section lays out our new framework for tracking market-implied CPI energy. For readers not wanting to get into the details of the methodology, they can skip to the final section, where we derive an updated "core" CPI fixings path from the modernized structure. We model each of the four major energy subcomponents (fuel oil, motor fuel, electricity, piped gas) separately, and then aggregate into a market-implied CPI energy path, which can be stripped out of the CPI fixings strip to get an ex-energy CPI fixings path. Moreover, because we are relying on the combination of daily realized data when possible, and augmenting with futures prices that adjust in real time, we are able to generate a high-frequency tracking of the market-implied CPI energy. This is fundamentally different from a true forecast, as it is purely mechanical and does not make any attempt to adjust for subjective nuances in the outlook. records.text: 10 September 2026 Asia Local Markets Weekly Deutsche Bank AG/Singapore Page 11 China Rates CNH CCS: Leave the party before it ends We recommend taking profit on our receive 5Y5Y CNH CCS trade. The receive-side tailwinds that supported the trade are fading. We expect to see receiving flows weaken in October; and for paying demand to subsequently strengthen in late Q4. Positioning too has become increasingly crowded. We expect market flows to rotate from receiving toward paying over the coming months: n Dim Sum issuance should slow in October. September is typically a heavy issuance month, supported by international banks completing funding ahead of the Q4 slowdown and strong demand from onshore lifers. Issuance activity falls sharply during the week-long Golden Week holiday and typically remains subdued afterwards, while onshore dim sum bonds buyers also moderate deployment heading into year-end. As a result, October issuance has averaged 27% below September over the past four years (Figure 15), implying fewer receive CCS flows. n Offshore RMB lending should also soften. In both cases there is a circularity. Bessent wants policy to correct the market because he believes policymakers know more than the market, while Warsh wants the market to inform policy while making policy less transparent for the market to understand. A more robust framework is the opposite: policymakers should be transparent about their objectives and rection function, allow markets to aggregate information about fundamentals, embrace market discipline, and intervene only when there is a clearly identified market failure rather than when they simply dislike a market signal. Initially, these operations will be financed from existing cash balances, with short-term bill issuance likely to play a larger role over time. records.text: 2 The Global Thinker | 10 September 2026 Everybody is talking Treasury Secretary Bessent and Fed Chairman Warsh introduced structural changes in the way they interact with markets. Bessent's more interventionist strategy might appear to contrast with Warsh's more laissez-faire approach. But both strategies share a common weakness: they implicitly assume policymakers can improve market outcomes by withholding information from markets rather than improving the underlying policy framework. Bessent's approach appears to rely on the government having superior information about the "correct" level of asset prices and being able to push markets toward that level through intervention. But markets aggregate information more efficiently than any policymaker. Intervention works to address a market failure, a coordination problem or a financial stability externality. It is never a substitute for poor fundamentals. In this case, intervention makes market prices less informative for an efficient allocation of capital. Warsh's approach runs into the mirror-image problem. If the Fed deliberately reveals less about its reaction function in the hope of learning from market prices, those prices become less informative precisely because investors must spend more resources guessing what the Fed will do. records.text: 10 September 2026 Asia Local Markets Weekly Page 10 Deutsche Bank AG/Singapore China Macro Bank recapitalisation: precautionary risk management Over the weekend, Beijing announced a RMB360bn capital injection package for SOE banks and insurance companies. Of the total, RMB300bn will be funded by the MoF, with the remaining RMB60bn provided by China Tobacco. Beyond the two SOE banks, the package also covers one policy bank and five insurance companies, accounting for roughly RMB100bn of support. The latest announcement effectively completes the recapitalization of all six major state-owned banks. Why recapitalize banks when CET1 ratios remain comfortably above regulatory requirements? In our view, the motivation is precautionary rather than a response to immediate capital needs. From 2026, regulators are expected to require full recognition of non-performing and overdue loans, increasing the need for capital buffers against potential asset quality deterioration. Stronger core Tier 1 capital positions should also support credit growth and policy lending objectives. With the recapitalization plan now formalized, the associated RMB300bn special CGB issuance (which was planned in May and June) will take place soon. Together with the recent increase in policy bank bond (PBB) issuance to fund the RMB800bn policy financing package, there have been some concerns about near-term supply pressure in the rates market. records.text: Fiscal Sustainability with Higher Rates and Higher Growth Unusually large primary deficits, the rise in the debt-to-GDP ratio to nearly its post-WW2 peak, and the rebound in interest rates from much lower rates last cycle have driven concern about the fiscal trajectory for a while. The sharp rise in interest rates this year amid the Iran war, continued high inflation, and strong demand for capital from the AI boom has heightened those concerns (Exhibit 1). In this week’s Analyst, we reassess the fiscal trajectory, ask how burdensome the existing debt is and how concerned we should be, estimate what it would take to get onto a sustainable trajectory both if we act now and if we act later, and consider how much a larger boost to growth from AI might help. Modeling the Fiscal Trajectory We analyze debt dynamics with the equation below for the change in the debt-to-GDP ratio, where r is the average nominal interest rate on outstanding government debt, g is nominal GDP growth, and the primary balance equals government revenues minus non-interest expenditures. The equation implies that stabilizing the debt-to-GDP ratio requires running a primary balance equal to r-g times debt-to-GDP . We then use our forecasts to project the path of debt-to-GDP . We forecast nominal GDP growth of just under 4.5% in the years ahead, boosted by stronger AI-led productivity growth, and we expect the primary deficit to average around 3% of GDP . If the issuer is allowed to reinvest cash flows, and there is "significant "embedded asset-liability management (ALM) risk" , then it does not meet the definition of a bond. records.text: 8 The Global Thinker | 10 September 2026 Japan: The good, the bad and the ugly Japan has a long history of foreign-exchange interventions with mixed results. While interventions can generate an immediate market reaction by forcing the unwinding of speculative positions, their effects have typically proven short-lived. In the absence of a meaningful adjustment in the monetary and fiscal policy mix, interventions have often amounted to little more than temporary patches. Ultimately, real exchange rates are determined by fundamentals. Japan's well-known structural challenges, including an aging population, weak productivity growth, and subdued potential output, continue to weigh on long-term growth prospects and are therefore consistent with persistent depreciation pressure on the yen over time. Recent history illustrates these limitations. In 2022, Japanese authorities spent more than ¥9 trillion supporting the currency. In 2024, interventions were even more aggressive, totaling roughly ¥15 trillion over a two-month period. In both instances, the impact on the exchange rate proved temporary. Once the effects of intervention faded, carry-trade dynamics re-emerged, reflecting the continued attractiveness of higher- yielding U.S. assets relative to domestic Japanese alternatives. The more recent joint intervention by Japan and the United States differs from previous episodes and can be analyzed through three lenses: the good, the bad, and the ugly. records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 5 Core goods inflation: We see core goods prices as likely to have risen by 0.34%M (0.78%Y). This is largely down to the very strong contribution from household goods from the July reading reversing. Market participants that we spoke to following the July print mostly thought that the price hike in one major seller's laptops and tablets was not captured by the ONS. However, we think this is only partially correct - tablet prices rose by 13%M in July, with the said (tablet) price hike thus fully passed through, in our view. We do model a 1.5%M rise in the data processing equipment category as pass-through of the end-June price hike in laptop prices has not, we think, been fully reflected in the data in July. A game console that has, per GfK, ~10% of UK market share saw its price hiked by ~40% at the start of August. Given that game consoles have a weight of 0.6ppt (the games, toys and hobbies category has a weight of 9ppt), we think the impact of this hike on core goods inflation is negligible. We model a flat contribution of clothing to the change in the annual rate of core goods inflation, with risks, we think, skewed to the downside. Services inflation: We forecast services inflation at 0.3%M (3.6%Y). The rise is almost entirely driven by base effects in air fares (on index day idiosyncracies, they rose by only 2%M last year). records.text: 2 Europe Economic Weekly | 11 September 2026 Weekly view September a “no brainer”, December a headache In line with what we expected, the ECB hiked all three policy rates by 25bp while being cautious on communication, with unchanged guidance (data-dependence, meeting-by- meeting, and no pre-commitment), and keeping the door open, implicitly in forecasts, to another hike in December. Communication was careful. This was clear when Lagarde avoided endorsing market pricing by giving a different answer than in July to a question on market pricing (and whether markets understood well the ECB’s reaction function). But the ECB’s forecast changes have surprised us to the hawkish side. Implicitly, the ECB is giving the signal that a December hike may be warranted, if their base case materializes (we are just not so convinced that their core inflation forecast of 2.6% in 4Q26 will, hence our decision to keep our call unchanged for now). The “mild” scenario would perhaps open the door for a halt at current policy rates, and the “adverse” scenario would open the door to a fourth hike. That’s a key point, the adverse scenario from the ECB would be consistent with 75- 100bp of total hikes, no more than that. And that assumes energy prices that are well above markets today. This is an implicit message, to us, that market pricing is too hawkish given that it prices more hikes with relatively more benign energy prices. Attorneys general taking more of a conciliatory approach when closure is on the horizon. While federal antitrust regulators continue to scrutinize healthcare consolidation, recent enforcement actions suggest a preference for targeted remedies over outright opposition in certain cases. For example, the FTC allowed Ascension's acquisition of AmSurg to proceed after requiring divestitures of seven ambulatory surgery centers in overlapping markets and imposing conditions on future acquisitions in those areas. This approach reflects a focus on addressing specific competitive concerns while permitting transactions to move forward. States also appear more willing to take a conciliatory approach when faced with hospital closure. In August, the Oregon Health Authority exempted the proposed combination of Salem Health and Santiam Memorial Hospital from its full market review process after concluding that Santiam faced a risk of insolvency during the third quarter. We can see this continuing as more hospitals face persistent financial pressures, making regulators increasingly reluctant to risk facilities closures to communities with limited healthcare alternatives. 11 September 2026 9 Barclays | Municipal Weekly

records.text: CDS Relative Value Systematic single-name screens – update With four weeks having passed, we update our systematic cheap and rich screens and take a look at the performance of the screens identified in our previous update. Top cheap and rich names We screen for cheap and rich names based on an algorithmic approach. For details on the methodological framework, please refer to Systematic single-name screens – review, 8 February 2019. Our screen for cheap names consists of a ranking based on 50% of the "spread momentum" metric (using a 375-day look-back period). It also uses 50% of the "stock price moving average" metric (using 20- and 100-day look-back periods). The first metric picks names where the current spread is above the average spread when normalising for realised volatility, while the second metric picks names that have seen improvement in their equity price. Our screen for rich names consists of a ranking based on 20% of the "spread momentum" metric (using a 375-day look-back period). It also uses 80% of the "stock price moving average" metric (using 20- and 100-day look-back periods). The first metric picks names where the current spread is below the average spread when normalising for realised volatility, while the second metric picks names that have not seen improvement in their equity price. records.text: Exhibit 12 makes a similar point while addressing the concern that a sustainable fiscal trajectory should be reasonably robust to uncertainty about future growth, interest rates, and deficits. Following a methodology used by IMF economists, we simulate thousands of economic and financial scenarios using shocks drawn from historical data. We then ask, at each point in the future, what primary balance would have to be realized on average (rather than targeted outside of recessions) over the subsequent 25 years to keep the debt-to-GDP ratio unchanged in the 10th, 50th, and 90th percentile most favorable scenarios. We draw two conclusions. First, the required primary balance becomes more positive and also more uncertain over time, rising in the median scenario by nearly 1p over the next decade. Second, the probability that the primary balance would have to exceed the largest primary surplus that has been sustained on average over a long period in the past (outcomes above the red line) grows meaningfully in the decades ahead on the current fiscal trajectory. Moreover, reaching that benchmark of the largest average primary surplus in history might prove much harder in the future as entitlement pressures rise. Similarly export prices for general/production/business machinery and transport equipment, which had remained largely flat or declined slightly in the 2010s, have been moving higher since 2020. Transport equipment export prices have dipped temporarily of late, which we suspect is an attempt to offset the impact of US tariff hikes on Japanese goods by lowering prices. During this period, the yen experienced a rapid depreciation in forex markets. Under normal circumstances, Japanese companies would be incentivized to reduce export prices on a contract currency basis. What actually occurred, however, was the opposite as prices turned upward. That turning point coincided roughly with the moment that domestic prices (CPI) began to rise. This suggests strongly that there was a fundamental shift in the pricing behavior of Japanese companies itself around 2020 not only for overseas shipments but in their strategies across both domestic and overseas markets. This newfound willingness of Japanese companies, long plagued by deflation, to raise prices coincided with a surge worldwide in AI demand. The resulting transformation of Japan from an exporter of deflation to one of inflation carries significant implications not only for the Japanese economy but for the global economy as a whole. Morgan Securities plc Alex Gallin (1-212) 270-5492 alex.gallin@jpmorgan.com JPMorgan Chase Bank NA Global Economic Research Androids dream of higher prices: The tech boost to CPI 10 September 2026 J P M O R G A N Measurement issues in US tech inflation The US data illustrate how basket composition and source data can amplify measured technology inflation. On a 3m/3m saar basis, US tech inflation stood at 15% in the July PCE price index but just 1% in CPI (Figure 10). Tech prices were still falling 3.2%oya in CPI while rising 8% in PCE. This gap does not appear to reflect a comparably large divergence in the underlying prices households face. How software is categorized in the two measures accounts for much of the difference. The CPI software category includes flash memory, or blank media, whose prices have surged as part of the semiconductor cycle despite being more appropri- ately classified as hardware. That CPI series is used as a source for the much larger software category in PCE, giving the flash-memory increase an outsized effect on measured PCE software inflation. The BEA plans to replace this source with three inputs this month: the existing CPI series and two PPI measures. Current estimates suggest that the change could reduce core PCE inflation by roughly 15bp on an over- year-ago basis. -20 -10 0 10 20 30 17 19 21 23 25 %3m/3m, saar Figure 10: US tech inflation Source: BEA, BLS, J.P. records.text: US Rates Weekly 11 September 2026 Citi Research 15 Vol: Slow and steady wins the short gamma race We maintain our bearish gamma and steeper vol slope bias on the premise that the pace of the possible rate hikes will be gradual. In recent years, 30y yield/equity correlation tends to decline and turn negative when yields move sharply higher. We recommend owning 6m30y OTM payer contingent lower SPX as a cheap hedge for the fiscal/supply tail risk. Short-dated vol could pullback amid gradual rate hike Even though today’s above consensus CPI print might be enough for the FOMC to hike next week, the relatively benign details, including the muted shelter and medical care components, likely would not cause the Fed to deviate from their slow and cautious approach. As we have argued over the past few months, it is the pace that really matters if the Fed ultimately hikes. A cautious Fed that is not pressured to act aggressively and beat the forwards should keep short-dated vol anchored in the near-term even if they do hike gradually. Hence, we maintain our bearish gamma bias on the premise that the benign CPI details would not be enough to justify an immediate follow-through even if the Fed hikes next week. However, we believe the medium-term economic and policy uncertainties should continue to be supportive of longer expiries and a steeper vol term structure. records.text: m FX measures As of reported data at the closure of FCNR window in end-August, total flows under the FX swap measures have added up to USD 137Bn. Once fully swapped with RBI (window till 11th Sep), these inflows, by themselves, would inject around INR 13Tn in liquidity. Part of these injections are offset by either RBI’s FX intervention or maturing FX forward positions which have reduced the net FX spot accrual. Current liquidity surplus stands around INR 9.7Tn (as of 2nd Sep) while durable liquidity surplus was last reported at INR 8Tn (as of 15st August). Over the next week, this surplus may increase even further once all the FX deposit flows are fully swapped into INR. This creates a major sterilization issue for RBI, leading to a discussion with major banks about instruments for durable absorption. CRR hike is a no-go as it would more than offset FX swap subsidy provided to banks for these flows. OMO sales are possible in small amounts but are difficult to scale-up without disrupting IGB markets. FX sell/buy swaps can be used to retire RBI forward shorts in <1y bucket (total of USD 44Bn) but that would raise concerns on spot reserves firepower available at RBI’s discretion. Longer-tenor VRRR absorption remains the most feasible solution, while keeping costs of sterilization lower and still leaving enough flexibility to manage overnight liquidity surplus (in SDF balance) to keep call rate close to the policy rate. 0 0.5 1 1.5 2 2.5 3 3.5 4 4.5 5 Jul-25 Sep-25 Nov-25 Jan-26

Despite likely fiscal consolidation, stuck at 7% of GDP deficits: In an unexpected turn of events, the long-awaited fiscal consolidation expected for 2027 had to be postponed on the back of the new reconstruction and support responsibilities arising from the earthquake hitting the country in August. Even though a fiscal adjustment by the government for about 1.5–2.0% of GDP continues to be our base case, such an adjustment would be offset by the reconstruction effort, which the government estimates will be worth around 1.5% of GDP (60–70% of that effort will probably be concentrated next year), keeping the deficit as high as 7% of GDP (similar to this year). Even though there has been significant noise coming from the government’s 2027 budget publication (showing a fiscal deficit of 9.4% of GDP), the government is also pointing to a final deficit of 7.2% of GDP after accounting for the likely fiscal adjustment (2.2% of GDP). Overall, the most relevant guidance from the budget is the post-adjustment estimated deficit, as the budget itself could be understood as a counterfactual without any fiscal action rather than a base case. records.text: Global Macro Strategy - Views and Trade Ideas 11 September 2026 Citi Research 8 Gamechanger #2: AI concerns become real Data center spending still booming – backlash isn’t a concern. Heading into the November 2026 midterm elections, data center development has become a highly charged, bipartisan political flashpoint, triggering a wave of local and state-level moratoriums across the United States. Local governments have enacted strict construction pauses, while at least 15 state legislatures have introduced severe regulatory restrictions. Yet, despite growing public and legislative concerns, the data center construction pipeline remains remarkably robust (Figure 17), fueled by the demand for AI infrastructure. Currently, speculative, early-stage projects are being canceled or delayed in local hearings, while late-stage projects with secured site control and power interconnection are moving forward aggressively. T o bypass grid constraints and local moratoriums altogether, hyperscalers are increasingly pivoting to direct investment (Amazon and Dominion Energy), and securing massive nuclear power purchase agreements (Meta and Constellation Energy) to ensure their pipelines continue to break ground. records.text: Source: BofA Global Research, World Bank BofA GLOBAL RESEARCH Financing demands rising, but lending channel stretched The renewed momentum behind capital market reform reflects Vietnam’s increasingly ambitious growth objectives. To achieve its double-digit GDP growth target for 2026-30, investment financial demands are projected at ≈$300bn/year, roughly double that of 2021-24. Meeting these primarily through the banking system will become increasingly challenging – credit-to-GDP ratio at 145% is closer to levels seen in more mature North Asian economies, and policymakers are increasingly reliance on looser macroprudential policies and special mechanisms to preserve credit growth. Significant room for capital markets to deepen Against this backdrop, Vietnam's capital markets remain underdeveloped relative to the size of its economy and banking system. The equity and corporate bond markets remain substantially smaller than outstanding bank credit, in contrast to regional peers. In our view, this partly reflects the relatively narrow institutional investor base. Despite rapid growth the past decade, the domestic fund management industry remains small at ≈6% of GDP (see Appendix), while investment mandate for pension fund VSS is highly conservative (>80% of holdings in government bonds). The general scheme covers around 90% of pensions and is funded by employee and employer contributions. Surplus contributions are channelled to a social security reserve fund (currently worth about EUR14bn, or 0.8% of GDP, according to the fund’s latest annual report), meant to be used to pay for years when the system runs a deficit. After a series of withdrawals from 2012 to 2019, the fund’s revenues have been boosted by an additional contribution (the Intergenerational Equity Mechanism), meant to ease the pressure caused by the retirement of the ‘baby boom’ generation. While two decades of reform have attempted to blunt the impact of an ageing population, the fiscal trajectory remains precarious. Almost all officials saw their scores rise, reflecting a greater openness to potential rate hikes. The average score for 2026 voters, as well as the average for all 19 officials, increased by 0.5 points to reach 7.2 —the highest level observed in our five-year sample. This marks the first time the average score has risen above 7.0, surpassing even the peak of the pandemic-era inflation period, which topped out at 6.8. This sustained upward trajectory over the past nine months underscores a collective hawkish shift in the Committee's risk assessment and an increasing perceived need for further policy action. The overall distribution of scores is heavily skewed toward the hawkish end of the spectrum, with 18 of the 19 officials scoring above the neutral threshold of 5.0. We do not think this would mark the start of a prolonged tightening cycle, bu t rather an attempt to signal the BoE’s commitment to keeping inflationary pressures contained, particularly in light of the resilience of the domestic economy and the duration of the energy -price shock. Going a gainst the grain of rate hikes , we expect the Central Bank of Brazil (BCB) to cut rates by 25bp at its meeting on 16 September. While geopolitical tensions between Iran and the US drive uncertainty and higher oil prices, the local outlook remains more stable. Q2 2026 data shows decelerating economic activity, evidenced by lower -than-expected household consu mption, and July data is showing a slowing labor market and reduced credit growth. We don’t expect BCB’s decision to meaningfully drive domestic assets. Rather, l ocal curves and FX will remain highly dependent on October’s election outcome. After the recent rally (with the market repricing higher the odds of Flavio Bolsonaro and then returning to a 50/50 outlook), we expect local assets to stabilize while new information comes in . Given the potential for volatility as we approach the first round ( 4 Oct), we prefer to remain on the sidelines for now. records.text: M Idea 4 September Projections: Higher Growth, Higher Inflation European Economics Team What to make of the updated projections: The key parameter of the September baseline projections was the cut-off date for the external assumptions. It was set on 19 August, in line with our expectations (17 August) and standard Eurosystem process. With that, the updated projections came in broadly in line with our views (Exhibit 3 ). Growth was revised higher, exactly as we thought, as the ECB took on board not only a solid 1H26 but also slightly lifted the expected path for the next quarters. On inflation, the revision was also up, as we expected, but a touch more pronounced. In particular, core was revised higher in 2027 and 2028 and headline projected still above target in 2028 (2.1%Y), ending the year at 2.2%Y in 4Q28. We note however that the outlook for wages was not revised much and that the ECB also mentions health regulated prices in Germany affecting EA inflation by 10bp in 2027. Likely, not all of the revision in core came from a more pessimistic view on the transmission of the energy shock through indirect effects in inflation. Lastly, with very large price changes since 19 August, the adverse scenario published today provides a good reference point, even though it entails much more persistent oil prices. This scenario illustrates the risks that headline HICP remains above target for longer. Exhibit 3: Inflation revised higher in 2028 2025 2026 2027 2028 2025 2026 2027 2028 202

records.text: 10 September 2026 Asia Local Markets Weekly Page 6 Deutsche Bank AG/Singapore Asia Strategy (2) What does JPY strength mean for rest of the region The ducks – valuations, policy convergence, repatriation flows - might finally be getting into a row for the yen. There are still plenty of ifs, and it could take a while for data to validate if this is more than another false start. But what if it is for real this time? What does it mean for rest of Asia? We look at 3 transmission channels: 1. The ‘competition’ channel - correlation with yen strength. Looking back at the last 10 years of Asia FX betas to JPY moves (Figure 3) shows KRW, THB and SGD with the highest beta to JPY strength (and somewhat symmetrical exposure to JPY weakness). There is a small intersection here – KRW – with currencies which are the most undervalued in the region (KRW, TWD, RMB), and with positive NIIPs . We have long argued that FX policy in Asia is influenced relatively more by TWIs – which includes JPY crosses – on the attitudes towards direction and level of currencies; and by the respective dollar crosses on managing the vol. The higher yielders down South (INR, IDR) are also cheap, but there is little evidence that they have benefited historically from big yen moves. If anything, they have shown disproportionately higher beta to JPY weakness, but fairly negligible beta to JPY strength. 2. The ‘carry unwind’ channel – vulnerability to yen as a funder. Episodes of JPY strength always lead to concerns

records.text: Jiuk Choi 10 September 2026 1 Insights Information Classification: General SGD: No Urgency for Further Tightening (For Now) Despite continued supply-side inflationary pressures, we expect MAS to keep its policy stance unchanged in October. Both headline and core inflation momentum moderated in July, implying that recent economic growth has yet to translate into meaningful demand-side pressure. Recent retail sales data also suggest relatively subdued domestic demand. While Singapore continues to benefit from the global AI boom, the latest economic data do not appear strong enough to justify a third consecutive tightening, and therefore we remain neutral on SGD. The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) utilizes an exchange rate-based monetary policy to promote price stability, as Singapore is a small and open economy with total trade exceeding 300% of GDP. Specifically, MAS adjusts a slope, level and width of the Singapore dollar nominal effective exchange rate (S$NEER) policy band (Figure 1). MAS tightened its monetary policy in both April and July by steepening the S$NEER appreciation slope. According to MAS’ September survey of professional forecasters, the market is narrowly divided over whether MAS will increase the slope again in October. Although uncertainty remains due to continuing supply-side inflationary pressure, we expect MAS to stay on hold in October, as both inflation momentum and economic activity have weakened. Covered bonds also represent a significant share of EU/EEA insurers’ exposures, but they are classified by EIOPA under a different category than government-related exposures discussed above. EIOPA data accounts for covered bonds under Corporate Bonds (CIC category 2) split between Common Covered bonds (sub-category 6) and Covered bonds subject to specific law (sub- category 7). As of Q2 26, EU/EEA insurers held €305bn of covered bonds – almost twice as much they held supranational or regional bonds – of which nearly four-fifths in German Pfandbrief (€136bn; 45%) and Danish covered bonds (€100bn; 33%). Their holdings also include relatively small exposures to Swedish (€24bn) and French covered bonds (€20bn; Figure 23). Whilst EU/EEA insurers’ covered bond holdings are sizeable, they have decreased by €207bn (40%) since Q4 17. German insurers have cut their covered bond holdings the most (-€127bn) followed by the French (-€64bn). Notably, of the main insurance undertakings holding covered bonds, Danish insurers were the only ones that meaningfully increased covered bond holdings in the past decade (+€18bn; Figure 24). Capping the long end of the curve effectively easy financial conditions and put more pressure on the Fed to hike down the road. Fiscal policy is stepping on a rake Fiscal policy is in disarray in developed economies and there is no political will in sight to address fiscal deficits. In the US, the deficit is north of 6% of GDP, half of that being the interest bill, 70% of spending is entitlements, and 15% is defense. Buying back long- term debt with short-term liabilities could potentially introduce rollover risk and further conditioning of monetary policy. Fiscal responsibility is a necessary condition for price stability. Fiscal dominance is not around the corner, but it is not far away either. Forward guidance is in the eye of the beholder Chairman Warsh wants to learn from markets and suppress forward guidance. But markets don’t price what the Fed should do, they price what they expect the Fed to do. And if the long end is influenced by US Treasury intervention, signals are even more distorted. The Fed should communicate its reaction function, which is the nominal anchor for the system. In our view, at Jackson Hole, Warsh ended up delivering too much guidance, which might end up costing the Fed degrees of freedom or credibility. 10 September 2026 Economics Global Table of Contents Everybody is talking 2 Why are interest rates moving higher? 2 Intervention in markets: a bad idea

records.text: extent of the Medicaid cuts became clear, hospitals started making deals again, especially giant systems divesting from non core hospitals and service segments. We think there is a distinction to be made between the current and the heavy M&A periods of the 1990s and 2010s: the previous periods were about consolidating to increase in size; the recent wave is more about surviving. This fundamental difference underscores why we believe that AGs will be more supportive this cycle than that of the 2010s. In the 1990s, hospitals merged mainly so they could have more bargaining leverage with insurance companies (here was some survival pressure mixed in, but the main prize was bargaining power). The 2010s presented the greatest incentives to becoming a large system. After the Affordable Care Act, being big came with real rewards: hospitals would be able to coordinate care, take on risk safely, afford expensive technology, and dominate a region. 2017 had a record 10 to 11 "mega-deals" in which the smaller partner still had over $1bn in revenue. The last few years flipped the motive. After COVID relief money ran out and costs (nurses, supplies, drugs) shot up, a lot of hospitals started bleeding money. They did not merge to conquer a market; they merged because they could not keep the lights on alone. Today was VaR shock as an already hawkishly priced market out- hawked itself. We expected the ECB may offer some nuance around further policy tightening but nothing came by and with President Lagarde ditching the concept of neutral rates, the invisible guardrails that could cap the tightening cycle also disappeared. This leaves the market firmly in the throes of energy price developments with nothing in way of central bank guidance to distinguish the scale of tightening needed in a pure supply shock. Admittedly the current terminal rate (c.3.3%) that pencils in c.80bp of further tightening appears excessive. But what is cheap can get cheaper and in the backdrop we find ourselves in, calling the peak in market pricing feels premature. However, today's market reaction suggests that a continued sell-off could lead to inversion further down the money market curve as shown by the move beyond Z7. We thus recommend initiating a ERZ7Z8 flattener (entry: -13bp target: -35bp stop: +0bp). records.text: European Rates Weekly 10 September 2026 Citi Research 5 This week, we provide a detailed overview of EU/EEA insurers’ Q2 26 asset exposures. Insurers have cut government bond holdings by more than €500bn since the end of ECB QE net purchases. Italian, Spanish, and Belgian insurers have cut the share of domestic EGBs’ of their GVT bond holdings the most, though they remain elevated and are in line with OAT s. Insurers’ supra holdings have almost doubled in the past decade, and some substitution of EGBs by supras holdings appear to have occurred. Insurers’ regional debt holdings, which are mostly held by German insurers, dropped sharply when ECB QE ended, but has stabilized since. This is also the case for their covered bond holdings, which are mostly held by German and Danish insurers. The big picture – fixed income makes up majority of EU/EEA insurers’ exposures. As of Q2 26, EU/EEA insurers’ aggregate exposures amounted to €9.594trn, up 1.3% from a year ago. Slightly less than half (47.3%) of these exposures were in fixed income (note this breakdown allocates debt and money market funds from Collective Investment Undertakings (CIU) to fixed income and equity funds to equity on a look-through basis) and slightly less than a third (28.8%) in equities (Figure 9). Cost-push pressures from higher crude import prices are already feeding through into domestic producer prices and are likely to push CPI inflation higher going forward. Pass-through is progressing more rapidly than in the past, extending not only from upstream to midstream stages of the supply chain, but also, more recently, to downstream sectors, including petrochemical intermediates and processed products (Exhibit 5; see Japan Viewpoint: Pipeline inflation pressures are broadening , 30 July). CPI inflation has been on a disinflationary trend over the past year, reflecting negative base effects from non-perishable food prices, but it appears to have already bottomed out. Presidential election blurs the medium-term outlook: Beyond this, there is still high uncertainty surrounding the fiscal trajectory following the presidential elections (May 2nd). Given rising interest rate payments, stabilizing the debt-to-GDP ratio would require fiscal consolidation worth around EUR 120bn (4% of GDP), now forecasted by 2032 by various presidential candidates. At this stage, the various candidates for the presidential election have not yet clearly outlined their medium-term fiscal policy, although several have already announced that they will roll back the pension reform. This could prove costly and thus requires strong fiscal arbitration elsewhere to finance it (see page 6). The capacity of any new elected president to deliver their economic policy will require benefitting from a majority in parliament. This is still uncertain. Any new president would likely call for new parliamentary elections, to take place possibly in the second half of June 2027. In the past, French voters have been rather consistent, providing a majority - or close to it - to the party of the President. We expect it will be still the case, helping to provide more visibility on the fiscal consolidation’s pace. We don't expect any evidence of "second-round effects" by November (or, for that matter, through 2026/7 more broadly). Having seen the economy in an 'ok place' last month, we now worry about the scale of tightening in the financial conditions and the impact of higher energy bills on consumer confidence. The global growth impulse has been very strong - but it might be tested by the recent market moves. This is not a set-up in which we see any more than 50bp worth of hikes as plausible. Going into next week, we still think if hikes are delivered, they might come in 1H27, with the BoE reacting to headline inflation edging towards 4.0-4.5%Y in this risk scenario (as of last night, our modelled peak in CPI inflation was ~3.5%Y). But we accept that should commodity prices remain at these levels, and the BoE comes into the November meeting unable to forecast headline inflation falling towards 2%Y by the end of 2027, action as early as November - on Pill's "risk management grounds" is very much possible. Considering the experience of March - a non- forecast meeting - we think that any hikes would be delivered at forecast meetings, where messaging can be better pitched to the broader market audience. records.text: United States: Interest Rates On the brink 10y UST yields are within striking distance of 5%, as the markets have reassessed the Fed's path higher while term premium is appropriately hovering near pre-GFC levels. We remain of the view that bonds are not cheap yet and catalysts for a rally do not appear imminent. Still not cheap enough With 10y Treasury yields approaching 5%, the obvious question is whether bonds have finally become cheap. We still do not think so. To answer that question, it helps to start from first principles. A 10y Treasury yield can be decomposed into two components. The first is the market's expectation for the path of short- term interest rates over the life of the note. The second is the term premium, the additional compensation investors require for holding duration rather than rolling Treasury bills. Any argument that yields have moved too far must therefore be an argument that one or both of these components is mispriced. The first thing to note is that most of this year's repricing has not come from term premium. It has come from expectations. Of the roughly 70bp increase in 10y yields year-to-date, term premium accounts for only around 15-20bp ( Figure 1). records.text: North America Economic Research 11 September 2026 J P M O R G A N www.jpmorganmarkets.com Economic and Policy Research Michael Feroli (1-212) 834-5523 michael.e.feroli@jpmorgan.com JPMorgan Chase Bank NA At the conclusion of next week’s FOMC meeting we expect that the Committee will increase the target range for the fed funds rate by 25bp to 3.75-4.0%. We think it’s a closer call than the market is pricing, but at the end of the day the Chair’s repeated stern warnings on inflation intolerance risk institutional credibility absent some action to back it up. While there may be a few Committee members who might not whole-heartedly endorse a hike next week, we expect no dissents. In the risk scenario of no action, we would expect another three hawkish dissents. In the dot plot, we look for the median to point to a year-end funds target of 4.0-4.25%, implying another hike this year on top of the expected hike next week. The risk scenario is a median looking for no further hikes beyond next week’s. Over the remainder of the forecast horizon, which will be extended to 2029 next week, we expect a gradual descent back to the longer-run dot, which we project will be revised up to 3.25%, if not higher. We don’t expect any meaningful changes in the post-meeting statement. For our part, after next week we are looking for one more hike in December. Setting aside the midterms, a credible case for passing in October is that it takes time to observe the effects of the hike on the economy. Inf

records.text: Global FX weekly | 11 September 2026 13 FX: The weakest link The outlook for GBP headed into the BoE meeting is complicated by several factors, the most significant of which is the weak correlation between GBP TWI and 10yr Gilts. Whilst this is not unique to the UK, it is difficult to anchor a view on the GBP reaction function through the BoE. We would be inclined to skew the risks to a weaker GBP given the high bar for the BoE to out-hawk market pricing which looks for 4 rate hikes over the coming year. Yet, given the breakdown in the link between GBP and gilts through this month, the distribution of GBP outcomes is wider than usual. Our base case, however, is that the BoE will indeed struggle to out-hawk market pricing and weigh on GBP though we doubt that the impact will be meaningful nor sustained. GBP has traded a relatively tight trading range since the start of the month as global developments drive broader sentiment, and markets continue to find the landing zone for USD. Against this backdrop, the vol outlook is likely to be a more important driver. GBP-specific risk premium continues to edge lower as is UK term premium, a sign that global rather UK-specific risk factors are at play. Though our base case suggests some asymmetry in GBP price action, one could make the following argument: BoE pricing is being heavily influenced by global factors rather than UK fundamentals and is essentially a misread. We also examined how these CRF baskets have performed through different economic regimes. In Figure 24, we show the last six El Niño instances and the changes in YoY food inflation in various G10 countries with liquid linker markets. As we mentioned earlier, usually, the El Niño weather pattern starts in the summer of first year and the inflationary impact in consumer price indices is seen in the following year. So, for the purpose of this exercise we define the impact of El Niño as the increase in yoy food inflation from the June of first year to the peak in YoY food inflation in the following calendar year. records.text: said, we consider the possibility of a 50bp hike or rate hikes at consecutive meetings (as recently hinted at by Hajime Takata in a speech) to be unlikely. While we view Fed policy as the most important variable, we will once again be paying close attention to the voting behavior of board members at this meeting. At the June meeting, dovish T oichiro Asada (appointed by the Takaichi administration) cast a dissenting vote against the rate hike. Whether the equally dovish new board member Ayano Sato also submits a dissenting vote will carry important implications (Figure 2). If the number of dissenting votes remains at one or fewer, it will be easier to project continued rate hikes even after the retirement of more hawkish members Naoki Tamura and Hajime Takata in July next year, with the probability of a terminal rate above 2% also increasing depending on Fed policy. On the other hand, should two or more dissenting votes be cast, the hurdle for continuing rate hikes from mid- next year onward could rise. If the Takaichi administration again appoints dovish successors to Mr. Tamura and Mr. Takata, dovish members would number four, sharply tilting the balance of the board in a dovish direction. While it is not ideal for the BoJ to continue raising rates in the face of multiple dissenting votes, a maximum of four dovish members out of nine would still allow rate hikes to continue. records.text: Please refer to important information at the end of the report and MAR disclosures Amidst a resilient macro backdrop, uncrowded positioning underpins the case for BTD in airlines. Unloved, highly shorted and uncrowded are powerful ingredients that typically underpin sudden, sharp right-tail moves. Airlines feature all three currently. An end to hostilities in the Middle East and a retracement in the price of crude would be the key macro catalysts for a squeeze. However, it is notoriously difficult to forecast how the situation might play out. That said, with the midterms approaching, we expect the Trump administration to focus on ways to ease prices at the pump and thus be more open to negotiating deals, even if they are only temporary. US macro/labor market resilience and seasonality add to squeeze risks, leading us to seek tactical BTD opportunities in airlines. From a flow perspective, institutional and retail option demand skews significantly bearish. We observed some short covering recently, but there is still plenty of scope for bears to close out their shorts further. Obviously, the flip side of this trade would be a short energy play. But with positioning in energy not overly stretched and the likelihood of sustainably higher oil prices over the medium term, the energy left tail is unlikely to be as steep as the airlines’ right tail, in our view. Japanese companies’ outward direct investment primarily consists of long-term investment involving local production, and profits earned locally are often reinvested. By contrast, much of the direct investment into Japan is thought to consist mainly of equity acquisitions by overseas investment funds8 , which may be more likely to lead to income outflows through demands for higher dividends and other channels. As we have argued before and elaborate on here, current pricing of neutral in the US is at the top end of – but still within – what we see as the plausible range. In particular, we think there is a reasonable case to make that nominal neutral could be 3.75-4.25%, 25-50bps above the assumption in our current forecast. That higher neutral rate would pass -through nearly 1:1 to 10y UST and, holding fixed our assumptions on term premia , imply a fair -value range of 5 -5.25%. For now, we treat this as an upside scenario rather than our baseline, as we look for more clarity on the path of inflation, the war, and fiscal policy. Until now, we had expected 2.5% to mark the peak in ECB rates. We expect the ECB to reverse this hike in Q4 2027 and then keep rates on hold at 2.5%. Current market pricing is significantly more hawkish and implies a further 75bp of tightening over the coming year. records.text: The 1990s: "We need to stick together. " Insurance companies (through managed care plans like HMOs and PPOs) started playing hardball and paying hospitals less. While a single small hospital had little power to negotiate, a big group of hospitals could say, "Pay us fairly or you lose all of us. " Accordingly, hospitals merged to get bargaining muscle, marking the first big wave. Late 1990s: The government cuts the check. In 1997, Congress passed the Balanced Budget Act of 1997, which slashed how much the government paid hospitals through Medicare (health insurance for older people) by about $112bn. Suddenly hospitals were treating lots of patients but making less money. Weak hospitals started looking for stronger partners to survive. After Congress softened the cuts with the Balanced Budget Refinement Act of 1999 and the Benefits Improvement and Protection Act of 2000, things calmed down for a while. 2010–2017: The big boom. The Affordable Care Act (the ACA, or "Obamacare") passed in 2010, and rewarded hospitals for being big by changing the goal from "do more" to "do it well. " Before the ACA, hospitals got paid for every single test, scan and procedure, so more care meant more money. The ACA started paying hospitals based on keeping patients healthy. Keeping a whole population healthy required doctors, specialists, labs and follow-up care working together, which is much easier when one big system owns all of it. Broadly speaking, (recognizing risks around what is said in the press conference), we think that if the Fed hikes, the curve is likely to modestly twist flatten, vol will come off, and mortgages will do well from this point. Market participants may feel like the Fed is willing to step in and control inflation, and delivering what is expected should be good for an asset that is structurally short vol. Yes, banks will have to question deposit durations, FX hedging costs will increase, and carry will go down, but much of that should be in the price. On the other hand, if the Fed surprised the market with a hold, even a hawkish one, we'd expect the curve to bear steepen and vol to pick up. Investors may worry about Fed independence, and risk assets could struggle. In particularly, we would expect the first reaction of mortgages to be underperformance despite a better backdrop from a carry perspective. However, in either case, our conviction level in the response function is not significantly high.

records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 7 Financial conditions: No longer easing Following the conflict in the Middle East and the uncertainty it brings to the next steps for monetary policy, we continue to track our FRB/US-based measure of financial conditions. As of the September 10 market close, financial conditions remained tighter than before the recent escalation in the Middle East, and no longer easier than at the time before the July FOMC meeting. Since the July FOMC meeting, financial conditions eased and reversed, now broadly unchanged. The index aims to capture how changes in asset prices weigh on future economic activity. It includes five daily variables: the 10-year Treasury yield, S&P 500 returns, the corporate BBB credit spread, the valuation of the U.S. dollar, and the price of oil. These are aggregated based on their estimated growth elasticities relative to the federal funds rate using the Federal Reserve's FRB/US model. As a result, the index can be interpreted as the equivalent change in the federal funds rate, expressed in basis points, required to generate a similar effect on economic activity. Since hostilities in the Middle East began on February 28, the tightening in financial conditions is equivalent to about a 53bp rise in the federal funds rate. This has reversed the easing seen earlier in the year, most of which was driven by a weaker U.S. dollar. Finally, because spread estimates are model-based and can occasionally produce unstable values, we trim observations of monthly spread changes that fall above the 99th percentile or below the 1st percentile. The resulting dataset contains about 1.7 million observations, of which 1.3 million are investment grade. To examine the relationship between systematic spread volatility and spread level, we apply the same framework used in our 2005 study. Monthly spread changes are grouped by sector (Financials, Industrials and Utilities), spread duration and spread level. The aim for these hospitals was less about survival and more about growing larger and more comprehensive. 2020–2022: COVID hits, everything freezes. During the pandemic, hospitals were completely overwhelmed and had less capacity to consider transactions. On top of that, the CARES Act of 2020 flooded even weak hospitals with cash for once, so there was less need to merge. Deals dropped to a low of 49 in 2021. 2023–2025: Trouble comes back. records.text: European Economic Perspectives11 September 2026 ab 12 What to expect from legislative elections? The extent to which the next president can implement his or her agenda − particularly with respect to passing budgets − will depend heavily on the composition of parliament. Without a parliamentary majority, any new president may become a "lame duck", at least on domestic matters. The next scheduled legislative elections are not due until June 2029, five years after the 2024 election. However, the traditional pattern under the Fifth Republic has been to hold legislative elections shortly after a presidential election. To do so in 2027, the newly elected president would need to dissolve the National Assembly, triggering elections within 20-40 days. If dissolution occurred immediately after taking office, legislative elections could take place as early as June 2027. Historically, presidential elections have often been followed either by a parliamentary majority aligned with the president − facilitating implementation of the government's programme, as during Macron's first term − or by a period of cohabitation, in which the opposition controls parliament and constrains the president's policy agenda, as under Jacques Chirac between 1997 and 2002. Since 2022, however, no party or bloc has secured an outright majority, forcing successive prime ministers to rely on fragile minority governments. records.text: M Update Morgan Stanley Research 3 G10 | Summary of Our G10 Currency Views USD Our view: Neutral Risk skew: Bearish Watch: FOMC Rates Decision, Retail Sales Over the past six months, EUR/USD has traded broadly in line with energy prices. The rise in Brent oil from the mid- $70/bbl area to the $100/bbl area over the past two months has coincided with a rise in EUR/USD from the mid 1.13 area to the 1.16 area, which is around where it traded in 2Q when oil was around $100/bbl. USD positive risks therefore include a rise in energy prices sharp enough that risk sentiment suffers as global growth expectations decline and a fall in energy prices to an extent that central bank pricing abroad (primarily in Europe) declines. In between those outcomes, a combination of relatively resilient global growth and elevated energy prices are likely to weigh on the USD, primarily versus risk-sensitive, high-yielding, energy-exporting currencies like AUD. We maintain a bearish skew on the USD as the ECB's forecasts may bolster pricing for additional tightening in Europe and our economists continue to call for a relatively patient Fed. Another lens is our regime framework, where rising real rates and breakevens over the past two months have aligned with carry trades doing well versus CHF; a continued rise in US real rates could weigh particularly on low yielders broadly. The AI boom is increasingly pertinent to USD flows. This cycle must persist to prevent the acceleration of institutional diversification . When capital moves away from the reserve currency nation, periphery assets are supported by the more narrow pipeline available to accommodate such larger- scaled capital inflows. Gold’s deep liquidity profile favours some capture. And, in the meantime, the geopolitical regime favours the recycling of reserves into gold, which itself is reflexively supportive for institutional adoption . The Hormuz conflict is the most potent threat to this dynamic: rising energy prices work against reserve recycling for energy importer nations. Physical flows are strengthening on this dip. records.text: US Credit Alpha Overview The Fed is a coin flip a week out, oil is spiking and Treasury yields sit at multi-year highs, yet credit isn't blinking. IG is absorbing heavy new supply, while HY's pullback looks like normalization from rich levels, not stress. CCCs are the exception, near two-year wides. Credit hasn't blinked The Fed is close to a coin flip, with Treasury yields already at multi-year highs. The market is pricing a 70% chance of a hike (as of mid-day Thursday), at the high end of the 50-70% range over the past ten days. This is unusually high uncertainty just one week out from an FOMC meeting. The vast majority of the time, the market has a 90%+ conviction level about the Fed's decision so close to a meeting. Barclays economists expects a hike in September and another one in December. Secretary Bessent's $6bn of longer-dated buybacks also failed to impress: the 2y is at 4.53%, the 10y at 4.92% and the 30y at 5.34% (as of Thursday mid-day). The yield curve is at multi-year highs, particularly in the long end: the 30y is at its highest level since 2007, and the 10y is only 7bp away from its post-GFC peak in 4Q23. The job market surprised to the upside, and CPI on Friday is the last gate before the decision. Payrolls and revisions were strong last week, and small companies are participating as well: the NFIB's hiring plans are at the high end of their four-year range.
