Time to hike (probably) Markets are pricing over 80bp of Fed hikes over the next 12 months. Oil is surging, and the ECB and BoJ are hiking despite weaker growth and much softer core inflation. We don’t think the Fed can credibly stay on hold, barring a very soft Aug CPI print. The SEP should show two hikes this year and one cut in 2027. Beyond this, we expect only modest tweaks. Assuming the Fed hikes, the key questions at the press conference will likely be about the future policy path and what has changed since July to justify a hike. The week ahead: All eyes on the Sep FOMC decision All eyes will be on the Sep FOMC meeting on Wed, where we expect the Fed to hike by 25bp. Additionally, we get retail sales for Aug on Wed as well. We also get import prices (Wed), the NAHB housing market index (Wed), housing starts (Thu), pending home sales (Thu) and industrial production (Fri). The Fed is in communication blackout until Sep 17 (Thu). There is no Fedspeak on the calendar yet for Fri, but we will be on the lookout for any updates.

The net effect is intensifying competition with both EM and DM manufacturers of higher-end products, which is fuelling G20 debates on trade imbalances. In parallel, a policy-led push for self-reliance in capital goods and intermediates has sharply reduced China’s imports of manufactured inputs. But import substitution has raised demand for primary commodities, and, amid rising trade frictions with the West, China has also moved to diver- sify sourcing to strengthen supply-chain resilience. For most EM Edge (the GCC and frontier EMs), this shift has been positive (EM Edge: The double-edged sword of Chinese growth). Given that exports are dominated by commodities, EM Edge has benefited from China’s move up the value chain, via stronger resource demand, without facing the same direct competition in advanced manufacturing. While export- ing more to China, EM Edge is importing cheaper goods. As EM Edge countries are generally less aligned with the West, they are increasingly “safer” counterparties for China’s efforts to diversify and de-risk its supply chain. In the post-GFC era, China combined trade integration with infrastructure development and financing via the Belt and Road Initiative. However, many of these projects ended up creating debt and debt service issues that required subsequent restructuring. Post-pandemic, the model is shifting again. Healey also indicated progress on PM Burnham’s signature policy ambition of greater devolution by announcing a Fiscal Devolution Road- map will be delivered alongside this autumn's budget to give more power and resources to local leaders, although this is unlikely to have significant implications for the overall fiscal metrics. As we have noted previously, the recent rise in gilt yields will mechanically reduce the fiscal headroom from £23bn to around £10bn, however the purpose of the headroom is to absorb shocks and given that the move in gilt yields reflects global factors (higher gas and oil prices and a broad increase in global real yields) rather than UK domestic factors we see little reason for the Chancellor to respond to reduced headroom via significant spending cuts or increased taxes. Given Healey’s message of ‘continuity’ around the UK’s overall fiscal stance and with likely more restrained and limited increases in taxation and spending, we are less con- cerned that the Budget will result in a significant increase in market pricing of UK fiscal risk premia. If the Budget is delivered along these lines it would likely leave in place around 0.5% of fiscal tightening. records.text: s, Treasury supply and changes in investor demand. Yet beneath the surface, the economy has continued to surprise to the upside. Labor markets have tightened, core inflation forecasts have drifted higher, and market pricing has shifted from expecting two Fed cuts at the beginning of the year to contemplating three to four hikes over the cycle. Even far-forward expectations have moved higher as investors reassess the neutral rate in an economy that continues to generate solid growth despite policy rates in the 3.5-3.75% range. In other words, investors are not demanding materially more compensation for taking duration risk. They are reassessing the level at which policy rates are likely to settle over the longer run. That distinction matters. If most of the move was attributable to term premium, one could plausibly argue that yields had overshot and become detached from the macroeconomic backdrop. But that is not what the data suggest. Instead, the market has spent much of the year repricing higher the path of future short rates and the long-run equilibrium level of interest rates. To argue that 10y yields are too high today is therefore to argue that the markets are pricing in too high a future path of policy rates, not simply that term premium has risen too far. 10 September 2026 3 FICC Research Interest Rates 10 September 2026 Anshul Pradhan +1 212 412 3681 anshul.pradhan@barclays.com BCI, US Demi Hu, CFA +1 212 526 7398 demi.hu@barclays.com BCI, US

With a reasonably hawkish BoJ hiking path already priced in, the risk that renewed fiscal concerns push JGB term premia higher and weaken the JPY at the same time warrants attention. Longer-term fundamental and supply/demand-based pressure for JPY depreciation is persistent and makes it difficult to see sustained JPY appreciation. Mid-2020: The RMB1 trillion anti-Covid special CGB program increased government n bond supply. 10y CGB yields rose alongside repo rates normalizing from pandemic lows towards the PBOC’s OMO target. Tighter funding conditions, rather than incremental supply alone, were likely an important driver of the bond sell-off. May-June 2022: Policymakers accelerated LGSB issuance, providing advance n guidance to largely complete the annual quota by end-June amid renewed Covid disruptions and property-sector weakness. However, 10y CGB yields were broadly stable initially and declined subsequently. The heavy issuance was accompanied by fiscal support, including large-scale VAT credit refunds, while weak growth reinforced expectations that monetary policy would remain accommodative. October-November 2023: Special refinancing LGBs and the additional issuance of n RMB 1tn central government bonds increased bond supply. records.text: icy Fiscal backing is a necessary condition for price stability. And fiscal policy is the Achilles heel of the US economy. The headline fiscal deficit will reach 6.5% of GDP next year, with 3.3% of GDP being the interest bill (and growing, see Exhibit 6). These numbers are simply too high for this stage of the cycle. Public debt is already above 120% of GDP and the Treasury is increasing the fraction of debt issuance on the front end of the curve to avoid validating much higher rates in the long end (Exhibit 7). The Operation Twist recently announced by Secretary Bessent moves in the direction of shortening the duration of government liabilities even further to contain the long end of the curve. A significant shortening of duration would condition the conduct of monetary policy absent fiscal consolidation. Gradually, the US is starting to check all the boxes that lead to fiscal dominance. Recently, President Trump urged the Fed to cut interest rates arguing that the US government is paying a higher interest rate than its credit rating would justify. Although not advisable, it is not unusual that Presidents express their views on monetary policy. However, pushing the central bank to cut rates to reduce the government’s interest bill is not a compelling argument, flirting with a case of fiscal dominance. However, the sell-off since July has weighed on the entire EUR term-structure with the belly of the curve underperforming the front-end despite the key catalyst continuing to be energy prices. For example, 2y2y ESTR is now higher than it was in the 2022 cycle whereas EUR2s5s10s fly has been steadily cheapening and is also approaching close to local highs. What’s even more striking is that despite the pure energy supply shock narrative with little demand-driven impulse for inflation and with terminal rate pricing having reached c.100bp above the ECB’s neutral rate estimate, the market prices virtually nothing in terms of reversing these hikes. For example, market pricing reflects a continuation of rate hikes into 2027, with only c.13bp of rate cuts priced between 2027 and 2028. This is in contrast to how market traded the rate path in 2022 and also in Q1 26. Figure 5 and Figure 6 show this contrast in how the market traded in 2022 versus what is happening this year. Pricing for the September meeting is around 100%, and the shape of the curve is consistent with subsequent rate hikes each quarter. What is deeply interesting is that the level for the January meeting equates to around 2.2 rate hikes relative to the current level. Nedopil (Griffith Asia Institute) argues that as policy-based lending has fallen, China’s engagement has pivoted toward energy, technology, construc- tion, and investment—especially in metal mining and pro- cessing—and, in Asia, toward building supply chains. In effect, even with sharply lower policy-bank lending, China is arguably more influential in shaping investment, trade corri- dors, and industrial development (notably mining) across EM and frontier markets. 2 Global Metals Weekly | 11 September 2026 Met coal supply crunch Met coal flips into deficit The metallurgical (‘met’) coal market has tightened dramatically over the past year, driven largely by China's crackdown on coal overproduction. As domestic output has declined, Chinese consumers have increasingly turned to imports, widening the import arbitrage and contributing to a sharp rally in both domestic and seaborne prices. While Indian steelmakers have remained on the sidelines in recent months due to elevated coal prices, underlying demand remains resilient. We now expect the market to move into deficit this year and remain tight into 2027. The key downside risks to our view are a reversal in China's production policy stance or a normalization of Mongolian coal flows into China. records.text: ECB Recap—Higher Rates Ahead The Governing Council hiked its policy rate by 25bp to 2.5% at today’s meeting, as widely expected. The new staff projections showed somewhat higher growth and more persistent inflation (Exhibit 1). The projections for core inflation, in particular, were raised by 0.1pp to 2.6% in 2027 and by 0.1pp to 2.3% in 2028. At the same time, the staff reiterated that the revisions to core inflation were mostly due to indirect (rather than second-round) effects, as projections for wage growth were revised only slightly higher. The staff also updated their milder, adverse and severe scenarios of alternative energy price paths. The scenarios were constructed under the same framework as in June (using the 25th, 75th and 95th percentile of option-implied distributions for oil and gas prices as of August 19th) and with similar assumptions on the strength of direct, indirect and second-round effects. President Lagarde noted that the decision to hike had been unanimous and once again described it as “robust”. This is consistent with our updated policy simulations, which show at least two hikes across all scenarios (Exhibit 2). Our simulations point to the policy rate reaching 2.75% under the staff’s new baseline, 3% under their adverse scenario, and 4% under the severe scenario. Higher real rates are the path of least resistance Interest rates are not historically high but normalizing to pre-2008 levels. The recent increase in long-term interest rates is driven by fundamentals: higher fiscal deficits post-pandemic and strong AI-related investment. The move is mostly in real rates and it is a global phenomenon rather than US-centric, concentrated in developed economies. Japan’s exit from YCC and heavy FX intervention is also putting pressure on global rates. Absent a collapse in AI-driven investment, lower fiscal deficits or widespread financial repression, the path of least resistance remains toward higher real interest rates. This is not a Draghi moment Interventions in financial markets are justified in cases of market failure, liquidity breakdown, externalities or coordination problems due to multiple equilibria. None of these conditions are present in US bond markets. This is not a Draghi moment. Intervention can end up being destabilizing and introduce moral hazard considerations by suppressing market signals. Intervention is not a substitute for addressing fundamentals. (Note: Weighted average is calculated as the sum of net debt, scaled by total LTM EBITDA, for each rating cohort. These are not computed at the firm level). For AAs, we find that net leverage has continued to trend down to historically low levels despite the ongoing AI capex buildout while interest coverage hovers at all-time highs. This reflects, in large part, the EBITDA growth which has occurred alongside the capex investment. As we have highlighted previously, we believe the technical factors in the credit market—such as issuer concentration limitations and market saturation considerations to the AI-theme broadly—will be the most pressing considerations in determining how much debt is issued into the syndicated credit market. records.text: M Idea 26 A note on methodology We use changes in month-to-month holdings to analyze overseas demand. To account for changes in market value each month, we adjust holdings changes by the Treasury's published monthly valuation changes for data from February 2023 to the present. For historical data without valuation change reporting, we approximate valuation changes using the MoM change in the Bloomberg Agency MBS index price. We subtract this change in portfolio value from the recorded month-on-month difference in portfolio value to determine if there was real buying or selling of mortgages that month. We note that the Treasury also publishes net transactions data, not adjusted for market value. There exists a substantial difference between our calculation of net flows from holdings data compared to the published net transactions data. Adjusting our calculations with the new monthly valuation change data seems to improve the correlation for recent data. The inconsistency between holdings data and transactions data has been previously acknowledged in a federal register, which also includes data improvement strategies. The Federal Reserve has similarly highlighted reconciliation challenges between the holdings data and the transactions data. Snowball equation to identify vulnerabilities: To chart the trajectory of a country’s debt-to-GDP ratio, though, two important considerations are ‘r–g’ and primary balances. These should be examined in tandem to assess the potential snowball effect arising from interest rates: i.e. when the weighted average interest rate paid by a government on its debt (r) exceeds the economy’s nominal growth rate (g), the interest rate bill compounds at a faster rate than the economy (or rather the tax base that will service the debt) grows. This on its own leads to a rise in debt-to-GDP unless the country runs a primary surplus above a certain level. In turn, even a country whose nominal growth exceeds its average interest rate faces a rising debt trajectory if its primary deficit is above a certain threshold. We use the ‘snowball effect’ equation to identify these key levels – the so-called DSPB (Figure 3). Below we identify which countries look more vulnerable from a debt sustainability point of view. CLO bond holdings inflect upwards Having declined through 2024 and much of 2025, European CLO allocations to corporate bonds appear to have found a floor this year and have even been trending higher in recent months. Bond holdings as a share of CLO portfolios bottomed out during Q1 26 and have since increased from a median 11.6% in March to 12.2% in August, albeit still below the peak allocations reached in 2023-24. Importantly, this increase is occurring against a much larger CLO market. As a result, bond holdings in absolute terms have already surpassed their previous highs, reaching a record €42bn as of August 2026 versus roughly €35bn at the 2023-24 peak ( Figure 2). And we expect OAT spreads to act, at least initially, as an anchor for the rest of the EGB complex – notably Italy. We think caution is particularly warranted because risk premia have scope to build from current lows. Indeed, the credit spline is no longer convex and even the AAA/AA slope has dropped. These factors may make EGB spreads prone to substantial repricing on a shift in market sentiment or a rise in French idiosyncratic risk. That said, contagion risks will likely be smaller than in the past, and we see a scenario where BTPs end the year at much richer levels than OATs. In the long run we are all older: Year-on-year budget decision have been the market focus in the last few years but the structural force of demographic decline and ageing population is building underneath the surface. This impacts public finances through higher pension and healthcare expenditures only partly offset by lower education costs. All four economies face these interlinked challenges – though these issues appear less severe in Germany. While we are not the first to study this issue, we note that official projections, such as the European Commission’s aging report, may rely on overly optimistic assumptions. Specifically, the assumption that potential growth will stabilize above 1% between 2040 and 2060 in these economies relies on a productivity boom that is not guaranteed, given the drag of demographic decline. Ageing costs are hard to time as a “market theme”. However, we see how the debate around the pension reform is at the forefront of French budget discussions. In Italy, after the 2011 reform the pension system has been ‘stabilized’, but we show that expenditure can rise higher than official projections currently assume. This, we think, should primarily constitute a growth problem. T o have an idea of how much households could allocate to bonds, we turn to the UK’s ISAs, the blueprint for Japan’s NISA program. Interestingly in the UK very little is allocated to Gilts, roughly 1%. What’s more interesting is that retail investors seem to i) trade Gilts quite tactically (Figure 28), having increased the allocation as the BoE was raising interest rates, and ii) also hold more corporate debt, given the higher yield despite the higher risk. Of course, demographically UK and Japan are very different, and perhaps risk-taking behavior also changes from country to country. Japan’s older population may mean that a higher bond allocation is possible. Still, the UK experience suggests the flows may be contained. Prepared for Cayla Buettner

Including these items, we estimate the FY27 initial budget at JPY146.5trn. The largest components are: (1) additional defence spending related to the revision of the three national security documents (submitted as an item request), and (2) the First Medium-Term National Resilience Implementation Plan (also submitted as an item request). For (1), we assume an additional JPY1.5trn based on estimates by our economics research team1 ; for (2), we assume an additional JPY1.9trn in line with FY26 implementation2 . In addition, there remains considerable upside risk from the "Strong and Prosperous Japan" Investment Framework, for which no upper limit has been imposed and under which ministries including METI and MLIT have submitted additional item requests. In estimating net new JGB issuance, two factors are particularly important: (i) revenue assumptions, and (ii) the size of the economic security component of the "Strong and Prosperous Japan" Investment Framework, which is to be managed through a special account. Regarding (i), we use the Cabinet Office's July 2026 medium-term fiscal projections3 , which assume FY27 "tax revenues and other revenues" of JPY98.8trn. NISA- related investment is typically concentrated at the start of the year when annual allowances reset, but investment trust flows have shown no slowdown even in H2 this year. By investment destination, flows into investment trusts targeting domestic assets increased in June and July, but slowed from August, with no sign of a shift back toward JPY assets (Figure 9). records.text: US Rates Weekly 11 September 2026 Citi Research 11 Inflation: The El Niño impact We study commodity prices in previous El Niño episodes to understand their impact on food inflation. Inflation indices in various linker-issuing developed markets have varying exposure to El Niño with US food inflation seeing very little impact. What gets impacted in El Niño? We are still in the early stages of this El Niño. Recently, we have received several questions on the possible impact of El Niño on commodity prices and what that could mean for food inflation in developed markets. Usually, El Niño weather patterns start in summer with ocean temperatures rising, and we see the weather disruptions and crop concerns in Q4. The actual impact on harvests becomes more visible in Q1 of the following year with food inflation in following months. So, we are still in the early stages of this El Niño cycle. Having said that, recent NOAA update, now assigns a greater than 90% probability of a very strong event and our commodity strategists see upside risks for agricultural commodity prices (see Global Commodities - Super El Niño and Geopolitical Supply Risks Reinforce Our Bullish Ags View and Raise Food Inflation Risks). records.text: 10 September 2026 Asia Local Markets Weekly Page 14 Deutsche Bank AG/Singapore Vietnam What is the USD/VND spot-fixing gap telling us? Recent VND resilience has likely been supported by (1) a narrower trade deficit, and (2) strong inflows from corporates raising external loans and converting proceeds into VND amidst high domestic funding costs. In this report, we examine what the USD/VND spot-fixing gap is telling us and why we maintain a cautious outlook on the currency. SBV's currency reaction function Wider USD/VND spot–fixing gaps have generally been followed by larger increases in SBV’s daily fixing over the subsequent 20–40 trading days (Figure 21). This suggests that the central bank gradually accommodates underlying depreciation pressure by allowing the fixing to catch up with spot. However, the relationship seems to break down when depreciation pressure is most acute. In fact, in the highest quintile of USD/VND spot–fixing gap, we find subsequent fixing increases over the next 20-40 trading days to be SMALLER than those observed even in the third quintile. This suggests a sort of inflection point beyond which SBV starts to lean MORE forcefully against VND depreciation pressures, particularly when spot is trading at the upper limit of its permitted trading range. Page 5 JGB: This Week in Review, The Week Ahead Our economists argue that Japan's export prices turned from two decades of decline to a rise around 2020, and that AI-related demand is now showing up in prices rather than volumes: a country that used to export deflation has started to export inflation. Firms raised contract-currency export prices through a sharp yen depreciation, at the same time as domestic prices turned, which makes this a structural claim about corporate pricing behavior. The most direct test of that claim in the rates market is the implied breakeven inflation (BEI) of inflation-linked JGBs (JGBi). As of 10 September the BEI curve is deeply inverted: 3.4% at 0.5 years, 2.3% at 4.5 years and 1.96% at 10 years. The 10-year BEI sits almost exactly on the BoJ's synthetic expected inflation of about 2.0%, leaving an inflation risk premium (IRP) of -9bp, and the 5y5y forward implied BEI is only 1.6-1.7%. JGBi #23 and #24 (1.5 and 2.5 years) trade at 1.7-1.8%, a deep trough against their neighbors: the "trough" created by the food tax cut is already priced ahead of the tax outline. The market accepts near-term inflation and the tax cut, but not a lasting shift in pricing behavior. European Overview Elevation Higher energy prices and firmer inflation expectations continue to push rates higher, with Bunds increasingly reflecting European-specific risks. Credit remains resilient, but deteriorating total returns and HY flow dynamics warrant closer monitoring as supply stays elevated. Many things are up over the week: supply in IG and HY, gas prices, oil prices, ECB inflation projections, rates globally, etc. For credit market performance, what matters is the durability (and speed) of these moves up and the underlying drivers. On energy prices, gas is making higher highs, well past the local peak in March and this is unlikely to revert in the near term even if the Iran-US crisis is "resolved" – EU aggregate gas storage is at 67% full as of 8 September versus the five-year seasonal norm of 84%. This feeds into ECB inflation projections, which were revised up for 2027 and 2028. The ECB now sees headline inflation averaging 3.0% in 2026, 2.5% in 2027 and 2.1% in 2028. As was priced, the ECB hiked by 25bp on Wednesday, citing upside risks to inflation. Going by market pricing, 1.6 more 25bp hikes are expected by year-end. 10yr Bund yields are also up, and since the rates sell-off accelerated on 25 August, Bunds seem to be selling off faster than USTs: based on a simple relationship over the past 12 months and changes from 25 August, 10yr Bunds are roughly 6bp higher than expected, given the UST yield change. We see limited scope for the market to price a meaningful probability of 50bp hikes at the front-end MPC meetings. All in all, we think the risks around the September meeting are broadly balanced. The rise in energy prices has clearly increased hawkish risks in terms of communication and messaging. On the flip side, we also expect the BoE to continue to focus on the still- modest risk of second-round effects stemming from the domestic backdrop, alongside the significant tightening already priced into valuations. Indeed, looking at the UK strip, market pricing now closely tracks the Bank staff’s illustrative model-based path under the July MPR Adverse scenario (see Exhibit 10 ). We also suspect the MPC will want to retain some near-term optionality and avoid triggering an even more hawkish market reaction, similar to what followed the March MPC. That said, ahead of the MPC, energy prices are likely to continue to drive money- market expectations, alongside broader repricing across other central banks. On the domestic front, incoming data could also shift the balance of risks ahead of the meeting itself.

records.text: e aftermath of the Global Financial Crisis was characterized by an unprecedented combination of financial repression, large-scale asset purchases by central banks, fiscal stimulus, excess global savings, and rapid globalization. Although fiscal policy subsequently became somewhat more restrained across advanced economies, these forces collectively contributed to an environment of exceptionally low interest rates that persisted for more than a decade. By the middle of the 2010s, however, this equilibrium had begun to shift. Global investment gradually recovered, globalization started to plateau, and fiscal positions in several advanced economies deteriorated. These developments marked the early stages of the secular rise in global interest rates. The pandemic accelerated this transition. In response to the unprecedented shock caused by COVID-19, policymakers deployed record monetary and fiscal stimulus. While these measures were effective in supporting the recovery, they were only partially reversed once economic activity normalized. EUR Our view: Neutral Risk skew: Bullish Watch: CPI, ZEW Survey Expectations We continue to see a constructive backdrop for EUR/USD, with relative rates increasingly the key driver. Since August, EUR/USD has tracked nominal yield differentials closely, suggesting the energy shock is being reflected in FX through rates rather than a direct terms-of-trade drag. The ECB meeting reinforces this dynamic: stronger growth and inflation projections drove further front-end repricing, while our economists now see upside risks to their on-hold call. This can continue to support EUR even with energy prices elevated. Cross-asset moves also suggest the terms-of-trade impulse remains visible, with NOK, AUD, and CAD rallying alongside oil and EUR outperforming CHF and SEK. However, further ECB hikes require evidence of persistent indirect or second-round inflation effects, which remains limited so far, leaving us neutral on EUR with a bullish risk skew. JPY Our view: Bearish Risk skew: Bearish Watch: BoJ Rates Decision, weekly MoF data, Nationwide CPI We have turned bearish on the JPY. USD/JPY has fallen sharply on expectations of GPIF portfolio changes. However, such expectations remain speculative at this stage, while the fundamental backdrop has not changed. Although uncertainty surrounding the September FOMC remains, concerns about US rate hikes driven by inflation are likely to persist as oil prices continue to rise

After falling from 5.8% of GDP in 2024 to 5.1% in 2025, largely due to stronger revenues, the budget deficit this year is expected to remain broadly unchanged around 5%, with risks likely to the upside. Fiscal outturns for H1 are broadly in line with this target as higher revenues were offset by higher expenditures. For 2027, we expect little change, with the government aiming for 4.9% of GDP , implying almost no tightening. In terms of specific measures, one focus will be on the temporary corporate tax surcharge on large firms. This was introduced in 2025 and subsequently extended. The natural slope is recalibration to 2.0% At 1.75%, we think that the policy rate still implies a mildly accommodative monetary policy stance. In our view, the ongoing economic recovery and a gradual strengthening of underlying inflation would support the case for one hike to 2.0%. We regard this as a natural recalibration of policy rather than a shift toward a restrictive stance. The exchange rate matters, too. Over the summer, the increasingly hawkish stance of major central banks put renewed depreciation pressure on the SEK. The ECB has already delivered policy tightening, while the FED should start its hiking cycle as early as September. A weaker SEK stemming from policy-divergence risks generating additional imported inflation pressures. A final 25bp hike would therefore also reduce the risk of further inflationary pressures amid FX depreciation. We still see no need for rates to turn restrictive We continue to view the expected move to 2.0% as the end of accommodative policy rather than the beginning of a broader tightening cycle. The slack in the Swedish economy should help contain second-round inflation effects, reducing the need for a sustained hiking cycle or a clearly restrictive policy stance. However, over this horizon, the search for yield contributed to this trend amid an excess savings glut . Today, the rise in long -end yields is telling you something else: capital is scarce . Mid-terms remain an issue that the market is increasingly likely to focus on, especially if prospects of post-election fiscal easing increase. records.text: 10 September 2026 Asia Local Markets Weekly Page 8 Deutsche Bank AG/Singapore Portfolio Strategy Adjustments to our portfolio We are making 3 adjustments to our portfolio this week; Re-striking our Long 3M USD/TWD put spread to 31.29/30.53 The case for a stronger TWD rests on three factors. First, portfolio inflows are returning as Taiwan remains one of the clearest beneficiaries of the global AI cycle. Improved AI sentiment has driven around $10bn of foreign equity inflows since August, reversing the heavy outflows seen in June and July. With investors still underweight Taiwan and AI-related exports continuing to support large trade and current account surpluses, the balance of flows remains supportive of TWD. Second, exporter USD selling appears to be picking up, providing an additional source of TWD demand. Seasonally, TWD tends to perform well into 4Q, coinciding with the strongest current account surplus of the year. We therefore expect exporter-related flows to remain a supportive factor in the months ahead. Third, structural USD demand from life insurers is gradually easing. Asset growth has slowed, policymakers are encouraging greater domestic investment, and ETF- related repatriation flows have reached $4.7bn QTD. Meanwhile, hedge ratios appear to have largely normalised following the sharp adjustment in 1Q, reducing the need for incremental USD hedging demand. records.text: The Global Thinker | 10 September 2026 5 Viewed through the lens of the global savings-investment framework, the recent increase in interest rates reflects a shift in equilibrium conditions. The global savings schedule has moved inward, while the demand for investment has increased. Higher interest rates are the natural outcome of this adjustment. More importantly, this framework helps explain why rates remained relatively contained for so long despite worsening fiscal positions. A prolonged period of exceptionally abundant savings created the illusion that fiscal trajectories were more sustainable than they actually were. A fundamentals-driven adjustment It is important to emphasize that the increase in real interest rates has, so far, been largely orderly. The evidence suggests a repricing driven primarily by economic fundamentals rather than by market dysfunction. In particular, the adjustment reflects a combination of a higher equilibrium real interest rate (r*) and rising risk premia. Notably, higher risk premia have emerged despite the still-low probability of nominal default on domestic-currency sovereign debt issued by advanced economies. Instead, investors appear increasingly concerned about the risk of losses in real terms. Such losses can arise through higher inflation, financial repression, or a combination of both. Generally higher-margin service lines include orthopedics, cardiovascular care, oncology, ambulatory surgery, imaging, laboratory services and specialty pharmacy, which typically generate stronger margins due to favorable reimbursement, high volumes and relatively efficient cost structures. Generally lower-margin service lines include acute care like emergency care and trauma, as well as behavioral health, obstetrics (labor and delivery), primary care and pediatrics. Systems including Dartmouth Health and MaineHealth have acquired or affiliated with community hospitals to deepen local market presence and strengthen referral networks, allowing them to capture more downstream volume in profitable specialties such as orthopedics, cardiovascular care, oncology, imaging, and ambulatory surgery. This assumption was wrong - the median MPC member did not push back against immediate tightening, and the April meeting repriced by ~15bp on the day. Following the meeting, Governor Bailey said the market was "getting ahead of itself". With the front end of the UK curve pricing ~45bp worth of hikes by year-end, it might seem a challenge for the BoE to "out-hawk" the market. Still, the hawkish risk scenario, we think, is one where there are hints that the vote for a hold was a "finely balanced" one for an internal MPC member. A very explicit acknowledgment that November tightening is now base case for the core of the Committee might also - in the extremis - crack the door open for a market conversation around a 50bp hike in November, or nudge the terminal rate to above 5%. To be clear, we don't think the BoE has any appetite to hike at an expedited pace or towards 5%, but, as noted, the market atmosphere is quite fluid. To state the obvious, much depends on the evolution of commodity prices into the meeting next week. If, as is our base case, the MPC simply reiterates the July MPC/TSC messaging, we think they would maintain sufficient optionality of acting at any of the upcoming meetings. records.text: global copper mine production declined by 1.1% in H1'26, mainly due to declines in Chile, Indonesia and the DRC. n China refined production in July slowed to the weakest growth rate since 2024, up 1.3% YoY and down 7% MoM on a daily output basis. Global refined output has fared better than mine supply this year, expanding by 2.4% in H1, largely due to capacity additions in China and Chinese smelters maximising scrap usage. Smelter maintenance activity is usually high in July, so the August data (expected late next week) should provide a clearer indication of whether this slowdown is temporary or the start of a broader moderation in refined output growth. Mine supply recovery potential in 2027 Based on latest company guidance and projections from Woodmac, mine supply could post a large recovery in 2027 (+5-6% YoY, +1.3 mt). This would represent the largest YoY growth since 2016 and largest absolute tonnage increase since 2013. Does this represent a material risk to copper prices? The relationship between annual mine supply growth and copper prices is relatively weak, and it is worth considering that even if achieved, the implied three-year mine supply CAGR (2024- 27) would only be ~2%, still below refined copper demand growth over the past 2-3 years of ~2.7% pa. records.text: Stuart Jenkins +44(20)7051-4700 | stuart.jenkins@gs.com Goldman Sachs International Global Markets Daily: Trading Policy Divergence in G10 FX 11 September 2026 | 12:55AM BST We highlight two rates-based signals for G10 FX markets that can help inform n discretionary trading views. First, we find that economies priced for greater policy tightening relative to G10 peers tend to see clear domestic currency outperformance, mostly explained by persistence in the pricing-in of hiking and cutting cycles over time. Second, systematically trading our economists’ modal central bank expectations relative to market pricing also generates positive FX returns over time. We view these two sets of signals as G10 FX strategies, and note that while both n deliver positive full-sample total returns, vol-adjusted performance is only particularly strong in certain periods (such as the sharp G10 tightening cycle of 2022-2023). Across a range of measures of rates vol and policy settings, we find that higher n absolute pricing of central bank action across the G10 is most clearly relevant for stronger returns in both strategies. The average level and dispersion of G10 policy rates, and the level of implied rates vol, are not statistically significant for either. The elevated current level of hike pricing for G10 central banks over the coming n two years implies to us that the current backdrop is well-suited to the use of both sets of signals. records.text: 6 Japan Viewpoint | 11 September 2026 Prime Minister Takaichi has not commented on the yen or monetary policy since the coordinated intervention. Thus, it remains uncertain whether her policy stance, which generally seemed to favor a weaker yen and lower rates, has truly changed. But the developments in July suggest that USD/JPY near 165 was a problem even for the Takaichi administration. We expect quarterly hikes to a terminal of 2% Given that growing expectations of faster rate hikes have been a key pillar of the recent yen rally, we think there is now a clearer path for the BoJ to deliver further hikes. Assuming that the BoJ delivers a 25bp hike in September, our base case calls for three additional hikes in December 2026 and March and July 2027, taking the policy rate to 2% (Exhibit 11). This assumes USD/JPY falls to 149 by end-2026 and 145 by end-2027, in line with our FX strategy team's forecasts. If the yen instead remains around 155 or above, we think the BoJ may ultimately need to raise rates to 2.5%. On the flipside, a global risk-off shock that strengthens the yen and weakens demand could end the cycle at 1.5%-1.75% (Exhibit 12; for details, see BoJ Watch: Faster hikes, higher terminal, 14 August 2026). As emerging tech industries are often in nascent stages of commercialisation or face uncertain downstream competitive landscapes, upstream and midstream suppliers of essential, high-barrier materials, components, tools and equipment can offer superior demand certainty, and benefit directly from the rapid industry capex growth. These companies have experienced sizable retracement from the June highs, presenting a good entry point for medium-term exposure. Trade ideas: We like going long BNPP China A-share Tech ‘Picks and Shovels’ thematic basket (BNPBCTPS), which comprises 49 representative stocks from the upstream and midstream sectors of policy-supported emerging industries. These companies operate in industries characterized by high technical barriers and stringent qualification requirements. While long positioning has cleaned up relative to recent levels (as seen on MSOPCADU Index), we still prefer patience into next week’s CPI. CAD has strengthened against weaker ToT currencies over the past two months (as seen in EUR/CAD), and has reacted little to the recent tariff escalations between the US and Canada. The tit-for-tat tariff approach rather than any genuine attempts to end existing trade agreements is a sign of a willingness to negotiate, in our view. records.text: Evidence of Supply Impact onto UST Yields and MBS Spreads Despite the magnitude of the move higher in longer-term UST yields this year, deviations from the levels implied by our framework for longer-term forwards have been contained. For the most part fundamentals—the shift in the expected Fed path, rising growth expectations, fiscal trajectory, and spillovers from abroad—have justified the broader trend higher in Treasury yields (Exhibit 3). That said, corporate borrowing is rising in order to finance investment that may be contributing to higher longer-term yields through its impact on fundamentals (via cyclical support, normalized sensitivity of yields to Treasury supply, and longer-run growth optimism). And as we have highlighted previously, a backdrop of heavier private sector borrowing raises the risk of more meaningful overshoots in longer-term yields versus fair value. Our standard rule of thumb is that a 1pp increase in US debt to GDP is worth 2-to-3bp of upward pressure on longer-term forward UST yields. Under our fiscal outlook, the trajectory for debt-to-GDP is adding about 5bp of upward pressure on longer-term forwards per year over the near-term. On a more granular basis, we previously documented evidence of a flow effect around long-end Treasury auctions, noting a tendency for long-end USTs to underperform on the curve and on asset swap, especially around refunding auctions. records.text: the Test of Time We examine the relationship between spread levels and the volatility of spread changes over the 20 years since our initial DTS study in 2005. We find that the relationship remains highly linear, with the slope close to that observed in the original study. This is a reprint of QPS FICC: Duration Times Spread (DTS): Standing the Test of Time published on September 10, 2026. • In 2005, we proposed DTS1 as a measure of credit portfolio risk based on evidence that the volatility of relative spread changes has remained more stable than that of absolute spread changes over the 1989-2005 period. • DTS has since become widely used for risk management and portfolio construction. Subsequent research has also demonstrated its applicability across a broad range of credit markets and geographies. • Here, we revisit the spread-volatility relationship underlying DTS using a new sample spanning the 20 years (2005-2026) since the 2005 study. • Our empirical analysis shows that the relationship remains highly linear, and the proportionality factor remains close to the value reported in 2005 (~10%). Evidence from 2005-2026 In 2005, we introduced DTS as a measure of credit portfolio risk. At the time, spread duration was the standard measure used to assess portfolio spread risk. Portfolio exposure was evaluated in terms of average spread duration, implicitly assuming that credit spreads move in parallel. An analysis of long-term trends in Japanese export prices (contract currency basis) suggests that the pricing behavior of Japanese corporations may be undergoing a structural change. A time-series analysis of Japanese export prices since 2000 (natural logarithm, contract currency basis) reveals a gradual downtrend until around 2020, since which prices have been on the rise. A breakdown of the three major categories of transport equipment, electrical & electronic machinery, and general/production/ business machinery finds that the most dramatic change has been in electrical and electronic machinery, which includes AI-related components. Prices in this category fell consistently from 2000 to around 2020, meaning effectively that Japan was exporting deflation. Prices then began a slow but steady uptrend, accelerating to a sharper rise in 2H 2025 and beyond. The next question is what happens to 5y5y rates after next week’s ‘first hike’ this cycle? First, 5y5y does not need to march higher in the months following the first hike. Institutes like the ifo criticize that the SVIK is being misappropriated for consumptive expenditure like tax cuts or social security funds crowding- out investment from the core budget. Indeed, details in the budget suggest that not all of the borrowing is used for “new” investment projects. Still, we think the government’s investment plan generates a significant growth impulse. Between 2025-2030 we estimate a cumulative fiscal impulse of 2.2% of GDP from defence and investment spending. Our assumption of an average multiplier of 0.7 still yields a GDP level that is 1.5% higher in 2030 compared to the counterfactual absent the government’s spending push. If combined with structural reforms, the multiplier could become even higher as this could crowd-in private investment. Given Germany’s benign fiscal position, debt sustainability is not a concern in the near term, and the positive growth impulse can stabilize debt levels in the long-run. In the near term we expect debt- GDP to reach close to 70% by end-2027 and expect debt-GDP increasing to 85% by the end of the decade as a structurally higher net borrowing requirement means rising debt levels. While this is a structural break from Germany’s fiscal stance, we think Germany remains fairly well positioned when it comes to debt sustainability concerns compared to its peers. In both the USD and EUR markets, there has been a bifurcation between improving net margins for IG firms and deteriorating net margins for HY issuers (Exhibit 3). In our view, this reflects the benefits of scale and diversification—especially in managing pressures related to cost inputs given the elevated prices of many commodities and broader price pressures. Notably, the bifurcation between North American IG and HY net margins became more pronounced beginning in 2023—a period which coincided with broad-based inflation and upward pressure on cost inputs (wages, etc.). It also coincided with the Federal Reserve’s rate-hiking cycle, which increased borrowing costs for floating rate issuers. By our estimates, 24% of USD HY issuers have some form of floating rate debt in their capital structures. In the EUR market, the bifurcation has materialized more recently, which we attribute to the renewed upward pressure on commodity prices. That said, a sharp deterioration in net margins was visible in EUR HY in early 2023, which coincided with the energy disruptions associated with the Russia-Ukraine conflict. A particularly important example concerns the treatment of supply shocks and whether they should continue to be largely ignored when they become increasingly frequent and persistent. This discussion was notably absent from Warsh's Jackson Hole remarks. In practice, explaining the reaction function is akin to explaining the effective Taylor Rule that guides policy decisions. No central bank follows a mechanical rule, and policymakers must always contend with uncertainty surrounding data quality, model specifications, and parameter estimates. Yet these uncertainties do not prevent the FOMC from making decisions. The more clearly policymakers explain their analytical framework and decision-making process, the more efficiently markets can incorporate new information and the less unnecessary noise contaminates asset prices. The discussion of supply shocks also raises a broader question regarding the inflation target itself. An inflation target is essential for accountability. However, it is well understood that optimal monetary policy should generally look through temporary supply shocks as long as inflation expectations remain well anchored. The challenge arises when the economy is repeatedly hit by supply disruptions. records.text: Our new treatment of imports raises our estimate of the growth impulse versus our prior calculations, as we adjust for re-exports and also estimate the share of computer imports being used for personal consumption instead of business investment. In addition to the total growth effects, we also separate out AI infrastructure spend—data centers, computing equipment, networking hardware, power infrastructure and related machinery —from AI adoption, for which software investment is our best economy-wide proxy. So far, infrastructure still dominates. Of the roughly 0.5pp contribution from AI- only investment to growth in 1H26, about 0.4pp came from infrastructure, with the remainder from adoption. The infrastructure contribution has accelerated from about 0.15pp in 2023 and -0.05pp in 2024 to 0.21pp in 2025 and 0.36pp in 1H26. We expect the mix to evolve as the cycle matures. Infrastructure spending is creating the supply-side capacity needed to develop and run AI applications; software spending should indicate whether AI is diffusing across the broader business sector. Adoption has picked up, but not decisively: software contributed about 0.18pp to growth in 2026, after 0.15pp in 2025 and 0.21pp in 2024. Our expectation is that infrastructure growth slows in 2027- 28 as the build-out matures, while adoption spending proves more persistent and potentially accelerates.

records.text: After softer growth momentum and slower-than-expected fiscal spending in H1 n 2026, government bond issuance—including both central and local government bonds —is picking up, echoing the July Politburo meeting’s call to accelerate fiscal spending. We expect total bond net issuance (both central and local) to rise meaningfully in the coming months, with monthly net issuance reaching 1% of GDP per month during September–October, up from a monthly average of around 0.6% of GDP in H1. In this note, we examine whether heavier bond supply could put upward pressure on bond yields and swap rates in China. Historical episodes suggest that higher government bond issuance has had mixed n effects on 10y CGB yields, with the yield response depending on a host of factors including PBOC liquidity management, the speed of fiscal-proceeds spending, as well as shifts in growth, inflation and policy rate expectations. Controlling for changes in growth and inflation expectations, and changes in the n interbank funding tightness relative to PBOC’s policy target, we estimate a larger sensitivity of yields at the front end of the CGB curve to net CGB issuance. By our estimates, a 0.2% of GDP acceleration in net CGB issuance is associated with a 4.8bp increase in the 1-year CGB yield, compared with 2.0bp in the 5-year CGB yield and 1.5bp in the 10-year CGB yield. The proposed pension reform is one of the most heatedly discussed items on the German government’s reform agenda (see Rentenkommission 2026 – BMAS and Bundestag). The part of the reform discussed at the panel was the proposed introduction of a funded component into pillar 1 – the statutory pension system, currently financed predominantly on a pay-as-you-go basis. The potential benefits of such a reform are substantial and extend beyond Germany: it could provide an impetus for similar reforms in other large European countries and help deepen European capital markets. But the concerns surrounding the reform are equally significant. These were well illustrated by a question from the audience at our conference: How would politicians deal with the fallout from, say, two negative years in stock markets if these occurred shortly after the introduction of the pension reform? Economic research offers some useful guidance. Beware of how to read markets As discussed earlier, real interest rates have been trending higher not only in the United States but across much of the global economy. But does a rise in real interest rates necessarily imply tighter financial conditions? Interestingly, Chairman Warsh appeared to offer two different interpretations. During the July press conference, he suggested that the FOMC's decision to remain on hold was partly justified by the market doing some of the Fed's work through higher yields and an effective tightening of financial conditions. By Jackson Hole, however, he argued that financial conditions were hardly restrictive. Beyond this apparent inconsistency lies a more fundamental question. If higher real interest rates are primarily the result of an investment boom, particularly in the United States, then they should not be interpreted as an exogenous tightening of financial conditions. Rather, they represent the endogenous market response to stronger demand for capital. In that case, higher real rates are not necessarily evidence of restrictive monetary conditions. If anything, they may be the consequence of financial conditions being sufficiently accommodative to support a surge in investment demand. That said, our sense is that a n October move is unlikely as the ECB has displayed a preference to move alongside projections meetings when more information is available. And the proactive response to the energy shock affords it the scope to proceed more gradually , in our view . In our base case of a gradual and uneven re -opening of the Strait of Hormuz, we see Brent crude trading between USD75 -100/bbl. This implies that flows will be choppy, but should slowly improve through the winter such that energy prices gradually come down over the next six months. In this scenario , we see the ECB opting to keep rates on hold at 2.75% until it is confident that the energy shock has passed. records.text: Higher Energy Prices, More Inflation, Slightly Weaker H2 Growth European TTF gas prices have surged again in recent weeks, almost doubling since the June lows. Given further delays to the normalisation of Persian Gulf LNG exports, our commodities team raised its Q4 TTF gas price forecast to 70 EUR/MWh (from 53 EUR/MWh before). They believe that the baseline remains for normalisation next year, but near-term risks remain to the upside, especially in the case of a cold winter. While they only raised their oil forecast modestly—Brent price projection up $5 to $85 in Q4— product spreads (especially for diesel) have widened further and risks to the crude oil price outlook likewise looks skewed towards higher prices (Exhibit 1). Higher energy prices are likely to weigh on growth in coming months, mainly via lower real income and household consumption growth. Also, Q3 is off to a softer start than the recent run-rate, as retail sales and industrial production dropped in July, most notably in Germany. As a result of weaker hard data, our Q3 tracking estimate has edged down and currently stands at 0.19%, indicating a modest slowdown from an average growth pace of +0.3% in H1 (Exhibit 2, left). Many of these components are relatively small and do not derail our near-term expectations for disinflation, but this AI-exposed basket makes up a larger share of spending for low-income, less-educated, and younger households. Over the longer run, productivity gains should be disinflationary, particularly where adoption is faster. Higher-income households spend a larger share on financial, professional and communication services, so they may experience AI-related services disinflation earlier. Putting the channels together, our base case remains that AI will lead to a modest, temporary increase in unemployment (around 0.2-0.5pp at the peak), but that task creation, wage gains, and wealth effects will more than offset this displacement. In this scenario, CHIC households benefit the most on net, as upside channels outweigh downside risks. Still, outcomes likely vary by career stage. Established, older professionals may be well positioned to capture AI-related productivity and asset-price gains while highly educated younger professionals may be more vulnerable. Weakness among younger entrants would likely have a smaller effect on aggregate consumption than a comparable disruption among established households that account for a large share of spending. Secondly, a minority government will find it hard to implement big changes, either to expand or consolidate the budget. Thirdly, the recent years without a budget have not only shown that the economy and fiscal metrics can continue to improve without discretionary fiscal intervention but have also allowed markets to price in this relative instability. Spain’s dependence on nominal growth to keep improving its fiscal outcomes poses a risk, as growth itself relies on some key engines that might be put to the test next year. An important growth driver of the Spanish economy in recent years has been immigration, which has helped expand the labour force, employment, incomes and private consumption. A change in the migration stance after the 2027 elections thus poses a risk to this trend continuing. We think this risk is more likely to materialise under a PP-led government supported by VOX (nationalist right), akin to other regional government agreements made earlier this year, such as in Andalucía. Losing such an important growth lever might make it harder for Spain to continue to use growth to keep reducing the debt without the need for consolidation. That requires a change in Japan's policy mix. Until now, that policy mix has been inconsistent with a stronger currency, as fiscal policy has retained an expansionary bias while monetary policy remains accommodative. There has been no sign since the intervention that the government intends to scale back its fiscal agenda, with Prime Minister Takaichi sticking to her promise of a consumption tax cut and a JPY370tn public-private investment roadmap. With fiscal policy retaining an expansionary bias over the medium term, the burden of adjusting the policy mix to support the yen falls primarily on the BoJ, at least in the near term (see Japan Viewpoint: Yen unlikely to prevail on defense alone: From FX intervention to rate hikes, 24 August 2026). Still, demographic changes will yield important challenges for Germany’s pay-as-you-go system as higher pension contributions drag on income. The Ifo and DRV estimate that without reform, pension contributions are expected to rise from 18.6% in 2025 to above 21.1% of gross wages by 2040 even as the pension level declines (Figure 1). In July 2026, the cabinet agreed on 33 reforms aimed at stabilising the statutory pension system, taking a first step away from the pay-as-you-go system by introducing a capital-market-based component. The package still needs to be approved by the Bundestag. Under current law, the pension level is expected to decline from 48% of average wages in 2026 to 46% by 2040. The pension commission estimates that their reforms could increase the pension level (ratio of standard pension to average wage) to 50% absent a strain on public finances. This would be due to measures like tying the life expectancy to retirement age, abolishing the option to retire at 63, increasing pension contributions by the private sector, and the introduction of a capital markets- based component. Absent reforms the ifo estimates that public expenditure on pension funds would need to rise by 54%, from EUR100bn in 2025 to EUR154bn by 2050 to stabilize pension levels. records.text: eted the decline in breakevens as evidence that the Fed no longer needed to tighten policy. But this reasoning confused cause and effect. The decline in inflation compensation was itself the endogenous response of markets to a perceived shift in the expected reaction function of the Federal Reserve. More broadly, market prices should not be treated as exogenous inputs into the policy process. They are equilibrium outcomes that reflect expectations about future policy. Changes in inflation breakevens, real rates, and risk premia often represent the market's assessment of how the central bank is likely to react to evolving economic conditions. Interpreting those variables correctly therefore requires understanding the underlying causality. A decline in inflation breakevens is not necessarily evidence that inflation risks have diminished. It may instead reflect increased confidence that the central bank will act forcefully enough to contain those risks. Reading causality in reverse can lead both policymakers and investors to draw precisely the wrong conclusions from market prices.
